lessons.title: Living together; getting things done with lassen
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In the last lesson you dealt with doctors and insurance. This lesson stays at home: the building you live in, the people next door, and what to do when something breaks. In a block of flats you rarely fix things yourself. You *have* them fixed: *Die Hausverwaltung lässt die Heizung reparieren.* And sometimes you need to *let* someone do something, or *make* them do it.

German does all of this with one verb, *lassen*. You met it in A2 (*Ich lasse mein Fahrrad reparieren*). Now you'll learn all its uses, its unusual perfect (*Ich habe das Fahrrad reparieren lassen*), and the pattern *sich lassen*, which you'll meet in instructions and complaints: *Das Fenster lässt sich nicht öffnen.*

## The four jobs of lassen

*lassen* is a strong verb: *ich lasse, du lässt, er lässt*; Präteritum *ließ*; perfect *hat gelassen* (but see below).

### 1. To leave

On its own, with a normal object, *lassen* means to leave something somewhere or in a certain state:

- *Ich habe meinen Schlüssel im Auto gelassen.* — I left my key in the car.
- *Lass mich in Ruhe!* — Leave me alone!
- *Lass die Tür bitte offen.* — Please leave the door open.

### 2. To have something done

*lassen* + infinitive at the end: somebody else does the work for you. This is the **[[causative]]** use, and the most important one in daily life:

- *Wir lassen die Wohnung renovieren.* — We're having the flat renovated.
- *Ich muss den Wasserhahn reparieren lassen.* — I need to get the tap repaired.
- *Er lässt sich die Haare schneiden.* — He's having his hair cut.

When it's something done to your own body or for you personally, add a dative reflexive pronoun: *Ich lasse mir die Haare schneiden. Lass dir das erklären!* (Get someone to explain that to you!) If you want to say who does the job, use *von*: *Wir lassen die Heizung von einem Handwerker prüfen.*

### 3. To let, allow

*lassen* + a person (accusative) + infinitive: you allow someone to do something.

- *Meine Eltern lassen mich allein in den Urlaub fahren.* — My parents let me go on holiday alone.
- *Lass mich das machen!* — Let me do that!
- *Lass uns gehen!* — Let's go!

*Lass uns …* / *Lasst uns …* is a common way of making a suggestion, a bit like *Wollen wir …?*

### 4. To make someone do something

The same pattern can mean that you cause or make someone do something. The context decides whether it's "let" or "make":

- *Die Lehrerin lässt uns jeden Tag einen Text schreiben.* — The teacher makes us write a text every day.
- *Der Vermieter lässt uns lange warten.* — The landlord keeps us waiting.

The chart helps you tell the four jobs apart: look at what comes with *lassen*.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: Which meaning of lassen?
  accDescr: Look at what comes with lassen. With only an object and no other verb, lassen means to leave, as in Ich lasse die Tür offen. With an infinitive where someone else does the work, it means to have something done, as in Ich lasse das Auto reparieren. With a person and an infinitive, it means to let or make someone do something, as in Lass mich helfen. With sich and an infinitive, it means that something can be done, as in Das Fenster lässt sich nicht öffnen.
  A{"What comes with lassen?"} -- "an object, no other verb" --> B["leave: Ich lasse die Tür offen."]
  A -- "a thing + infinitive" --> C["have something done: Ich lasse das Auto reparieren."]
  A -- "a person + infinitive" --> D["let or make someone: Lass mich helfen."]
  A -- "sich + infinitive" --> E["can be done: Das Fenster lässt sich nicht öffnen."]
```

### Word order

*lassen* works like a modal verb: it takes the second position, and the other infinitive goes to the end.

| | position 2 | | end |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Ich* | *lasse* | *das Auto morgen* | *reparieren.* |
| *Wann* | *lässt* | *du dir die Haare* | *schneiden?* |
| *Wir* | *müssen* | *die Heizung* | *reparieren lassen.* |
| *…, weil ich* | | *das Auto* | *reparieren lasse.* |

## The perfect: hat … reparieren lassen

When *lassen* is used with another infinitive, its perfect uses the infinitive *lassen*, not the participle *gelassen*. You get two infinitives at the end, the same pattern as with modal verbs (*hat … machen müssen*):

- *Ich habe die Waschmaschine reparieren lassen.* — I had the washing machine repaired.
- *Sie hat ihren Sohn allein fahren lassen.* — She let her son go alone.
- *Wir haben uns beraten lassen.* — We got advice.

Without another infinitive, the normal participle is used: *Ich habe meine Brille zu Hause gelassen.* — I left my glasses at home.

In main clauses this perfect is completely normal in speech, so use it. In writing you will also see the Präteritum: *Sie ließ die Waschmaschine reparieren.* Only the subordinate clause is awkward: in standard German *haben* comes before the two infinitives (*…, dass ich das Auto habe reparieren lassen*), and many speakers avoid it by rephrasing (*…, weil das Auto in der Werkstatt war*). Recognize that subordinate-clause form; you don't need to build it.

## sich lassen: "can be done" *(receptive)*

*sich lassen* + infinitive means that something *can* be done, almost like a passive with *können*. It's very common in complaints and instructions:

- *Das Fenster lässt sich nicht öffnen.* — The window won't open / can't be opened.
- *Der Mangel lässt sich leicht beheben.* — The defect can easily be fixed.
- *Das lässt sich machen.* — That can be done. (= OK, no problem.)
- *Darüber lässt sich streiten.* — That's debatable.

## Living together in a building

A block of flats in Germany usually has a *Hausordnung* (house rules) and a *Hausverwaltung* (property management company) that looks after the building for the owner. You call them when there's a *Mangel* (defect): the *Heizung* (heating) doesn't work, the *Wasserhahn* (tap) drips, a window is *undicht* (leaks), or there's *Schimmel* (mould) in the bathroom. They send a *Handwerker* or *Handwerkerin* (tradesperson) to *beheben* (fix, remedy) it.

If the landlord doesn't fix a serious defect, tenants in Germany may have the right to a *Mietminderung* (rent reduction). Before you pay less rent, though, get advice: the local *Mieterverein* (tenants' association) helps its members for a small yearly fee.

Many conflicts are about shared spaces: the *Treppenhaus* (stairwell), the *Hof* (courtyard), the *Mülltonnen* (bins). Common complaints: a *Kinderwagen* (pushchair) or bikes are *abgestellt* (left, parked) in the hall, someone *grillt* on the balcony, a dog barks, the *Klingel* (doorbell) is broken, post ends up in the wrong *Briefkasten* (letterbox). Most of this can be solved with a friendly conversation. If not, a neutral person can *vermitteln* (mediate) until both sides *sich einigen* (come to an agreement). Some towns offer free *Vermittlung* (mediation) between neighbours, and an *Einigung* (agreement) reached that way usually lasts longer than one forced by a lawyer.

Here are the shared parts of a typical building:

![A block of flats with the shared parts labelled: das Treppenhaus (the stairwell in the middle), die Klingel (the doorbell panel next to the front door), der Briefkasten (the letterboxes on the other side of the door), der Balkon (a balcony on the first floor), die Mülltonne (two bins) and der Hof (the courtyard beside the building).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *Der Wasserhahn tropft seit einer Woche.* — The tap has been dripping for a week.
- *Könnten Sie den Mangel bitte bis Freitag beheben lassen?* — Could you please have the defect fixed by Friday?

## Reading: a blog post

> *Mein Haus, meine Nachbarn*
>
> Als ich vor zwei Jahren in dieses Haus gezogen bin, kannte ich niemanden. Im Treppenhaus haben wir uns gegrüßt, mehr nicht. Das hat sich im letzten Winter geändert. Die Heizung war drei Tage lang kaputt, und es war eiskalt. Die Hausverwaltung war telefonisch nicht zu erreichen. Frau Özdemir aus dem Erdgeschoss hat dann eine Liste im Hof aufgehängt, und alle Mieter haben unterschrieben. Am nächsten Tag hat die Verwaltung endlich einen Handwerker geschickt und die Heizung reparieren lassen.
>
> Seitdem ist das Zusammenleben anders. Wir haben eine Chatgruppe gegründet, in der wir uns gegenseitig helfen. Wer eine Bohrmaschine braucht, kann sie bei Herrn Lang ausleihen. Herr Lang lässt sich dafür beim Einkaufen helfen, weil er nicht mehr gut laufen kann. Die Familie im dritten Stock lässt ihren Kinderwagen zwar immer noch im Flur stehen, aber jetzt redet man darüber, statt Zettel an die Tür zu kleben.
>
> Natürlich gibt es auch Streit. Im Sommer wollte ein Nachbar jeden Abend auf dem Balkon grillen, und die Leute über ihm haben sich über den Rauch beschwert. Frau Özdemir hat vermittelt, und wir haben uns geeinigt: Gegrillt wird nur am Wochenende und nur bis zehn Uhr. Das war ein guter Kompromiss.
>
> Im September haben wir zum ersten Mal ein Nachbarschaftsfest im Hof gefeiert. Jeder hat etwas mitgebracht, und die Kinder durften bis spät draußen bleiben. Ich habe gelernt: Eine Gemeinschaft entsteht nicht von allein. Aber ein bisschen Hilfsbereitschaft und Toleranz machen das Leben in einem großen Haus viel angenehmer.

Translation:

> *My building, my neighbours*
>
> When I moved into this building two years ago, I didn't know anyone. We said hello in the stairwell, nothing more. That changed last winter. The heating was broken for three days and it was freezing. The property management company couldn't be reached by phone. Mrs Özdemir from the ground floor then put up a list in the courtyard, and all the tenants signed it. The next day the management finally sent a tradesman and had the heating repaired.
>
> Since then, living together has been different. We set up a chat group where we help each other. Anyone who needs a drill can borrow it from Mr Lang. In return Mr Lang gets help with his shopping, because he can't walk well any more. The family on the third floor still leaves their pushchair in the hall, but now people talk about it instead of sticking notes on the door.
>
> Of course there are arguments too. In the summer one neighbour wanted to barbecue on his balcony every evening, and the people above him complained about the smoke. Mrs Özdemir mediated and we came to an agreement: barbecues only at the weekend, and only until ten o'clock. That was a good compromise.
>
> In September we had a neighbourhood party in the courtyard for the first time. Everyone brought something, and the children were allowed to stay outside until late. I've learned that a community doesn't happen by itself. But a bit of helpfulness and tolerance make life in a big building much more pleasant.

Notes: *war nicht zu erreichen* (couldn't be reached) is *sein + zu*, a passive-like form from lesson 18. *Gegrillt wird nur am Wochenende* is a passive without a subject (lesson 17). *entstehen* means "to come into being, arise". Find the uses of *lassen*: *reparieren lassen* (had it done), *lässt sich helfen* (lets people help him), *lässt … stehen* (leaves standing).

## Being helpful and polite

Some useful words for the friendly side of living together:

- *Die neuen Nachbarn sind sehr hilfsbereit.* — The new neighbours are very helpful.
- *Frau Lang hat freundlicherweise unsere Pakete angenommen.* — Mrs Lang kindly took in our parcels.
- *Wir tolerieren den Lärm am Wochenende, aber nicht nachts.* — We put up with the noise at the weekend, but not at night.
- *Kann ich mir deine Leiter ausleihen?* — Can I borrow your ladder?

*ausleihen* is separable and works in both directions: *sich etwas ausleihen* is to borrow, *jemandem etwas ausleihen* is to lend: *Ich leihe dir mein Fahrrad aus.* Neighbours who take in each other's parcels and lend each other tools often notice how much easier the *Zusammenleben* gets. Want a *Haustier* (pet)? Check your rental contract first.

## Pronunciation

- *lässt*: short *ä* like in *Bett*; *ließ*: long *ie*, sharp *ß*.
- *Treppenhaus*: TREP-pen-haus; *Hausverwaltung*: HAUS-ver-wal-tung, stress on the first part as in most compounds.
- *Schimmel*: SCHIM-mel, short *i*.
- *beheben*: be-HE-ben, long *e*.

## Common mistakes

- Using *machen* for "have something done": ~~Ich mache meine Haare schneiden.~~ → *Ich lasse mir die Haare schneiden.*
- Putting *zu* before the infinitive: ~~Ich lasse das Auto zu reparieren.~~ *lassen*, like modals, takes a bare infinitive.
- The perfect with *gelassen* and another verb: ~~Ich habe das Auto reparieren gelassen.~~ → *Ich habe das Auto reparieren lassen.* (Some native speakers do say it, but it's not standard.)
- The vowel change: *du lässt, er lässt* (not ~~lasst~~, which is *ihr lasst*).
- *ausleihen* vs *leihen*: both exist; *ausleihen* is especially common for libraries and for borrowing.
- *der Mangel* has an umlaut in the plural: *die Mängel*.

## Key points

- *lassen* + object: to leave (*Ich lasse die Tür offen*).
- *lassen* + infinitive: to have something done (*Ich lasse das Fahrrad reparieren*); with a dative reflexive for yourself (*Ich lasse mir die Haare schneiden*).
- *lassen* + person + infinitive: to let or make someone do something (*Lass mich helfen. Er lässt uns warten.*). *Lass uns …!* = Let's …!
- Perfect with two infinitives: *Ich habe die Heizung reparieren lassen*; but *Ich habe den Schlüssel im Auto gelassen*.
- *sich lassen* + infinitive = can be done: *Das Fenster lässt sich nicht öffnen.*
- Defects go to the *Hausverwaltung*; for advice on your rights, ask the *Mieterverein*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Travel and the German-speaking regions; giving a short presentation
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

German is spoken in Germany, Austria, most of Switzerland, Liechtenstein, parts of Belgium and Italy, and Luxembourg. Each of these places has its own regions, dialects and *Spezialitäten*, and tourism is a big part of their economies. This lesson gives you the words to talk about them.

It also teaches two practical skills. The first is grammar: the little words *hin* and *her*, which tell you whether a movement goes away from the speaker or towards them (*Komm herein! Geh hinaus!*). The second is speaking: how to give a short, well-structured presentation on a topic, with an introduction, your own experience, the situation in your home country, pros and cons, and a conclusion. This is exactly what the second part of the Goethe-Zertifikat B1 speaking test asks for (lesson 30), and it's also a skill you'll use at work and in courses.

## The German-speaking regions

| country | parts | example |
|---|---|---|
| Germany | 16 *Bundesländer* (federal states) | *Bayern, Sachsen, Nordrhein-Westfalen* |
| Austria | 9 *Bundesländer* | *Tirol, Steiermark, Wien* |
| Switzerland | 26 *Kantone* (cantons) | *Zürich, Bern, Graubünden* |

*Das Bundesland* is a compound of *der Bund* (federation) and *das Land*. Switzerland is divided into *Kantone*; German is the main language in most of them, but French, Italian and Romansh are spoken in others.

The *Alpen* (Alps, plural only) cover most of Austria and much of Switzerland and reach into the far south of Germany. Germany's highest mountain, the Zugspitze, is just under 3,000 metres; the highest in Austria, the Großglockner, is almost 3,800. In a *Gebirge* (mountain range) you'll find *Gipfel* (summits), *Hütten* (mountain huts) where hikers eat and sleep, and *Seilbahnen* (cable cars) that take you up without the climb.

Every region has a *Dialekt* or *Mundart* (both mean dialect; *Mundart* sounds more traditional). In German-speaking Switzerland, almost everyone speaks Swiss German in daily life and writes standard German. In northern Germany, older people in the countryside may still speak *Plattdeutsch*. You don't need to speak a dialect, but it helps to know that people will switch to standard German for you if you ask: *Könnten Sie bitte Hochdeutsch sprechen?*

Some sentences with the words of this lesson:

- *Jedes Bundesland hat seine eigenen Ferien.* — Every federal state has its own school holidays.
- *Käsespätzle sind eine typische Spezialität aus dem Allgäu.* — Cheese noodles are a typical speciality of the Allgäu.
- *Der Tourismus ist für die Region sehr wichtig.* — Tourism is very important for the region.
- *Die Saison beginnt im Dezember und endet im April.* — The season starts in December and ends in April.
- *In der Hauptsaison sind die Hotels voll und teuer; in der Nebensaison ist es ruhiger.* — In the high season the hotels are full and expensive; in the low season it's quieter.
- *Wien ist ein beliebtes Reiseziel für Touristen und Touristinnen aus aller Welt.* — Vienna is a popular destination for tourists from all over the world.
- *Im Restaurant gibt es nur regionale Produkte.* — The restaurant only has regional produce.

## hin and her: away and towards

German marks the direction of a movement with two small words:

- *hin* = away from the speaker, "there"
- *her* = towards the speaker, "here"

You know them already from *wohin?* (where to?) and *woher?* (where from?). In speech the question word is often split: *Wo gehst du hin?* — Where are you going? *Wo kommst du her?* — Where do you come from?

These words combine with prepositions to make **[[directional adverbs]]**, which are often used as separable prefixes:

| away from the speaker | towards the speaker | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *hinauf* | *herauf* | up |
| *hinunter* | *herunter* | down |
| *hinein* | *herein* | in |
| *hinaus* | *heraus* | out |
| *hinüber* | *herüber* | over, across |

The choice depends on where the speaker is:

- You're at the bottom of the stairs, your friend is at the top. You call up: *Ich komme gleich hinauf!* — I'm coming up in a second! Your friend calls down: *Komm herauf!* — Come up (here)!
- Someone knocks on your door: *Herein!* — Come in! You're inside, so the movement is towards you.
- A sign on an old train window: *Bitte nicht hinauslehnen.* — Please don't lean out.
- *Kannst du die Kiste bitte herunterbringen? Ich bin unten im Keller.* — Can you bring the box down, please? I'm down in the cellar.
- *Die Kinder laufen in den Garten hinaus.* — The children run out into the garden (away from me, inside the house).
- *Wir sind mit der Seilbahn hinaufgefahren und zu Fuß heruntergekommen.* — We went up by cable car and came down on foot (said by someone now at the bottom).

The picture shows the four most common directions from the point of view of one speaker upstairs: what comes up or in moves towards her (*her-*), what goes down or out moves away from her (*hin-*).

![A two-storey house. The speaker is in a room upstairs. A person climbing the stairs towards her is labelled herauf; a key dropped from her window to a friend in the garden is labelled hinunter; a cat walking into her room is labelled herein; a dog running out of the front door downstairs is labelled hinaus.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Spoken short forms

In everyday speech, Germans don't think about *hin* and *her* very much. They say *rauf, runter, rein, raus, rüber*, which come from the *her-* forms but are used for both directions:

- *Ich geh mal kurz raus.* — I'm just popping out.
- *Kommst du rein?* — Are you coming in?
- *Wir fahren morgen auf den Berg rauf.* — We're going up the mountain tomorrow.

In writing and in the exam, use the full forms when the direction is clear; in conversation the short forms are completely natural.

### Fixed expressions

Some uses have become idioms: *Wo ist mein Handy hin?* (Where has my phone got to?), *Wo hast du das her?* (Where did you get that from?), *hin und her* (back and forth), and *hin und zurück* (there and back, return ticket). And one you'll need for presentations: *Ich möchte darauf hinweisen, dass …* — I'd like to point out that …

## Giving a short presentation

In a short presentation (*eine Präsentation* or *ein kurzer Vortrag*) you speak for about three minutes about a question, such as *Sollte man im Urlaub lieber in die Berge oder ans Meer fahren?* A clear structure makes it easier for you and for your listeners. In a course or at work you'd have slides (*Folien*); in the exam you get five "slides" printed on paper, one for each part below. Each part has its typical phrases.

The five parts always come in this order:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The five parts of a short presentation
  accDescr: A short presentation goes in five steps. First the introduction, for example In meiner Präsentation geht es um. Second, your own experience, for example Ich habe selbst erlebt, dass. Third, the situation in your home country, for example In meinem Heimatland. Fourth, advantages and disadvantages with your opinion, for example Einerseits, andererseits. Fifth, the conclusion, for example Abschließend möchte ich sagen.
  A["1 Einleitung: In meiner Präsentation geht es um …"] --> B["2 Eigene Erfahrung: Ich habe selbst erlebt, dass …"]
  B --> C["3 Heimatland: In meinem Heimatland …"]
  C --> D["4 Vor- und Nachteile, Meinung: Einerseits … andererseits …"]
  D --> E["5 Schluss: Abschließend möchte ich sagen, …"]
```

### 1. Introduction (die Einleitung)

- *In meiner Präsentation geht es um das Thema …* — My presentation is about …
- *Ich möchte heute über … sprechen.* — Today I'd like to talk about …
- *Zuerst erzähle ich von meinen eigenen Erfahrungen, danach …* — First I'll talk about my own experiences, then …

### 2. Your own experience

- *Ich habe selbst erlebt, dass …* — I have experienced myself that …
- *Als ich in … war, habe ich …* — When I was in …, I …
- *Ich persönlich …* — Personally, I …

### 3. The situation in your home country

- *In meinem Heimatland ist das ganz anders / ähnlich.* — In my home country it's quite different / similar.
- *Bei uns in … ist es üblich, dass …* — Where I come from, it's usual that …
- *Viele Leute in … finden, dass …* — Many people in … think that …

### 4. Pros and cons, and your opinion

- *Ein Vorteil ist, dass … Ein Nachteil ist, dass …* — One advantage is that … One disadvantage is that …
- *Einerseits …, andererseits …* — On the one hand …, on the other hand …
- *Erstens …, zweitens …, außerdem …* — Firstly …, secondly …, also …
- *Meiner Meinung nach … / Ich bin der Meinung, dass …* — In my opinion …

### 5. Conclusion (der Schluss)

- *Abschließend möchte ich sagen, dass …* — To conclude, I'd like to say that …
- *Zusammenfassend kann man sagen: …* — In summary, you can say: …
- *Vielen Dank fürs Zuhören. Haben Sie noch Fragen?* — Thank you for listening. Do you have any questions?

*einerseits … andererseits* work like *deshalb* or *trotzdem*: when they start the clause, they fill position 1 and the verb comes right after: *Einerseits ist die Hauptsaison teuer, andererseits ist das Wetter dann am besten.*

## A model presentation

Ana is from Portugal and lives in Munich. Her course asked her to *präsentieren* a short talk on the question: *Urlaub in der Hauptsaison oder in der Nebensaison?*

> Guten Tag! In meiner Präsentation geht es um die Frage, ob man lieber in der Hauptsaison oder in der Nebensaison Urlaub machen sollte. Zuerst erzähle ich von meinen Erfahrungen, dann spreche ich über die Situation in Portugal, und am Ende nenne ich Vor- und Nachteile.
>
> Letzten Sommer bin ich im August in die Alpen gefahren. Das war ein Fehler: Auf jeder Hütte waren Hunderte von Touristen, und an der Seilbahn haben wir eine Stunde gewartet, bis wir hinauffahren konnten. Im Oktober war ich dann noch einmal in derselben Region. Es war ruhig, die Wirtin auf der Hütte hatte Zeit für uns, und der Blick vom Gipfel war fantastisch.
>
> In meinem Heimatland ist der Tourismus sehr wichtig, vor allem an der Küste im Süden. Im Sommer kommen so viele Urlauber, dass die Einheimischen manchmal kaum noch einen Parkplatz finden. Deshalb wirbt die Region inzwischen auch für den Winter.
>
> Einerseits hat die Nebensaison viele Vorteile: Es ist billiger, ruhiger, und man lernt die Leute besser kennen. Andererseits ist das Wetter nicht so sicher, und manche Restaurants und Museen sind geschlossen. Für Familien ist es außerdem schwierig, weil die Kinder nur in den Ferien freihaben.
>
> Abschließend möchte ich sagen: Wer flexibel ist, sollte in der Nebensaison reisen. Das ist besser für die Reisenden und für die Menschen, die dort wohnen. Vielen Dank fürs Zuhören!

Translation:

> Hello! My presentation is about whether it's better to go on holiday in the high season or the low season. First I'll tell you about my experiences, then I'll talk about the situation in Portugal, and at the end I'll give some pros and cons.
>
> Last summer I went to the Alps in August. That was a mistake: there were hundreds of tourists at every mountain hut, and at the cable car we waited for an hour before we could go up. Then in October I went to the same region again. It was quiet, the landlady at the hut had time for us, and the view from the summit was fantastic.
>
> In my home country, tourism is very important, especially on the coast in the south. In summer so many holidaymakers come that the locals sometimes can hardly find a parking space. That's why the region now advertises the winter too.
>
> On the one hand, the low season has many advantages: it's cheaper and quieter, and you get to know the people better. On the other hand, the weather is less reliable, and some restaurants and museums are closed. It's also difficult for families, because the children only have time off in the school holidays.
>
> To conclude, I'd like to say: if you're flexible, you should travel in the low season. That's better for the travellers and for the people who live there. Thank you for listening!

Notes: *dieselbe Region* (the same region) is written as one word. *Hunderte von Touristen* is "hundreds of tourists". *die Einheimischen* are the locals (an adjectival noun, lesson 5). *werben für* is to advertise, promote. Notice how each paragraph matches one of the five parts.

## Pronunciation

- *Tourismus*: tu-RIS-mus; *Tourist*: tu-RIST, stress on the last syllable.
- *Saison*: sä-ZONG, or with a French nasal ending, in Germany and Switzerland; in Austria (and parts of south-east Germany) it's se-SOHN, with a sharp *s* and a plain *n* (plural there: *Saisonen*).
- *Spezialität*: shpe-tsi-a-li-TÄT, stress on the last syllable, like all nouns in *-ität*.
- *hinein, heraus*: stress on the second part: hi-NEIN, he-RAUS.

## Common mistakes

- Mixing up *hin* and *her*: you're in the room and want someone to come in: ~~Komm hinein!~~ → *Komm herein!*
- Using *Bundesland* for Switzerland: the Swiss have *Kantone*.
- Forgetting the verb after *einerseits*: ~~Einerseits es ist teuer.~~ → *Einerseits ist es teuer.*
- Reading a written text aloud in a presentation. Use short notes and speak freely; that's what listeners and examiners expect.
- Leaving out the conclusion. Even one sentence (*Abschließend möchte ich sagen, …*) makes the talk sound finished.
- *die Alpen* is plural only: ~~die Alpe~~ (that's a mountain pasture in some regions).

## Key points

- Germany and Austria have *Bundesländer*, Switzerland has *Kantone*.
- *hin* = away from the speaker, *her* = towards the speaker: *hinauf/herauf, hinein/herein, hinaus/heraus*. In speech: *rauf, rein, raus, runter*.
- A short presentation has five parts: *Einleitung*, own experience, situation in your home country, *Vor- und Nachteile* with your opinion, *Schluss*.
- *einerseits … andererseits*, *erstens … zweitens*, *abschließend*: verb right after them.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Writing at B1: e-mails, forum posts and formal letters
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At A2 you wrote short messages with three content points. At B1 the texts get longer and more varied: an e-mail to a friend about something that happened, a post in an online *Forum* where you give your opinion, a polite message to a teacher or a landlord, and the letter everyone needs sooner or later, the complaint. These are also the three writing tasks of the Goethe-Zertifikat B1 (lesson 30).

This lesson shows you how to choose the right **[[register]]**, how to build a short text that reads as one piece rather than a list of sentences, the conventions of formal letters, and the spelling and comma rules that cost the most marks. For each type of text there is an original model you can learn from, and the reference sheet for this module collects the phrases.

## Three registers

| | informal | semi-formal | formal |
|---|---|---|---|
| to whom | friends, family, people you say *du* to | people you know but say *Sie* to: a teacher, a colleague, a neighbour | a company, an office, people you don't know |
| *Anrede* (opening) | *Liebe Mia, / Lieber Tom, / Hallo Sam,* | *Liebe Frau Kraus, / Lieber Herr Ott,* | *Sehr geehrte Frau Kraus, / Sehr geehrter Herr Ott, / Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren,* |
| *Grußformel* (closing) | *Viele Grüße / Liebe Grüße / Bis bald* | *Viele Grüße / Freundliche Grüße* | *Mit freundlichen Grüßen* |
| style | short sentences, *ja, mal, doch*, exclamation marks | polite and friendly | complete sentences, *würde, könnte*, no slang |

A **[[semi-formal]]** message mixes the two: you say *Sie* and stay polite, but you can be warm and personal, because you know the reader. *Liebe Frau Kraus* sounds friendly; *Sehr geehrte Frau Kraus* sounds like an office.

The chart helps you choose:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: Choosing the register of a letter or e-mail
  accDescr: Ask who you are writing to. To a friend or family member, someone you say du to, write informally: Liebe Mia, and close with Liebe Grüße. To someone you know but say Sie to, such as a teacher or neighbour, write semi-formally: Liebe Frau Kraus, and close with Viele Grüße. To a company, an office or a stranger, write formally: Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, and close with Mit freundlichen Grüßen. In an online forum, use no opening or closing, or just Hallo zusammen.
  A{"Who will read it?"} -- "a friend: du" --> B["informal: Liebe Mia, … Liebe Grüße"]
  A -- "someone you know: Sie" --> C["semi-formal: Liebe Frau Kraus, … Viele Grüße"]
  A -- "a company or office" --> D["formal: Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, … Mit freundlichen Grüßen"]
  A -- "an online forum" --> E["no opening or closing, or just Hallo zusammen"]
```

After the opening, put a comma, and start the next line with a small letter (unless it's a noun or *Sie*):

> Liebe Frau Kraus,
>
> vielen Dank für Ihre Nachricht.

*Sie, Ihnen, Ihr* are always capitalized. *du, dich, dein* can be written with a small or a capital letter in letters; both are correct.

## Building a text, not a list

An 80-word text with eight separate sentences of the form *Ich … Ich … Ich …* reads like a list. Examiners and readers want connections. Three tools help:

1. Change what comes first. Put a time or a reason at the start: *Letzte Woche … Deshalb … Zum Glück …*
2. Use connectors from this course: *weil, obwohl, damit, sodass, trotzdem, deshalb, außerdem, einerseits … andererseits, nicht nur … sondern auch*.
3. Refer back with pronouns and *da*-words: *Darüber habe ich mich sehr gefreut. Das hat mich geärgert.*

Two words that make formal writing tighter: *sowie* (as well as, and also) and *beziehungsweise*, written *bzw.* (or, or rather, respectively):

- *Bitte bringen Sie Ihren Ausweis sowie eine Kopie des Vertrags mit.* — Please bring your ID as well as a copy of the contract.
- *Ich kann am Montag bzw. am Dienstag kommen.* — I can come on Monday or Tuesday.

For a longer letter, give each point its own *Absatz* (paragraph). In e-mails, an empty line between paragraphs is enough.

## Model 1: an informal e-mail

Task: a friend has moved and wants to know how your new job is going. Tell her what happened in your first week, what you like, and suggest a visit.

> Liebe Jana,
>
> danke für deine Mail! Schön, dass du dich in Leipzig schon so wohlfühlst. Bei mir gibt es auch Neuigkeiten: Seit Montag arbeite ich in der Buchhandlung am Markt. Die erste Woche war anstrengend, weil ich viel lernen musste, aber die Kollegen sind sehr nett. Am besten gefällt mir, dass ich Kunden beraten darf. Gestern hat mich eine Frau nach einem Krimi gefragt, und ich wusste sofort, welchen sie meinte!
>
> Hast du Lust, mich im Mai zu besuchen? Dann zeige ich dir meinen Laden.
>
> Liebe Grüße
> Sofia

(about 90 words) Notice: each of the three points gets two or three sentences; there's a reason with *weil*, a past event, and a question at the end that asks for an answer.

## Model 2: a forum post

Task: in an online forum on a city website, people discuss the question: *Sollte die Innenstadt für Autos gesperrt werden?* Write your opinion.

> Ich finde die Idee grundsätzlich gut, aber man sollte sie gut planen. Einerseits wäre die Luft in der Innenstadt viel besser, und Fußgänger und Radfahrer hätten mehr Platz. In meiner Heimatstadt gibt es schon seit Jahren eine autofreie Zone, und die Geschäfte dort sind heute beliebter als früher. Andererseits müssen ältere Menschen und Familien mit kleinen Kindern weiter in die Stadt kommen können. Deshalb brauchen wir vorher bessere Busse und genug Parkplätze am Stadtrand. Mein Fazit: Ja, aber Schritt für Schritt.

(about 80 words) A forum post has no *Anrede* or *Grußformel*, or only a short *Hallo zusammen*. Take a clear position (*Stellung nehmen*) in the first sentence, give a reason and an example from your own experience, mention the other side, and end with a short *Fazit* (conclusion). In the exam, you may also have to react to another user's comment: *Ich stimme Max zu, dass … / Ich sehe das anders als Max.*

## Model 3: a semi-formal message

Task: you can't come to your course tomorrow. Write to your teacher, apologize and ask for the homework.

> Liebe Frau Brandt,
>
> leider kann ich morgen nicht zum Kurs kommen, weil ich einen Termin beim Facharzt habe. Das tut mir sehr leid. Könnten Sie mir bitte die Hausaufgaben per E-Mail schicken?
>
> Vielen Dank und viele Grüße
> Tariq Hassan

(about 40 words) Short, polite, all points covered. *Könnten Sie …?* is the key polite form. If you want to *hinzufügen* (add) a detail, one sentence is enough: *Ich hole den Stoff bis nächste Woche nach.*

## Formal letters: complaints and inquiries

A formal letter has a fixed shape: *Absender* (sender: your name and address) at the top, then the *Empfänger* (recipient), the place and date (*München, 12.03.2027*), a *Betreff* (subject line, no full stop), the *Anrede*, the text in paragraphs, the *Grußformel* and your name. In an e-mail, the address block is left out.

The picture shows where each part goes on the page:

![The layout of a formal letter: the sender's name and address at the top left, the recipient's address below it, the place and date on the right, a bold subject line, the opening Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, the text in paragraphs, the closing Mit freundlichen Grüßen, a handwritten signature and the typed name.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The two most common reasons to write one are an *Anfrage* (inquiry: you *anfragen* or *sich erkundigen*, ask for information) and a *Reklamation* (complaint about a product or service). In a complaint you say what you bought, what is *mangelhaft* (defective) or *beschädigt* (damaged), and what you want: a repair, an *Ersatz* (replacement), a *Umtausch* (exchange) or your money back.

### Model 4: a complaint

> Betreff: Reklamation – Bestellung Nr. 48213
>
> Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren,
>
> am 2. März habe ich in Ihrem Online-Shop einen Wasserkocher bestellt. Das Paket ist gestern angekommen, aber leider war der Wasserkocher beschädigt: Der Deckel ist gebrochen und lässt sich nicht schließen.
>
> Mit Bezug auf Ihre Garantiebedingungen bitte ich Sie um einen kostenlosen Ersatz bzw. um die Rückzahlung des Kaufpreises. Fotos vom Schaden sowie die Rechnung finden Sie im Anhang. Bitte teilen Sie mir außerdem mit, ob ich das Gerät zurückschicken soll und wer die Kosten dafür trägt.
>
> Ich möchte betonen, dass ich bisher mit Ihrem Kundendienst immer sehr zufrieden war. Ich hoffe, dass Sie mein Anliegen schnell bearbeiten, und freue mich auf Ihre Antwort.
>
> Mit freundlichen Grüßen
>
> Nadia Petrova

Translation:

> Subject: Complaint – order no. 48213
>
> Dear Sir or Madam,
>
> On 2 March I ordered a kettle from your online shop. The parcel arrived yesterday, but unfortunately the kettle was damaged: the lid is broken and won't close.
>
> With reference to your guarantee terms, I would ask you for a free replacement or a refund of the purchase price. You will find photos of the damage and the invoice attached. Please also let me know whether I should send the appliance back and who will pay the costs.
>
> I'd like to stress that I have always been very satisfied with your customer service so far. I hope you can deal with my request quickly and look forward to your reply.
>
> Yours faithfully,
>
> Nadia Petrova

Notes: *mit Bezug auf* (with reference to) + accusative is a formal way to *erwähnen* (mention) a document. *das Anliegen* is a request or concern, a polite formal word. *bearbeiten* is to deal with, process. *lässt sich nicht schließen* is the *sich lassen* of lesson 27. The firm will hopefully *beantworten* your letter, or *reagieren* (react) with a *Rückfrage* (a question back to you).

### Phrases for formal letters

| purpose | phrase |
|---|---|
| reason for writing | *Ich wende mich an Sie, weil … / Ich schreibe Ihnen wegen …* |
| asking for information | *Ich möchte mich nach … erkundigen. Könnten Sie mir bitte mitteilen, ob/wann …?* |
| complaining | *Leider muss ich mich über … beschweren. Leider war … beschädigt / mangelhaft.* |
| demanding | *Ich bitte Sie, … / Ich erwarte, dass …* |
| apologizing | *Ich bedauere sehr, dass … / Bitte entschuldigen Sie die Unannehmlichkeiten.* |
| closing | *Für Ihre Hilfe danke ich Ihnen im Voraus. Ich freue mich auf Ihre Antwort.* |

*bedauern* is a formal "regret, be sorry": *Wir bedauern die Verspätung.* *sich wenden an* + accusative is "to turn to, contact": *Wenden Sie sich bitte an unseren Kundendienst.* A *Stellungnahme* is a written statement of your position, for example when an office asks for your side of a story.

## Spelling and commas: the rules that cost marks

- Nouns have capitals, including nouns made from verbs and adjectives: *beim Lesen, etwas Neues, das Gute*.
- Commas before every subordinate clause: *Ich hoffe, dass … / …, weil … / …, obwohl … / …, die …* — and after it if the main clause continues: *Wenn du Zeit hast, komm vorbei.*
- Commas before infinitive groups with *um, ohne, statt*: *Ich schreibe Ihnen, um mich zu erkundigen.*
- No comma before *und* or *oder* joining two short parts: *Ich habe angerufen und eine Nachricht hinterlassen.*
- *dass* vs *das*: *dass* starts a clause after a verb of saying or thinking; *das* is an article or pronoun. If you can replace it with *dieses* or *welches*, it's *das*.
- *ß* vs *ss*: *ß* after a long vowel or a diphthong (*Grüße, heißen*), *ss* after a short vowel (*müssen, dass*).

## Pronunciation

- *Reklamation*: re-kla-ma-TSION; *Stellungnahme*: STEL-lungs-nah-me, stress on the first part.
- *beziehungsweise*: be-TSIE-hungs-wei-se; in speech, some people even say the abbreviation letter by letter: *beh-tsett-veh*.
- *Anliegen*: AN-lie-gen.

## Common mistakes

- Capital letter after the opening: ~~Liebe Frau Kraus, Vielen Dank …~~ → *vielen Dank …* (small letter).
- Mixing registers: *Sehr geehrte Frau Kraus … Liebe Grüße* or *Hallo Herr Ott* in a complaint. Pick one level and stay there.
- A full stop or comma after the *Grußformel*: ~~Mit freundlichen Grüßen,~~ → no punctuation in German.
- Writing *sie* for the polite "you": ~~Könnten sie mir helfen?~~ → *Könnten Sie mir helfen?*
- Missing out a content point. In the exam, every point counts. Tick them off before you finish.
- Starting every sentence with *Ich*.

## Key points

- Three registers: informal (*Liebe Mia, Liebe Grüße*), semi-formal (*Liebe Frau Kraus, Viele Grüße*), formal (*Sehr geehrte …, Mit freundlichen Grüßen*).
- Comma after the opening, small letter on the next line; no punctuation after the closing.
- Make a text, not a list: vary the first position, use connectors, refer back.
- A forum post: position, reason, example, the other side, *Fazit*.
- A complaint: what, when, what's wrong, what you want, attachments, closing.
- Comma before every subordinate clause and *um … zu* group.

lessons.title: The Goethe-Zertifikat B1 and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the last lesson of German B1. It explains what B1 means, describes the best-known exam at this level, the Goethe-Zertifikat B1, with strategies for each part, and reviews the grammar of the whole course. Its questions cover the whole course. You don't need to take the exam, but B1 is the level many people need for work, study or residence, so it's worth knowing how it works. Check the current requirements with the office or employer that asks for it.

## What B1 means

B1 is the third of the six levels of the **[[CEFR]]** (Common European Framework of Reference for Languages), and the first of the two "independent user" levels. The framework describes each level with **[[can-do statements]]**. In plain words, someone at B1:

- understands the main points when people speak clear standard language about familiar things: work, school, free time, the news on topics they know;
- can deal with most situations that come up while travelling where the language is spoken;
- can write simple, connected texts on topics they know or care about;
- can describe experiences, events, hopes and plans, and give short reasons and explanations for opinions.

At A2 you got by in routine situations; at B1 you can tell stories, argue, describe precisely, follow the news on familiar topics and handle offices, doctors, landlords and formal letters. Fast speech, dialects and unfamiliar abstract topics are still hard; that is the job of B2.

## The Goethe-Zertifikat B1

The adult exam is modular: there are four *Module* (modules), and you can take all four on one day or only the ones you need.

| module | time | what you do |
|---|---|---|
| Lesen (reading) | 65 minutes | 5 parts: a blog or other personal text; press articles; matching people's situations to ads; readers' opinions on a topic; rules or instructions |
| Hören (listening) | about 40 minutes | 4 parts: short announcements and messages; a monologue such as a guided tour; an informal conversation; a discussion on the radio |
| Schreiben (writing) | 60 minutes | 3 tasks: an informal e-mail (about 80 words); a forum post giving your opinion (about 80 words); a semi-formal e-mail (about 40 words) |
| Sprechen (speaking) | about 15 minutes, plus 15 minutes to prepare | in pairs: plan something together; present a topic; react to your partner's presentation and answer questions on your own |

![The four modules of the Goethe-Zertifikat B1: Lesen 65 minutes in 5 parts, Hören about 40 minutes in 4 parts, Schreiben 60 minutes with 3 tasks of about 80, 80 and 40 words, Sprechen about 15 minutes in pairs plus 15 minutes of preparation in 3 parts. Each module has 100 points and is passed with 60.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Each module is scored out of 100 points and passed with 60. The grades are the same as at A2:

| points | grade |
|---|---|
| 90–100 | sehr gut (very good) |
| 80–89 | gut (good) |
| 70–79 | befriedigend (satisfactory) |
| 60–69 | ausreichend (sufficient, a pass) |

Because the modules are separate, you can repeat only the one you failed. Modules passed within one year can usually be listed together on one combined certificate, sometimes for an extra fee; how this works depends on the exam centre, so ask before you register. Dates, fees and rules can change too.

The Goethe-Institut publishes free official practice material:

- [Model test for adults (Modellsatz, PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/pro/relaunch/prf/materialien/B1/b1_modellsatz_erwachsene.pdf)
- [Practice test for adults (Übungssatz, PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/pro/relaunch/prf/materialien/B1/B1_Uebungssatz_Erwachsene.pdf)
- [Interactive online practice](https://bfu.goethe.de/b1_mod/index.php)
- [Official exam rules (Durchführungsbestimmungen, PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/pro/relaunch/prf/en/Durchfuehrungsbestimmungen_B1.pdf)

Other B1 exams, such as telc Deutsch B1 and the ÖSD Zertifikat B1, and the *Deutsch-Test für Zuwanderer* used in German integration courses, test the same level with different tasks.

## Strategies for each module

### Lesen

- Read the *Aufgabenstellung* (task instructions) and the questions first. Every *Anweisung* tells you exactly what to do: *Lesen Sie die Aussagen 1 bis 6. Sind sie richtig oder falsch?*
- In true/false tasks, look for the sentence in the text that matches the *Aussage* (statement), then compare carefully. Small words decide: *nur, noch nicht, kaum, nicht mehr, alle, manche*.
- In matching tasks, you *zuordnen* (match) situations to ads. Underline the key need of each person, and remember that one situation may have no matching ad. Check whether an ad really *zutrifft* (applies) to all of the need, not only one word.
- In the readers' opinions part, decide for each person whether they are for or against something. Watch for *zwar … aber*, *einerseits … andererseits* and *obwohl*: the main opinion often comes after them.

### Hören

- Read the questions before each recording and *markieren* (mark) or *unterstreichen* (underline) the key words.
- In announcements, the last information counts: *Der Zug fährt heute nicht von Gleis 3, sondern von Gleis 5.*
- In conversations and discussions, keep track of who says what: each *Sprecher* or *Sprecherin* has a position. Note a word for each person as you listen.

### Schreiben

- Lesson 29 is your preparation. For each task, plan for two minutes: a short *Gliederung* (outline) with the content points in order.
- Cover every point. Doing the task, with all its *Inhalt* (content), is one of the main marking criteria, so a missing point costs marks however good your German is.
- Choose the right register: friend → informal; forum → neutral; teacher or landlord → semi-formal.
- Show what you can do: one or two subordinate clauses, a connector or two, a polite Konjunktiv II. Write sentences you are sure of; a simple, correct *Formulierung* is better than a complicated wrong one.
- Save five minutes to check *Rechtschreibung* (spelling), capitals, verb position and commas.

### Sprechen

The speaking module runs like this:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How the B1 speaking test runs
  accDescr: The speaking module starts with 15 minutes of preparation on your own. Then, in part 1, you and your partner plan something together. In part 2, each of you presents a topic for about three minutes. In part 3, after each presentation, the partner reacts and asks a question, and the presenter answers questions from the partner and the examiner.
  A["15 minutes of preparation, on your own"] --> B["Teil 1: plan something together with your partner"]
  B --> C["Teil 2: present your topic, about 3 minutes"]
  C --> D["Teil 3: your partner reacts and asks; you answer questions"]
  D --> E["Then the same for your partner's presentation"]
```

- In the 15 minutes of preparation, write keywords, not full sentences. Nobody wants to hear you read.
- In the planning task, the examiners want a real conversation: suggest, react, disagree politely, agree. Use your partner's ideas: *Gute Idee, und dann könnten wir …*
- For the presentation, follow the five-part structure from lesson 28: introduction, own experience, home country, pros and cons with your opinion, conclusion. *Gliedern* (structure) your talk out loud: *Zuerst …, dann …, zum Schluss …*
- When your partner has finished, react: say something positive or ask a question. Then answer the questions you're asked.
- If you can't find a word, describe it: *Das ist ein Ding, mit dem man …* Being able to *sich ausdrücken* (express yourself) around a gap is a B1 skill.

## How the writing and speaking are marked

Examiners don't count mistakes. They look at a few broad questions:

- Did you do the task? (all points covered, the right register, the right length)
- Is the text or talk well connected? (connectors, references back, a clear order)
- How wide is your *Wortschatz* (vocabulary) and your range of *Ausdrücke* (expressions)?
- How correct is the *Grammatik*, and do mistakes get in the way of understanding?
- In speaking: pronunciation, and whether you really interact with your partner.

So a text with a few small errors that is clear, complete and *angemessen* (appropriate) for the reader gets a good *Punktzahl* (score). A text that's perfect but misses a point or uses the wrong register loses points.

## Dialogue: planning together

Two learners, Lukas and Amira, practise the first speaking task. Their class wants to give a farewell party for their teacher.

> Amira: Lukas, wir sollen ja die Abschiedsfeier für Frau Brandt organisieren. Wann wollen wir die Feier machen?
>
> Lukas: Ich würde sagen, am letzten Kurstag, also am Freitag. Dann sind noch alle da.
>
> Amira: Das finde ich gut. Aber nicht im Kursraum, oder? Der ist so klein.
>
> Lukas: Stimmt. Wie wäre es mit dem Café gegenüber? Wir könnten dort einen Tisch reservieren.
>
> Amira: Hm, ich bin nicht sicher. Das ist ziemlich teuer, und wir sind zwanzig Leute. Was hältst du davon, wenn jeder etwas zu essen mitbringt und wir im Park feiern?
>
> Lukas: Gute Idee, aber was machen wir, wenn es regnet?
>
> Amira: Dann fragen wir die Schule, ob wir den großen Raum im Erdgeschoss benutzen dürfen. Das kann ich übernehmen.
>
> Lukas: Super. Und ein Geschenk brauchen wir auch. Ich schlage vor, dass wir ein Buch über unsere Stadt kaufen und alle etwas hineinschreiben.
>
> Amira: Das ist schön persönlich. Ich sammle das Geld, und du kaufst das Buch?
>
> Lukas: Einverstanden. Also: Freitag, Park oder Erdgeschoss, Essen von allen, und ein Buch mit Widmungen.

Translation:

> Amira: Lukas, we're supposed to organize the farewell party for Ms Brandt. When shall we have it?
>
> Lukas: I'd say on the last day of the course, so on Friday. Everyone will still be there then.
>
> Amira: I think that's good. But not in the classroom, right? It's so small.
>
> Lukas: True. How about the café opposite? We could book a table there.
>
> Amira: Hm, I'm not sure. It's quite expensive, and there are twenty of us. What do you think about everyone bringing something to eat and having the party in the park?
>
> Lukas: Good idea, but what do we do if it rains?
>
> Amira: Then we'll ask the school whether we can use the big room on the ground floor. I can take care of that.
>
> Lukas: Great. And we need a present too. I suggest we buy a book about our town and everyone writes something in it.
>
> Amira: That's nice and personal. I'll collect the money and you buy the book?
>
> Lukas: Agreed. So: Friday, the park or the ground floor, food from everyone, and a book with dedications.

Both speakers make suggestions (*Wie wäre es mit …? Was hältst du davon, wenn …? Ich schlage vor, dass …*), disagree politely with a reason, solve a problem, share the jobs and sum up: that is what examiners want to hear. *die Widmung* is a dedication; *übernehmen* is to take on, take care of.

## Review of the course

| topic | core idea | lessons |
|---|---|---|
| Präteritum | *fand, schrieb, fuhr, stand auf* for written stories | 1 |
| Plusquamperfekt, nachdem | *Nachdem sie gegessen hatte, ging sie.* | 2 |
| time clauses | *während, seit, bis, sobald, solange* | 3 |
| Futur I | *Es wird regnen. Er wird wohl krank sein.* | 4 |
| weak and adjectival nouns | *den Kollegen; ein Deutscher, die Erwachsenen* | 5 |
| concession | *obwohl, trotzdem, zwar … aber* | 6 |
| purpose | *um … zu, damit, ohne … zu, statt … zu* | 7 |
| reason and consequence | *da, falls, sodass; deshalb, daher* | 8 |
| two-part connectors | *entweder … oder, weder … noch, sowohl … als auch* | 9 |
| comparison | *je mehr, desto besser; das schnellere Auto* | 10 |
| relative clauses | *der Mann, dem …; die Leute, mit denen …; wo, was* | 11, 12 |
| genitive | *des Mannes, wegen des Wetters, trotz, während* | 13, 14 |
| participles, unpreceded adjectives | *das reparierte Rad; mit frischem Brot* | 15 |
| passive | *wird gebaut, wurde gebaut, muss gebaut werden* | 16–18 |
| opinions, da- and wo-words | *Ich bin der Meinung … Worüber? Darüber.* | 19 |
| news style, nominal phrases | *die Einführung des Gesetzes* | 20 |
| Konjunktiv II | *Wenn ich Zeit hätte … Hätte ich das gewusst …* | 21–23 |
| verbs, adjectives, nouns with prepositions | *sich beschäftigen mit, stolz auf, die Angst vor* | 24 |
| infinitive constructions | *scheinen zu, brauchen nicht zu* | 25 |
| reported speech, Konjunktiv I | *Sie sagt, sie komme. Er fragt, ob …* | 26 |
| lassen | *Ich lasse die Heizung reparieren.* | 27 |
| hin and her, presentations | *Komm herein! Einerseits … andererseits* | 28 |
| writing | register, connectors, formal letters | 29 |

If you remember only three things from B1, make them these: the verb's position tells the reader what kind of clause they're in (second, end, or first); the Konjunktiv II is how German is polite, imagines, and regrets; and connectors turn sentences into a text.

## What comes next: B2

At B2 you'll understand the main ideas of complex texts, including technical discussions in your own field, and talk with native speakers without strain on either side. The grammar continues with the Konjunktiv I used actively, more participle constructions (*die von der Stadt gebaute Brücke*), noun-heavy written style, and more connectors. The biggest change, though, is vocabulary, and the best way to build it is to read and listen to real German every day, mainly things you enjoy. The reading list for this course is a good start, and regular review keeps what you have learned.

## Exam and study language

These words come up in instructions, in feedback and in your own planning:

- *Insgesamt hat die Prüfung vier Module.* — Altogether the exam has four modules.
- *Der Text war inhaltlich gut, aber die Rechtschreibung war schwach.* — The text was good in terms of content, but the spelling was weak.
- *Formulieren Sie Ihre Meinung in zwei oder drei Sätzen.* — Put your opinion into words in two or three sentences.
- *Im Hörtext geht es hauptsächlich um das Wohnen.* — The listening text is mainly about housing.
- *Wie bereitest du dich auf die Prüfung vor?* — *Ich lerne jeden Tag neue Wörter, und am Wochenende mache ich eine Wiederholung.* — How are you preparing for the exam? — I learn new words every day, and at the weekend I do a review.
- *Die Vorbereitung dauert ungefähr drei Monate.* — The preparation takes about three months.
- *Die Prüferin hat mir viele Fragen gestellt.* *Der Prüfer war sehr freundlich.* — The examiner asked me lots of questions. The examiner was very friendly.
- *Meine Strategie: zuerst die Fragen lesen, dann den Text.* — My strategy: read the questions first, then the text.
- *Mein Niveau ist jetzt B1.* — My level is now B1.

## Pronunciation

- *Modul*: mo-DUL, stress on the second syllable (not like English "module").
- *Niveau*: ni-WOH, from French; the *-eau* is a long *o*.
- *Grammatik*: gram-MA-tik, stress on the second syllable.
- *Formulierung*: for-mu-LIE-rung, stress on *-lie-* like all *-ieren* verbs and their nouns.

## Common mistakes

- In Lesen, choosing an ad because one word matches. It has to fit the whole situation.
- In Schreiben, writing 150 words for an 80-word task. Longer isn't better; it only gives you more room for mistakes and less time to check.
- Learning set phrases for the presentation but not practising them aloud. Say your introduction and conclusion until they feel automatic.
- *die Prüfung bestehen* (pass) vs *die Prüfung machen / ablegen* (take): *Ich habe die Prüfung gemacht* only says that you took it. If you passed, say *Ich habe die Prüfung bestanden.*

## Key points

- B1 = an independent user on familiar topics: you can follow the main points, travel, write connected texts, and describe experiences and plans with reasons.
- The Goethe-Zertifikat B1 has four modules (Lesen 65 min, Hören about 40 min, Schreiben 60 min, Sprechen about 15 min plus 15 min preparation), each out of 100, passed with 60.
- Modules can be taken and repeated separately.
- Read the task first, cover every point, choose the right register, react to your partner.
- Practise with the free official model tests.
