lessons.title: Reported speech in full: Konjunktiv I and the replacement rule
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 26 you learned to report what someone said in everyday German (*Sie hat gesagt, dass sie morgen kommt*) and to recognize a few news forms: *er sei, er habe, es gebe*. This honors lesson completes the picture. You'll see the whole Konjunktiv I, the rule journalists use to decide between Konjunktiv I, Konjunktiv II and *würde*, how past, future, questions and requests are reported, and what the choice of verb (*behaupten*, *einräumen*, *bestätigen* …) tells you about a statement. At the end you'll turn a news report back into the German you'd use with a friend.

Using the Konjunktiv I actively is a B2 skill, so most of this lesson is about reading. If you did the honors lesson on sources and claims in module 4, you already know *laut*, *zufolge* and the hearsay *sollen*; here the focus is on the verb forms.

## Why the news needs its own form

Compare two sentences from a newspaper:

- *Die Brücke ist sicher, sagte der Bürgermeister.*
- *Die Brücke sei sicher, sagte der Bürgermeister.*

Both report the mayor's words. In the first, the main clause *Die Brücke ist sicher* looks like a plain fact; only the added *sagte der Bürgermeister* shows whose view it is. In the second, the verb itself says "this is someone's statement": *sei* marks it as reported, and the newspaper doesn't vouch for it.

The big advantage shows up in longer texts. Once a reporter has named the speaker, every following sentence in the Konjunktiv I still belongs to that speaker, with no need to repeat "he said":

> *Der Bürgermeister verteidigte die Entscheidung. Die Brücke sei sicher. Man habe sie erst im Frühjahr geprüft. Es gebe keinen Grund zur Sorge.*

In English you'd have to keep adding "he said" or "according to him". In German the verb form carries it. As soon as the text switches back to the indicative, the newspaper is speaking again.

Two things to keep in mind. First, the quote itself, in quotation marks, is **[[direct speech]]**: *„Die Brücke ist sicher", sagte er.* It keeps the speaker's exact words and the indicative. Second, the indicative is also correct in reported speech, and many papers use it after a clear verb of saying (*Er sagte, dass die Brücke sicher ist*). The Konjunktiv I is the more careful, more formal choice, typical of news agencies, quality papers and the radio news.

## The forms in full

The Konjunktiv I is built from the infinitive stem plus the endings *-e, -est, -e, -en, -et, -en*. Only *sein* is irregular. The forms marked * are the same as the normal present tense:

| | sein | haben | werden | können | kommen |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | *sei* | *habe** | *werde** | *könne* | *komme** |
| du | *sei(e)st* | *habest* | *werdest* | *könnest* | *kommest* |
| er / sie / es | *sei* | *habe* | *werde* | *könne* | *komme* |
| wir | *seien* | *haben** | *werden** | *können** | *kommen** |
| ihr | *seiet* | *habet* | *werdet* | *könnet* | *kommet* |
| sie / Sie | *seien* | *haben** | *werden** | *können** | *kommen** |

In practice you'll meet two groups: the third person singular of every verb (*er habe, sie komme, man könne, es gebe*) and all the forms of *sein* (*sie seien*). The *du* and *ihr* forms sound old-fashioned and are rare; you only need to recognize them. Stem-changing verbs keep the infinitive vowel: *er gebe* (not *gibt*), *sie fahre* (not *fährt*), *er wisse* (not *weiß*). That's a handy way to spot them.

## The replacement rule

What if the Konjunktiv I looks exactly like the indicative, as in *sie haben* or *wir kommen*? Then the reader can't see that the sentence is reported, so writers follow a **[[replacement rule]]** (*Ersatzregel*):

1. Use the Konjunktiv I if it is different from the indicative: *er komme, er habe, sie seien*.
2. If it isn't, use the Konjunktiv II: *sie hätten, sie kämen, wir müssten*.
3. If the Konjunktiv II looks like the Präteritum too (as with all regular verbs: *sie arbeiteten*), use *würde* + infinitive: *sie würden arbeiten*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The replacement rule for reported speech in the news
  accDescr: Start with the Konjunktiv I. If its form is different from the normal present indicative, use it, for example er komme or er sei. If it looks the same, as with sie kommen or sie haben, use the Konjunktiv II instead, for example sie kämen or sie hätten. If the Konjunktiv II also looks like the simple past, as with sie arbeiteten, use würde plus infinitive, for example sie würden arbeiten.
  A["Form the Konjunktiv I"] --> B{"Different from the indicative?"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["Use it: er komme, er sei, er habe"]
  B -- "no" --> D["Form the Konjunktiv II"]
  D --> E{"Different from the Präteritum?"}
  E -- "yes" --> F["Use it: sie kämen, sie hätten"]
  E -- "no" --> G["Use würde + infinitive: sie würden arbeiten"]
```

So in a news article a Konjunktiv II doesn't always mean "unreal" or "would". *Die Ärzte sagen, sie hätten zu wenig Zeit* simply reports *„Wir haben zu wenig Zeit."* The context tells you which job it's doing. In speech and informal writing, many people go straight to the Konjunktiv II or *würde* for all reported speech; that's normal too.

## Time: only three choices

Reported speech has fewer tenses than direct speech:

| original | reported (Konjunktiv I) |
|---|---|
| present: *„Ich komme."* | *er komme* |
| any past: *„Ich kam." / „Ich bin gekommen." / „Ich war gekommen."* | *er sei gekommen* |
| future: *„Ich werde kommen."* | *er werde kommen* |

Every past tense becomes *habe* or *sei* + participle: *„Wir hatten keine Wahl"* → *sie hätten keine Wahl gehabt* (*sie haben gehabt* would look like the indicative, so the rule switches to *hätten*). A Konjunktiv II in the original stays as it is: *„Wir hätten früher informieren müssen"* → *man hätte früher informieren müssen*.

## Questions and requests

Reported questions work as in lesson 26, with the verb in the Konjunktiv I at the end:

- *„Wann wird die Brücke geöffnet?"* → *Sie fragte, wann die Brücke geöffnet werde.*
- *„Gibt es einen Ersatzbus?"* → *Er wollte wissen, ob es einen Ersatzbus gebe.*

Requests and instructions use *sollen* (or, for a polite request, *mögen*):

- *„Nehmen Sie die Nordbrücke!"* → *Die Polizei sagte, man solle die Nordbrücke nehmen.*
- *„Bitte haben Sie Geduld."* → *Der Sprecher bat, man möge Geduld haben.*

With a plural subject the replacement rule applies again: *sie sollen* looks like the indicative, so you read *sie sollten*: *Er forderte die Anwohner auf, sie sollten den Umweg nehmen.*

## The reporting verb tells you more

The verb that introduces a statement is chosen with care, and it often reveals how the reporter sees it. These **[[reporting verbs]]** are worth knowing:

| verb | meaning | what it suggests |
|---|---|---|
| *sagen, erklären, mitteilen* | say, state, announce | neutral |
| *betonen* | stress | the speaker finds it important |
| *behaupten* | claim | the reporter keeps a distance; maybe it isn't true |
| *bestätigen* | confirm | it was said before; now it's official |
| *einräumen* | admit | something unpleasant for the speaker |
| *bestreiten, dementieren* | deny | *dementieren*: officially deny a report |
| *warnen (vor)* | warn | a danger |
| *fordern* | demand, call for | a demand on someone else |

*Der Minister behauptete, er habe von nichts gewusst* sounds much more doubtful than *Der Minister erklärte, er habe von nichts gewusst*. And *Die Firma räumte ein, dass Fehler gemacht worden seien* tells you the firm didn't want to say it. A short official statement is a *Pressemitteilung* (press release); exact words in quotation marks are a *Zitat* (quotation). If someone gives a view, they *äußern sich* (comment): *Die Stadt wollte sich nicht äußern.* — The city declined to comment.

The picture shows these signals in a short article:

![A short local news article headed Brücke bleibt gesperrt, with the reporting signals highlighted: the Konjunktiv I verb sei, the reporting verb erklärte, a direct quotation in German quotation marks, the source phrase Einem Gutachten zufolge, and the distancing adverb angeblich.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1: From direct to reported speech

A city spokesman speaks at a press conference. Report his words in news style.

1. *„Die Brücke ist nicht sicher."* — *ist* → Konjunktiv I *sei* (different from *ist*): *Er sagte, die Brücke sei nicht sicher.*
2. *„Wir haben die Schäden erst im März entdeckt."* — the speaker is the city, so *wir* becomes *die Stadt* (third person singular). Past → *habe* + participle: *Er räumte ein, die Stadt habe die Schäden erst im März entdeckt.* *einräumen* fits: it's an admission.
3. *„Die Arbeiten dauern mindestens acht Wochen."* — Konjunktiv I *sie dauern* = indicative; Konjunktiv II *sie dauerten* = Präteritum; so *würde*: *Die Arbeiten würden mindestens acht Wochen dauern.*
4. *„Wann wird die Brücke wieder geöffnet?"* (a resident's question) — *ob*/question word + Konjunktiv I: *Eine Anwohnerin wollte wissen, wann die Brücke wieder geöffnet werde.*
5. *„Nutzen Sie die Fähre!"* (to the residents) — a request, plural: *Er forderte die Anwohner auf, sie sollten die Fähre nutzen.*

### Example 2: Whose view is it?

Read the short report and decide which sentences belong to the speaker and which to the newspaper.

> *(1) Der Vermieterverband kritisierte die neuen Regeln für Nebenkosten. (2) Sie seien viel zu kompliziert. (3) Kleine Vermieter hätten dafür keine Zeit. (4) Viele Eigentümer dächten deshalb an einen Verkauf. (5) Die Regeln treten am 1. Juli in Kraft.*

1. Sentence 1 is in the indicative: the newspaper reports a fact, namely that the association criticized the rules.
2. *seien* (Konjunktiv I): the association's view, not the paper's.
3. *hätten* (replacing *haben*, which would look like the indicative): still the association.
4. *dächten* (Konjunktiv II of *denken*, replacing *denken*): still the association. Nobody has checked whether owners really want to sell.
5. *treten … in Kraft* (indicative): the newspaper's own information. The date is a fact.

### Example 3: Back to everyday German

You read the news and tell a friend about it. Konjunktiv I would sound stiff in conversation, so turn it into *dass* + indicative, or into Konjunktiv II if you doubt it.

- News: *Der Minister erklärte, die Renten seien sicher. Er habe nie etwas anderes behauptet.*
- To a friend: *Der Minister hat gesagt, dass die Renten sicher sind und dass er nie etwas anderes behauptet hat.*
- With doubt: *Er hat behauptet, die Renten wären sicher.* (You don't quite believe him.)

The perfect (*hat gesagt*) replaces the Präteritum of the news (*erklärte*), as usual in speech.

## Reading: a residents' meeting

> *Lindenbrücke: Anwohner verlieren die Geduld*
>
> Seit drei Wochen ist die Lindenbrücke gesperrt, und viele Anwohnerinnen und Anwohner sind verärgert. Bei einer Bürgerversammlung am Dienstag kritisierten sie vor allem die Informationspolitik der Stadt. Man habe erst aus der Zeitung von der Sperrung erfahren, sagte eine Ladenbesitzerin aus der Altstadt. Seitdem kämen kaum noch Kunden in ihr Geschäft.
>
> Baubürgermeister Klaus Wendt räumte Fehler ein. Die Stadt hätte die Bürger früher informieren müssen. Die Sperrung sei aber notwendig gewesen: Ein Gutachten habe gezeigt, dass der Beton an mehreren Stellen beschädigt sei. Er betonte, die Sicherheit gehe vor.
>
> Ein Anwohner wollte wissen, ob die Stadt eine Fähre oder einen Ersatzbus einsetzen werde. Wendt antwortete, man prüfe beide Möglichkeiten. Eine Entscheidung werde es bis Ende des Monats geben. Die Anwohner forderte er auf, sie sollten bis dahin den Umweg über die Nordbrücke nehmen.
>
> Die Bauarbeiten beginnen nach Angaben der Stadt im Juni.

Translation:

> *Lindenbrücke: residents are losing patience*
>
> The Lindenbrücke has been closed for three weeks, and many residents are angry. At a public meeting on Tuesday they criticized above all the way the city handled information. People only found out about the closure from the newspaper, said a shop owner from the old town. Since then, she said, hardly any customers had come into her shop.
>
> Klaus Wendt, the deputy mayor for building, admitted mistakes. The city should have informed people earlier, he said. But the closure had been necessary: an expert report had shown that the concrete was damaged in several places. He stressed that safety came first.
>
> One resident wanted to know whether the city would provide a ferry or a replacement bus. Wendt answered that both options were being examined. There would be a decision by the end of the month. Until then, he asked the residents to take the detour over the Nordbrücke.
>
> According to the city, the construction work will begin in June.

Notes: *kämen* replaces *kommen* (which would look like the indicative). *hätte … informieren müssen* was already Konjunktiv II in the original (*„Wir hätten früher informieren müssen"*), a real regret, so it stays. *vorgehen* means to take priority; *einsetzen* to put into service; *der Umweg* is a detour; *die Bürgerversammlung* is a public meeting for residents. The last sentence is indicative with a source: the city's plan, reported as information.

## Common mistakes

- Reading *er sei* or *sie habe* as a mistake or as a command. It's reported speech: "he is, (he says)".
- Reading every Konjunktiv II in the news as "would" or "unreal". In reported speech, *sie hätten* often just stands for *sie haben*.
- Translating the Konjunktiv I with a present tense in English after "said". English normally shifts back: *Er sagte, er sei krank* = "He said he *was* ill."
- Forgetting that every past becomes *habe/sei* + participle: ~~er war gekommen~~ → *er sei gekommen*.
- Using the Konjunktiv I in your own conversation. In speech, *dass* + indicative or the Konjunktiv II is natural; save the Konjunktiv I for formal writing at B2.
- Taking *behaupten* as neutral. It signals distance; *sagen* or *erklären* is the neutral choice.

## Key points

- The Konjunktiv I (*er sei, er habe, es gebe, man könne*) marks a statement as reported; a whole paragraph in it still belongs to the named speaker.
- Endings *-e, -est, -e, -en, -et, -en*; stem-changing verbs keep the infinitive vowel (*er gebe, sie fahre*).
- Replacement rule: Konjunktiv I → if identical, Konjunktiv II → if identical to the Präteritum, *würde* + infinitive.
- Three times only: *er komme*, *er sei gekommen*, *er werde kommen*.
- Questions: *ob*/question word + Konjunktiv I; requests: *solle(n)*, polite *möge*.
- Reporting verbs carry a view: *behaupten* (doubt), *einräumen* (admission), *bestätigen*, *dementieren*.
- In conversation, turn news German back into *dass* + indicative.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Letters from offices and landlords: reading Amtsdeutsch
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Living on your own in a German-speaking country means post: from the town hall, the health insurance fund, the landlord. In lesson 29 you learned to *write* formal letters; this honors lesson is about *reading* the ones that come to you, and acting on them in time. Their style has a nickname, *Amtsdeutsch* ("office German"), in English **[[officialese]]**: long nouns, fixed phrases, abbreviations and passive forms. It looks hard, but it uses a small toolkit you already know from lesson 18 (*sein* + *zu*) and lesson 20 (nominal style), plus one new pattern, the light verb construction.

If you did the German A2 honors lesson on official letters, you already know their layout, the most common abbreviations and how to read a reminder. This lesson goes further: how deadlines are counted, how to write an objection yourself, the light verb constructions of formal German, and how to check the yearly service-charge bill from your landlord. The legal details here are simplified and describe Germany; they are not legal advice. When in doubt, a *Beratungsstelle* or the *Mieterverein* (lesson 27) can help.

## The parts of an official decision

When an office decides on something you applied for, or something you have to pay, it sends a *Bescheid* (an official decision). A *Bescheid* is binding: if you don't object in time, it stands. Here is a quick review of its parts:

![An official letter from the road traffic office of the fictional town of Musterstadt to Elif Kaya. Labels point to the Aktenzeichen (file number) at the top right, the bold subject line, the decision Ihr Antrag wird abgelehnt, the reasons under Begründung, the Rechtsbehelfsbelehrung that explains how to object, and Im Auftrag above the signature.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *das Aktenzeichen* (Az.): the file number. Quote it in every reply and phone call; it's how the office finds your case.
- *der Sachbearbeiter / die Sachbearbeiterin*: the official dealing with your case, often with a phone number.
- *der Betreff*: what the letter is about, as in lesson 29.
- the decision itself: your application *wird bewilligt* (is approved) or *wird abgelehnt* (is rejected), or an amount *wird festgesetzt* (is fixed).
- *die Begründung*: the reasons.
- *die Rechtsbehelfsbelehrung*: information on how you can challenge the decision, and by when. Always read this part.
- *Im Auftrag* (i. A.): the person signs on behalf of the office.

## Deadlines and objections

The Rechtsbehelfsbelehrung in the picture says: *Gegen diesen Bescheid kann innerhalb eines Monats nach Bekanntgabe Widerspruch erhoben werden.* That means you can lodge an objection (*Widerspruch einlegen* or *erheben*) within one month of being notified.

*Bekanntgabe* (notification) isn't the date on the letter. A letter sent by ordinary post counts as delivered a few days later: under the federal rules, since 2025, on the fourth day after posting (before that it was the third), and state offices follow similar rules. Because the details vary, the safe habit is simple: treat the date on the letter as the start, and act well within a month.

A *Widerspruch* must be in writing (a signed letter; some offices also accept other forms) or *zur Niederschrift*, which means you go to the office and an official writes it down for you. In some states and for some kinds of decisions there is no *Widerspruch*, and you have to go straight to the administrative court (*Klage* at the *Verwaltungsgericht*). You don't need to know which cases those are: the Rechtsbehelfsbelehrung of your letter tells you.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: What to do when an official decision arrives
  accDescr: Read the subject line and the decision. If you agree, do what the letter asks by the date it gives, such as paying or sending a document. If you disagree, find the deadline in the Rechtsbehelfsbelehrung, write a Widerspruch that quotes the Aktenzeichen and gives your reasons, and send it in time, keeping proof that you sent it. If anything is unclear, ask the Sachbearbeiter or a Beratungsstelle before the deadline runs out.
  A["Read the Betreff and the decision"] --> B{"Do you agree?"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["Do what it asks by the date given"]
  B -- "no" --> D["Find the deadline in the Rechtsbehelfsbelehrung"]
  D --> E["Write a Widerspruch: Aktenzeichen, reasons, signature"]
  E --> F["Send it in time and keep proof"]
  B -- "not sure" --> G["Ask the Sachbearbeiter or a Beratungsstelle, before the deadline"]
```

### Example 1: Answering the Bescheid

Elif Kaya applied for a residents' parking permit (*Bewohnerparkausweis*). The car belongs to her sister, so it isn't registered in her name, and the office rejected the application because a confirmation from the registered keeper (*die Halterin*) was missing. The letter is dated Monday, 3 May 2027.

1. Deadline: a month after notification. Posted on 3 May, the letter counts as delivered on Friday, 7 May, so the month ends on Monday, 7 June. To be safe, Elif plans to send her objection by the end of May.
2. What she can do: the missing document is the whole problem, so she could simply apply again with it. She can also lodge a *Widerspruch* and attach the document, which asks the office to look at the same case again. She chooses that.
3. Her letter, formal, with the file number in the subject line:

> Betreff: Widerspruch gegen Ihren Bescheid vom 03.05.2027, Az. BP-2027-0418
>
> Sehr geehrter Herr Brandt,
>
> hiermit lege ich Widerspruch gegen den oben genannten Bescheid ein. Das Fahrzeug gehört meiner Schwester, aber ich nutze es dauerhaft. Die Bestätigung der Halterin habe ich diesem Schreiben beigefügt. Ich bitte Sie, meinen Antrag erneut zu prüfen.
>
> Mit freundlichen Grüßen
>
> Elif Kaya

(*hiermit* = hereby; *oben genannt* = above-mentioned; *das Schreiben* = the letter, a formal word.) She sends it by registered post (*Einschreiben*) or hands it in and asks for a stamp with the date of receipt, so she has proof.

## Officialese decoded

### Nominal style

Lesson 20 showed how written German packs actions into nouns. Official letters do it constantly, often with a preposition at the front (*nach Eingang*, *bei Nichtzahlung*, *zur Vermeidung*). Turn the noun back into a verb and the sentence becomes plain German:

| officialese | plain German | English |
|---|---|---|
| *Im Falle einer Ablehnung …* | *Wenn wir Ihren Antrag ablehnen, …* | if your application is rejected |
| *Unter Vorlage Ihres Ausweises …* | *Wenn Sie Ihren Ausweis zeigen, …* | on presentation of your ID |
| *Zur Vermeidung weiterer Kosten …* | *Damit keine weiteren Kosten entstehen, …* | to avoid further costs |
| *Nach Prüfung Ihres Antrags …* | *Nachdem wir Ihren Antrag geprüft haben, …* | after examining your application |
| *Bei Rückfragen …* | *Wenn Sie Fragen haben, …* | if you have any questions |

### Light verb constructions

A **[[light verb construction]]** (*Funktionsverbgefüge*) is a noun plus a verb that has lost most of its own meaning: the noun carries the meaning. *einen Antrag stellen* doesn't "put" anything; it simply means *beantragen*, to apply. They sound formal and are everywhere in official German:

| light verb construction | simple verb | English |
|---|---|---|
| *einen Antrag stellen* | *beantragen* | to apply |
| *Widerspruch einlegen* | *widersprechen* | to object |
| *eine Entscheidung treffen* | *entscheiden* | to decide |
| *in Anspruch nehmen* | *nutzen* | to make use of |
| *zur Verfügung stellen* | *geben, bereitstellen* | to provide |
| *zur Kenntnis nehmen* | *bemerken, registrieren* | to note |
| *in Kraft treten* | *gültig werden* | to come into force |

You don't need to use them yourself; *Ich möchte widersprechen* is perfectly correct. But *Ich lege Widerspruch ein* is what offices expect, and it's worth learning as a phrase.

### Passive and sein + zu

Offices rarely say who acts. Lesson 18's *sein* + *zu* is their favourite way to give an order: *Der Betrag ist bis zum 15.07. zu überweisen* = *Sie müssen den Betrag bis zum 15.07. überweisen.* *Die Unterlagen sind beizufügen* = you must enclose the documents. The passive does the same job without the "must": *Ihr Antrag wird abgelehnt.*

### Abbreviations

Besides *Az.*, *i. A.*, *ggf.* (*gegebenenfalls*, if necessary) and *Anl.* (*Anlage*, enclosure), you'll meet these:

| abbreviation | full form | English |
|---|---|---|
| *z. Hd.* | *zu Händen* | for the attention of |
| *i. V.* | *in Vertretung* | standing in for (the person in charge) |
| *o. g.* | *oben genannt* | above-mentioned |
| *bzgl.* | *bezüglich* | regarding |
| *gem.* | *gemäß* | in accordance with |
| *Abs.* | *Absatz* | paragraph, subsection (of a law) |

*§ 556 Abs. 3 BGB* reads "Paragraf 556, Absatz 3 des Bürgerlichen Gesetzbuchs" (the German Civil Code).

### Example 2: Translating a sentence into plain German

*„Bei nicht fristgerechter Vorlage der Nachweise wird Ihr Antrag gem. § 66 SGB I ggf. abgelehnt."*

1. *Bei … Vorlage der Nachweise*: *bei* + noun = *wenn*; *die Vorlage* comes from *vorlegen* (to present). → *Wenn Sie die Nachweise … vorlegen*.
2. *nicht fristgerecht* = not in time (*die Frist* + *gerecht*, "fitting"). → *Wenn Sie die Nachweise nicht rechtzeitig vorlegen*.
3. *gem. § 66 SGB I*: the legal basis, a section of the social security code. You can skip it to understand the sentence.
4. *ggf.* = *gegebenenfalls*, "possibly, where applicable".
5. Plain German: *Wenn Sie die Nachweise nicht rechtzeitig schicken, kann es sein, dass wir Ihren Antrag ablehnen.* — If you don't send the documents in time, we may reject your application.

## The service-charge bill: die Nebenkostenabrechnung

Your rent in Germany usually has two parts: the basic rent and the *Nebenkosten* (service charges: heating, water, rubbish collection, cleaning the stairwell, the caretaker and so on). For the *Nebenkosten* you pay a fixed *Vorauszahlung* (advance payment) every month. Once a year the landlord or the *Hausverwaltung* adds up the real costs and sends the *Nebenkostenabrechnung*. If the real costs were higher than your advance payments, you owe a *Nachzahlung* (additional payment); if they were lower, you have a *Guthaben* (credit), which is paid back or set against the next rent.

Some rules worth knowing (simplified; Austria and Switzerland differ):

- The landlord has to send the bill within twelve months of the end of the billing period. For a bill for 2026, that means by 31 December 2027. A bill that comes later usually can't demand a *Nachzahlung*.
- You have twelve months from receiving it to raise objections, and you may ask to see the *Belege* (receipts) behind it.
- After a bill, the landlord can adjust the monthly advance payment to a fitting amount.

## Reading: a letter from the property management

> Betreff: Nebenkostenabrechnung 2026, Mieteinheit Lindenweg 7, 2. OG links
>
> Sehr geehrte Frau Kaya,
>
> anbei erhalten Sie die Nebenkostenabrechnung für den Abrechnungszeitraum 01.01.2026 bis 31.12.2026. Ihre Vorauszahlungen betrugen 12 × 210,00 € = 2.520,00 €. Ihr Anteil an den Kosten beträgt 2.687,40 €. Daraus ergibt sich eine Nachzahlung in Höhe von 167,40 €.
>
> Der Betrag ist innerhalb von 30 Tagen nach Erhalt dieser Abrechnung auf das unten genannte Konto zu überweisen. Aufgrund der gestiegenen Heizkosten wird Ihre monatliche Vorauszahlung ab dem 01.03.2027 auf 225,00 € angepasst.
>
> Die Belege können nach vorheriger Terminvereinbarung in unserem Büro eingesehen werden. Bei Rückfragen steht Ihnen Ihre Sachbearbeiterin, Frau Lenz, gern zur Verfügung.
>
> Mit freundlichen Grüßen
>
> i. A. M. Lenz
> Hausverwaltung Muster GmbH
>
> Anl.: Abrechnung (3 Seiten)

Translation:

> Subject: Service-charge bill 2026, flat Lindenweg 7, 2nd floor left
>
> Dear Ms Kaya,
>
> Please find enclosed the service-charge bill for the billing period 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2026. Your advance payments came to 12 × €210.00 = €2,520.00. Your share of the costs is €2,687.40. This results in an additional payment of €167.40.
>
> The amount must be transferred to the account given below within 30 days of receiving this bill. Because heating costs have risen, your monthly advance payment will be adjusted to €225.00 from 1 March 2027.
>
> The receipts can be inspected in our office by prior appointment. If you have any questions, your contact, Ms Lenz, will be glad to help.
>
> Yours sincerely,
>
> pp. M. Lenz, Muster property management
>
> Encl.: bill (3 pages)

Notes: *anbei* = enclosed; *OG* = *Obergeschoss* (upper floor); *betragen* = to amount to; *sich ergeben* = to result; *in Höhe von* = to the amount of; *einsehen* = to inspect; *die Terminvereinbarung* = making an appointment. Find the nominal style (*nach Erhalt, nach vorheriger Terminvereinbarung, bei Rückfragen*), the *sein* + *zu* order (*ist … zu überweisen*), the passives (*wird … angepasst*, *können … eingesehen werden*) and the light verb construction (*steht … zur Verfügung*).

### Example 3: Checking the numbers

1. Advance payments: 12 × 210,00 € = 2.520,00 €. Costs: 2.687,40 €. Costs are higher, so it's a *Nachzahlung*: 2.687,40 € − 2.520,00 € = 167,40 €. The letter is right.
2. Is the new advance payment fair? 2.687,40 € ÷ 12 ≈ 223,95 € a month, so 225,00 € roughly matches last year's real costs.
3. Another tenant paid 12 × 160,00 € = 1.920,00 € and her share was 1.812,60 €. Costs are lower, so she has a *Guthaben* of 1.920,00 € − 1.812,60 € = 107,40 €.

Remember the German number format: a comma for decimals and a point for thousands (*2.687,40 €*).

## Common mistakes

- Waiting for the deadline to "start" when the letter arrives late, or calculating it to the last day. Act well within a month of the date on the letter.
- Phoning instead of writing. A call can help you understand, but a *Widerspruch* has to be in writing or *zur Niederschrift*.
- Forgetting the *Aktenzeichen* in a reply. Without it, your letter may take weeks to reach the right desk.
- Reading *ist … zu überweisen* as "is to be transferred (some day)". It's an instruction: you must transfer it.
- Mixing up *Nachzahlung* (you pay) and *Guthaben* (you get money back).
- Reading *i. A.* as a name. It means the person signs on behalf of the office or company.

## Key points

- A *Bescheid* has an *Aktenzeichen*, a decision, a *Begründung* and a *Rechtsbehelfsbelehrung*; read the last one first if you disagree.
- *Widerspruch einlegen*: usually within a month of notification, in writing; quote the *Aktenzeichen*; keep proof.
- Officialese = nominal style (*nach Eingang*, *bei Nichtzahlung*), light verb constructions (*einen Antrag stellen*, *zur Verfügung stellen*), *sein* + *zu* and the passive.
- Learn the abbreviations: *Az., z. Hd., i. A., ggf., bzgl., gem., Abs., Anl.*
- *Nebenkostenabrechnung*: real costs minus advance payments = *Nachzahlung* (positive) or *Guthaben* (negative).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Die Kurzgeschichte: reading a modern short story
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 1 you learned to write stories in the simple past and met the words for books: *der Roman, der Autor, die Figur, die Handlung, das Kapitel*. In lesson 2 the past perfect let you step back in time inside a story. This honors module puts that grammar to work on real reading: literature, history and society. It starts with the most typical German school text of all, the **[[short story]]** (*die Kurzgeschichte*).

Almost every pupil in Germany, Austria and Switzerland reads short stories in class. You'll learn what makes a Kurzgeschichte, read one written for this course, find its turning point and its gaps, and write the standard German school summary, the *Inhaltsangabe*, a skill you can use for any film, report or meeting.

## Where the Kurzgeschichte comes from

The word is a translation of the English "short story". After 1945, young German writers came home to bombed cities and wanted a new, plain way of writing. The language of the Nazi years had been full of big words; they wanted short sentences, everyday language and ordinary people. Many of them admired American writers such as Ernest Hemingway, whose stories were now translated into German.

Their stories about hunger, ruins and soldiers coming home are called **[[rubble literature]]** (*die Trümmerliteratur*; *die Trümmer* = ruins, rubble). Two names you'll meet in every German school book:

- Wolfgang Borchert (1921–1947) wrote his stories in the two years between the end of the war and his early death. In *Das Brot* (written in 1946), an old couple meet in the kitchen at night in a time of hunger; one of them has secretly eaten a slice of bread, and neither says so.
- Heinrich Böll (1917–1985) started with short stories about the war and its aftermath and later wrote novels. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1972.

Today's Kurzgeschichten are about anything, but the form those writers shaped is still what schools teach. (*die Literatur* is literature; *die Erzählung* is a general word for a narrative text, usually longer than a Kurzgeschichte.)

## What makes a Kurzgeschichte

German teachers use a checklist of typical features (*Merkmale*). It's a simplification: many famous stories break one or two of the rules. But it tells you what to look for.

| feature | German term | what it means |
|---|---|---|
| sudden start | *unvermittelter Anfang* | no introduction; we're dropped into the action (*Als Jana aus dem Bus stieg, …* Who is Jana?) |
| open ending | *offener Schluss* | the story stops without telling us how things end |
| turning point | *der Wendepunkt* | one moment changes the situation or what a character understands |
| short time | *kurze erzählte Zeit* | minutes or hours, rarely more than a day |
| few characters | *wenige Figuren* | often two or three ordinary people, sometimes without names |
| everyday language | *Alltagssprache* | short sentences, simple words, a lot of dialogue |
| gaps | *Leerstellen* | important things are not said; the reader has to fill them in |

The **[[open ending]]** and the gaps are why readers argue about short stories. A fairy tale closes every door (*Und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, dann leben sie noch heute*); a Kurzgeschichte leaves them open on purpose. The **[[turning point]]** is usually small: a sentence, a look, an object. Nothing explodes, but afterwards a character sees the world differently.

The difference shows clearly if you draw how the tension (*die Spannung*) rises and falls:

![Tension over time. A grey dashed fairy-tale curve starts at zero, rises and falls back to zero. A blue short-story curve starts halfway up, rises to the turning point, falls a little and stops in the air with a dotted line and a question mark. Labels: unvermittelter Anfang, Hauptteil, Wendepunkt, offener Schluss.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Text: Der Zettel

Read the story first without the translation. It was written for this course.

> Als Jana aus dem Bus stieg, regnete es schon wieder. Sie zog die Kapuze über den Kopf und lief los. Seit drei Wochen ging sie jeden Dienstag nach der Arbeit zu ihrem Vater. Er wohnte immer noch in der Wohnung, in der sie aufgewachsen war, im vierten Stock, ohne Aufzug.
>
> Er öffnete die Tür, bevor sie klingeln konnte. „Du kommst zu spät“, sagte er. Sie kam nicht zu spät. Sie kam wie immer um sechs. Sie trug die Einkaufstasche in die Küche und wollte die Milch in den Kühlschrank stellen. Dort standen schon drei Flaschen Milch, alle ungeöffnet.
>
> „Hast du heute schon gegessen?“, fragte sie.
>
> „Natürlich“, sagte er und setzte sich vor den Fernseher. Der Fernseher war aus.
>
> Auf dem Küchentisch lag ein Zettel. Oben stand in seiner ordentlichen Schrift: *Dienstag kommt Jana. Milch kaufen.* Darunter, etwas schiefer: *Dienstag kommt Jana.* Und ganz unten, kaum noch zu lesen, nur: *Jana.*
>
> Sie las den Zettel zweimal. Dann faltete sie ihn klein zusammen und steckte ihn in ihre Jackentasche. Im Wohnzimmer erzählte ihr Vater von einem Fußballspiel, das sie vor zwanzig Jahren zusammen im Stadion gesehen hatten. Er wusste noch jedes Tor, jeden Namen, sogar das Wetter.
>
> „Papa“, sagte sie, „nächste Woche komme ich schon am Montag. Und am Donnerstag auch.“
>
> Er sah sie an, als hätte sie etwas Seltsames gesagt. Dann lächelte er. „Montag ist gut“, sagte er.
>
> Draußen regnete es weiter. Jana blieb sitzen, bis es dunkel wurde.

In English:

> When Jana got off the bus, it was raining again. She pulled her hood over her head and set off. For three weeks she had been going to her father's every Tuesday after work. He still lived in the flat she had grown up in, on the fourth floor, with no lift.
>
> He opened the door before she could ring. "You're late," he said. She wasn't late. She came at six as always. She carried the shopping bag into the kitchen and was going to put the milk in the fridge. There were already three bottles of milk there, all unopened.
>
> "Have you eaten yet today?" she asked.
>
> "Of course," he said, and sat down in front of the television. The television was off.
>
> On the kitchen table there was a note. At the top, in his neat handwriting: *Tuesday Jana is coming. Buy milk.* Below it, a little more crooked: *Tuesday Jana is coming.* And right at the bottom, hardly readable, just: *Jana.*
>
> She read the note twice. Then she folded it up small and put it in her jacket pocket. In the living room her father talked about a football match they had watched together at the stadium twenty years ago. He still remembered every goal, every name, even the weather.
>
> "Dad," she said, "next week I'll come on Monday. And on Thursday too."
>
> He looked at her as if she had said something strange. Then he smiled. "Monday is good," he said.
>
> Outside it went on raining. Jana stayed sitting there until it got dark.

Words to note: *die Kapuze* (hood), *ungeöffnet* (unopened), *ordentlich* (neat, tidy), *schief* (crooked), *zusammenfalten* (to fold up), *lächeln* (to smile). *als hätte sie etwas Seltsames gesagt* is *als ob* with the verb moved forward (lesson 23): "as if she had said something strange". *etwas Seltsames* is an adjectival noun after *etwas* (lesson 5).

The grammar is the grammar of every written story: the simple past for the events (*stieg, zog, lief, öffnete, las, faltete*), the past perfect for what happened before (*aufgewachsen war, gesehen hatten*), and the perfect only inside the dialogue (*Hast du gegessen?*), because people speak in the perfect.

### Example 1: Finding the features

Go through the checklist with *Der Zettel*.

1. Sudden start: the first sentence names Jana as if we knew her. We learn who she is only bit by bit.
2. Short time and few characters: one evening, two people.
3. Everyday language: short sentences, ordinary words, short dialogue.
4. The turning point: the note. Before it, Jana notices small strange things (the milk, the TV that's off). The note shows her, and us, what they mean. Her reaction comes right after it: she hides the note and decides to come more often.
5. Gaps: the story only hints at the illness (*andeuten*: *Die Geschichte deutet die Krankheit nur an*); the word never appears. Nobody says "Dad is getting forgetful". The reader works it out from three bottles of milk and a name written three times. Why does she put the note in her pocket? To keep it? So that he doesn't see it again? The text doesn't say.
6. Open ending: the last scene (*die Szene*) shows Jana sitting in the dark. Will he remember Monday? What happens next? We don't find out.

Notice that the gaps don't make the story vague: a good Kurzgeschichte is exact about things and silent about feelings.

## Who tells the story?

The **[[narrator]]** (*der Erzähler, die Erzählerin*) is the voice that tells the story. It isn't the same as the author (*der Autor, die Autorin*), the real person who wrote it. Two main types:

- A **[[first-person narrator]]** (*der Ich-Erzähler*) is a character in the story and says *ich*: *Als ich aus dem Bus stieg, regnete es.* We only know what this person knows and thinks.
- A **[[third-person narrator]]** (*der Er-Erzähler / Sie-Erzähler*) talks about the characters as *er* and *sie*: *Als Jana aus dem Bus stieg …*. This narrator can stay close to one character, as in *Der Zettel*, where we see everything through Jana's eyes, or can know everything about everyone.

The perspective (*die Perspektive*) decides what the reader may know: in *Der Zettel* we never learn what the father thinks.

## Writing an Inhaltsangabe

The **[[Inhaltsangabe]]** (summary of the content) is the standard German school summary. It follows strict rules, and teachers mark them:

- Present tense (*Präsens*), even though the story is in the past. The past perfect becomes the perfect: *Sie war hier aufgewachsen* → *Sie ist hier aufgewachsen*.
- No direct speech. Turn quotations into reported speech with *dass* or a verb such as *behaupten, fragen, versprechen* (lesson 26). German schools often expect the Konjunktiv I here (*Er behauptet, sie komme zu spät*), a form you only need to recognize at B1; *dass* + indicative, as in this lesson, is correct German.
- Your own words, short and in order. Leave out details that don't matter.
- No opinion. No *spannend*, no *traurig*, no "I think". Interpretation comes afterwards, in a separate part.
- An introduction sentence with title, author, text type and theme: *In der Kurzgeschichte „…“ von … geht es um …*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How to write an Inhaltsangabe
  accDescr: Seven steps from top to bottom. Read the story twice. Mark the beginning, the turning point and the ending. Write an introduction sentence with title, author, text type and theme. Retell the main events in order in the present tense. Turn direct speech into reported speech. Leave out your own opinion and small details. Finally check the tense and that there are no quotation marks.
  A["Den Text zweimal lesen"] --> B["Anfang, Wendepunkt und Schluss markieren"]
  B --> C["Einleitungssatz: Titel, Autor, Textsorte, Thema"]
  C --> D["Die wichtigsten Ereignisse im Präsens nacherzählen"]
  D --> E["Direkte Rede in indirekte Rede umwandeln"]
  E --> F["Keine eigene Meinung, keine Details"]
  F --> G["Prüfen: Präsens? Keine Anführungszeichen?"]
```

### Example 2: An Inhaltsangabe of Der Zettel

Step 1, the introduction sentence. The theme is not "milk" or "rain"; it's what the story is about underneath:

*In der Kurzgeschichte „Der Zettel“ geht es um eine junge Frau, die merkt, dass ihr Vater immer vergesslicher wird.*

Step 2, the main events in the present tense. Compare the story's sentences with the summary:

| story (past, direct speech) | Inhaltsangabe (present, reported) |
|---|---|
| *Seit drei Wochen ging sie jeden Dienstag zu ihrem Vater.* | *Jana besucht ihren Vater seit einigen Wochen jeden Dienstag.* |
| *„Du kommst zu spät“, sagte er.* | *Er behauptet, dass sie zu spät kommt, obwohl das nicht stimmt.* |
| *Dort standen schon drei Flaschen Milch.* | *Im Kühlschrank findet sie mehrere ungeöffnete Flaschen Milch.* |
| *Auf dem Küchentisch lag ein Zettel …* | *Auf einem Zettel hat ihr Vater immer wieder ihren Namen geschrieben, immer unordentlicher.* |
| *„Nächste Woche komme ich schon am Montag.“* | *Jana steckt den Zettel ein und verspricht, nun öfter zu kommen.* |

Step 3, the ending, without opinion: *Der Vater freut sich darüber. Die Geschichte endet offen.*

Put together, that's a complete Inhaltsangabe of about 70 words, without the rain, the hood, the football match or any word like *traurig*. Note *hat … geschrieben*: what happened earlier is in the perfect.

## Common mistakes

- Writing the Inhaltsangabe in the past: ~~Jana besuchte ihren Vater~~ → *Jana besucht ihren Vater.* Summaries of stories, films and books are in the present.
- Quoting: ~~Er sagt: „Du kommst zu spät.“~~ → *Er behauptet, dass sie zu spät kommt.*
- Giving your opinion in the summary: ~~Die Geschichte ist sehr traurig.~~ That belongs in the interpretation, not the Inhaltsangabe.
- Mixing up narrator and author: in a first-person story, *ich* is the narrator, not necessarily the author.
- Naming the topic instead of the theme: ~~Es geht um Milch und einen Zettel.~~ Say what the story is really about: *Es geht um eine Tochter, die merkt, dass ihr Vater vergesslich wird.*

## Key points

- The Kurzgeschichte grew out of the rubble literature after 1945 (Borchert, Böll), with plain language and ordinary people.
- Typical features: sudden start, open ending, a turning point, a short time, few characters, everyday language and gaps the reader must fill. It's a checklist, not a law.
- The narrator is the voice in the text, not the author: first-person (*ich*) or third-person (*er/sie*).
- An Inhaltsangabe is in the present tense, without quotations or opinions, and starts with title, author, text type and theme.
- Stories use the simple past and past perfect; their dialogue uses the perfect; their summaries use the present and perfect.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Gedichte: reading poems by Eichendorff and Heine
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 13 one of the genitive examples was *Goethes Gedichte*, Goethe's poems. This lesson opens the world of German poetry. (If you did the honors lesson on stories in German A2, you already met Goethe's *Wandrers Nachtlied*; here you go further.) Poems are short, so they're perfect for a learner: you can read one in five minutes and learn it by heart in a week. Both poems in this lesson are among the best known in German.

Poems are also hard in a special way. They use old forms (*hätt'*, *die Lande*), unusual word order and words chosen for their sound. This lesson gives you the tools: the words for talking about a poem, the three common rhyme patterns, and a method for turning poetic German into everyday German. Then you read Joseph von Eichendorff's *Mondnacht* and part of Heinrich Heine's *Die Lore-Ley*. Both are long out of copyright, so you read the original texts.

## Talking about a poem

| German | English | note |
|---|---|---|
| *das Gedicht* | poem | plural *die Gedichte* |
| *der Dichter, die Dichterin* | poet | |
| *die Strophe* | stanza, verse (a group of lines) | |
| *die Zeile, der Vers* | line | |
| *der Reim, sich reimen* | rhyme; to rhyme | *Herz reimt sich auf Schmerz.* |
| *das Reimschema* | rhyme scheme | |
| *die Stimmung* | mood, atmosphere | |
| *auswendig lernen* | to learn by heart | |
| *vortragen* | to recite, perform | *trägt vor, trug vor, hat vorgetragen* |

A **[[stanza]]** (*die Strophe*) is a group of lines, separated from the next group by an empty line. A **[[line]]** of verse is *eine Zeile* or *ein Vers*. Watch out: German *Vers* means one line, while English "verse" often means a whole stanza (as in "the second verse of a song"). For a song's stanza, German says *die Strophe*.

## Three rhyme schemes

To describe how a poem rhymes, give each new rhyme sound a letter: the first is *a*, the next new sound *b*, and so on. Lines that rhyme get the same letter. That pattern is the **[[rhyme scheme]]** (*das Reimschema*). Three schemes are so common that they have names:

- **[[Couplet rhyme]]** (*der Paarreim*), *aabb*: lines rhyme in pairs.
- **[[Alternate rhyme]]** (*der Kreuzreim*), *abab*: every other line rhymes; the rhymes "cross" (*kreuzen*).
- **[[Enclosed rhyme]]** (*der umarmende Reim*), *abba*: one pair of rhymes "embraces" (*umarmt*) another.

![Three columns of four lines each, drawn as bars with the rhyme letter at the end. The first column is labelled Paarreim, a a b b. The second is labelled Kreuzreim, a b a b. The third is labelled umarmender Reim, a b b a. Lines with the same rhyme have the same colour.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A small example of couplet rhyme, written for this course:

> Im Garten blüht der erste Baum,\
> der Winter war ein langer Traum.\
> Die Kinder rennen aus dem Haus,\
> der Frühling ruft: „Kommt alle raus!“

*Baum / Traum* is *a*, *Haus / raus* is *b*: *aabb*. (In the garden the first tree is blooming, the winter was a long dream. The children run out of the house, spring calls: "Everybody come out!")

A rhyme starts at the last stressed vowel: *Nacht* and *sacht* rhyme from the *a* onwards, *Felder* and *Wälder* from the *e* / *ä*.

## Text 1: Eichendorff, Mondnacht

Joseph von Eichendorff (1788–1857) was one of the great poets of German Romanticism, the movement that loved nature, night, longing and the feeling of being far from home. He published *Mondnacht* (Moonlit Night) in 1837, and Robert Schumann set it to music in 1840. The text here is in modern spelling; Eichendorff wrote *geküßt*, *Daß* and *müßt'*.

> Es war, als hätt' der Himmel\
> Die Erde still geküsst,\
> Dass sie im Blütenschimmer\
> Von ihm nun träumen müsst'.
>
> Die Luft ging durch die Felder,\
> Die Ähren wogten sacht,\
> Es rauschten leis die Wälder,\
> So sternklar war die Nacht.
>
> Und meine Seele spannte\
> Weit ihre Flügel aus,\
> Flog durch die stillen Lande,\
> Als flöge sie nach Haus.

A plain translation: *It was as if the sky had quietly kissed the earth, so that, in the shimmer of blossom, she now had to dream of him. The air moved through the fields, the ears of grain swayed gently, the forests rustled softly, so starry-clear was the night. And my soul spread its wings wide, flew through the silent lands, as if it were flying home.*

Words: *der Schimmer* (shimmer, glow), *die Blüte* (blossom), *die Ähre* (ear of grain), *wogen* (to sway, surge like waves), *sacht* (gently), *rauschen* (to rustle, murmur), *die Seele* (soul), *der Flügel* (wing).

Two things to notice first. The grammar you know from lessons 21–23 frames the poem: *als hätt' der Himmel … geküsst* and *als flöge sie* are *als ob* sentences with the verb moved forward, in Konjunktiv II: "as if the sky had kissed", "as if it were flying". The poem opens and closes with a comparison to something unreal. And the poem uses grammatical gender: *der Himmel* is masculine and *die Erde* feminine, so *sie* (she, the earth) dreams *von ihm* (of him, the sky). In English the love story disappears; in German it's built into the articles.

The old and poetic forms are all still understandable (honors lesson 25h2 has more one-word Konjunktiv forms like *flöge*):

| in the poem | everyday German | what happened |
|---|---|---|
| *hätt'* | *hätte* | final *-e* dropped for the rhythm |
| *müsst'* | *müsste* | final *-e* dropped (Konjunktiv II of *müssen*) |
| *leis* | *leise* | final *-e* dropped |
| *flöge* | *würde fliegen* | Konjunktiv II of *fliegen*, today rare in speech |
| *die Lande* | *die Länder, das Land* | old poetic plural of *Land* |
| *nach Haus* | *nach Hause* | final *-e* dropped |

Dropping a sound like this is called **[[elision]]** (*die Elision*); in old texts it's often marked with an apostrophe: *hätt', müsst'*. The *-e* at the end of *nach Hause* and *zu Hause* is an old dative ending that survives in everyday German (also *im Grunde*, *auf dem Lande*); older poems use it much more: *im Walde, dem Manne*. Don't copy these forms into your own e-mails: *flöge* and *die Lande* sound 200 years old.

### Example 1: The rhyme scheme of Mondnacht

Write down the last word of each line and give letters. Stanza 1:

1. *Himmel*: new sound, *a*
2. *geküsst*: new sound, *b*
3. *Blütenschimmer*: *a*? *Himmel* and *Schimmer* share the stressed vowel and the *mm*, but end differently (*-el*, *-er*). This is an **[[impure rhyme]]** (*der unreine Reim*): close enough for the ear, not identical. Count it as *a*.
4. *müsst'*: rhymes with *geküsst*, *b*

Stanza 2: *Felder* / *Wälder* (*e* and *ä* sound the same here, *c*), *sacht* / *Nacht* (*d*). Stanza 3: *spannte* / *Lande* (impure again, *e*), *aus* / *Haus* (*f*).

The scheme is *abab cdcd efef*: three stanzas of alternate rhyme (*Kreuzreim*), four lines each. Rhyme is about sound, not spelling: *Felder* and *Wälder* rhyme perfectly even though one has *e* and the other *ä*.

Now look at lines 9 and 10: *Und meine Seele spannte / Weit ihre Flügel aus*. The sentence doesn't stop at the end of line 9; it runs on into line 10. This is called **[[enjambment]]** (*der Zeilensprung*). Here it even splits a separable verb: *spannte … aus* (from *ausspannen*, to spread out). When you read aloud, don't stop after *spannte*; let the voice carry on, and the wings open with the sentence. What the last line means, a soul longing for a home on earth or in heaven, the poem doesn't say. Many readers hear both; that's interpretation, and you're free to disagree.

## Text 2: Heine, Die Lore-Ley

Heinrich Heine (1797–1856) was born in Düsseldorf into a Jewish family and lived in Paris from 1831 until his death. He wrote *Die Lore-Ley* in 1824, and it became famous through his collection *Buch der Lieder* (Book of Songs, 1827). The Loreley is a steep rock on the Rhine, and its story is a *Sage* (legend) near St. Goarshausen, where the river is narrow and was dangerous for boats. Heine's poem tells of a beautiful woman who sits on the rock, combs her golden hair and sings, and the boatman below looks up at her instead of at the rocks. With a melody by Friedrich Silcher (1837) it became one of the best-known German songs.

The first stanza:

> Ich weiß nicht, was soll es bedeuten,\
> Dass ich so traurig bin;\
> Ein Märchen aus alten Zeiten,\
> Das kommt mir nicht aus dem Sinn.

And the last:

> Ich glaube, die Wellen verschlingen\
> Am Ende Schiffer und Kahn;\
> Und das hat mit ihrem Singen\
> Die Lore-Ley getan.

Translation: *I don't know what it should mean that I am so sad; a tale from olden times won't leave my mind. … I believe the waves in the end swallow up the boatman and his boat; and that is what the Lorelei did with her singing.*

(The spelling is modernised here: Heine wrote *Daß* and *gethan*, as everyone did before the spelling reforms. In 1901 *th* became *t* in words like *tun*; in 1996 *daß* became *dass*.)

Words: *die Welle* (wave), *verschlingen* (to swallow up, devour), *der Schiffer* (boatman), *der Kahn* (small boat), *aus dem Sinn kommen* (to leave one's mind; compare the proverb *Aus den Augen, aus dem Sinn*: out of sight, out of mind).

A small joke hides in the first stanza: the speaker calls the story *ein Märchen aus alten Zeiten*, but the Loreley legend wasn't old at all. The writer Clemens Brentano invented it in a ballad in 1801, only about 20 years before Heine's poem. A story told about the poem is also uncertain: it's often said that during the Nazi era, when Heine's books were banned, songbooks printed *Die Lore-Ley* as by "an unknown poet". Researchers who have searched the school books and anthologies of the time have found little or no evidence for it, so treat it as a legend about a legend.

### Example 2: From poetic word order to everyday German

Poems bend word order for rhythm and rhyme. To understand a line, rewrite it in normal German.

1. *Ich weiß nicht, was soll es bedeuten, dass ich so traurig bin.* An indirect question like *was …* normally sends the verb to the end (lesson 26): *Ich weiß nicht, was es bedeuten soll, dass ich so traurig bin.* Heine keeps main-clause order, which sounds spoken and gives the line its rhythm.
2. *Ein Märchen aus alten Zeiten, das kommt mir nicht aus dem Sinn.* The *das* repeats the subject, as in speech. Everyday: *Ein altes Märchen geht mir nicht aus dem Kopf.*
3. *Und das hat mit ihrem Singen die Lore-Ley getan.* The object *das* stands first, and the subject *die Lore-Ley* comes last, right before the participle, so that the name falls at the end of the poem. Everyday order: *Und die Lore-Ley hat das mit ihrem Singen getan.* Same meaning, but the surprise is gone.

The method for any line: find the verb (or the two parts of the verb), find the subject (who or what?), then put them in the order you'd use in a letter.

## How to read a poem

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How to read a poem in German
  accDescr: Six steps from top to bottom. Read the poem aloud. Ask who is speaking, where and when. Find the stanzas and the rhyme scheme. Rewrite old forms and unusual word order in everyday German. Describe the mood and the images. Finally form your own interpretation.
  A["Das Gedicht laut lesen"] --> B["Wer spricht? Wo? Wann?"]
  B --> C["Strophen und Reimschema finden"]
  C --> D["Alte Formen und Wortstellung in Alltagsdeutsch umschreiben"]
  D --> E["Stimmung und Bilder beschreiben"]
  E --> F["Eine eigene Deutung finden"]
```

Read aloud first, because rhyme and rhythm are sounds, and learn a poem by heart the same way: stanza by stanza, out loud.

## Common mistakes

- *der Vers* is one line, not a stanza. "The second verse of the song" is *die zweite Strophe*.
- Copying old forms into your own writing: ~~Ich hätt' gern Zeit~~ → *Ich hätte gern Zeit.* ~~durch die Lande reisen~~ → *durch das Land reisen.*
- Writing *daß* because you saw it in an old poem. Since 1996 the standard spelling is *dass*.
- Stopping at the end of every line when you read aloud. With enjambment, the sentence goes on.
- *der Dichter* is a poet (or a great writer, in a solemn way); a writer in general is *der Schriftsteller* (lesson 1).
- Rhymes are for the ear: don't look only at the spelling. *Felder* rhymes with *Wälder*.

## Key points

- *das Gedicht, die Strophe* (stanza), *die Zeile / der Vers* (line), *der Reim, das Reimschema*.
- Rhyme schemes: *Paarreim aabb, Kreuzreim abab, umarmender Reim abba*. Give each new sound a new letter.
- Old poetic forms: dropped *-e* (*hätt', leis*), old plurals (*die Lande*), Konjunktiv II forms like *flöge*, dative *-e* (*im Walde*). Understand them; don't use them.
- Poems change word order for rhythm and rhyme. Find verb and subject, then rewrite the line in normal order.
- Eichendorff's *Mondnacht* (1837): *abab cdcd efef*, a comparison in Konjunktiv II, with impure rhymes and enjambment. Heine's *Die Lore-Ley* (1824): a "tale from olden times" that was invented in 1801.

lessons.title: Erinnerungskultur: how Germany remembers
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 2 you met Herr Brandt, who crossed into West Berlin on the night of 9 November 1989, and the words for history: *der Krieg, die Diktatur, die Flucht, der Zeitzeuge*. In lesson 17 you learned the passive in the past (*Die Mauer wurde 1961 gebaut*), and in lesson 13 the genitive. This lesson puts all three together in the texts you'll see in every German town: memorial plaques, memorial days and the small brass stones in the pavement called *Stolpersteine*.

The theme is serious. Germany's way of remembering the crimes of the Nazi era (1933–1945) is a large part of its public life, and a visitor or a new resident meets it everywhere. The language is also special: short, formal and full of passives, because it is about people to whom things were done.

## Erinnerungskultur: remembering in public

*Die Erinnerungskultur*, the **[[culture of remembrance]]**, means all the ways a society remembers its past in public: memorials, memorial days, museums, school lessons, speeches. In Germany the word mostly refers to remembering the Nazi era and the Holocaust (*der Holocaust*, also *die Shoah*), the murder of about six million European Jews, and the persecution (*die Verfolgung*, from *verfolgen*) of Sinti and Roma, political opponents, gay men, people with disabilities and many others. In German you'll read *die Verbrechen des Nationalsozialismus*, the crimes of National Socialism.

A longer word you'll see in newspapers is **[[Vergangenheitsbewältigung]]**: *die Vergangenheit* (the past) + *die Bewältigung* (coping with, mastering, from *bewältigen*). It means coming to terms with the past. Many people now prefer *die Aufarbeitung* (working through), because a past like this can't really be "mastered".

It didn't start at once. A simplified overview:

- In the 1950s West Germany rebuilt, and many people preferred not to talk about the past.
- The Frankfurt Auschwitz trials (1963–1965) put former camp staff in court and in the newspapers.
- Around 1968 a young generation asked their parents what they had done.
- On 8 May 1985 Federal President Richard von Weizsäcker called the end of the war a *Tag der Befreiung*, a day of liberation, for the Germans too. The speech became a turning point in public memory.
- In 2005 the *Denkmal für die ermordeten Juden Europas* (Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe), with its 2,711 concrete blocks, opened in the centre of Berlin.

## Memorial days

A *Gedenktag* is a day of remembrance (*gedenken* = to commemorate). The most important:

| date | what is remembered |
|---|---|
| 27 January | 1945: the Auschwitz camp is liberated by the Soviet army. A German day of remembrance for the victims of National Socialism since 1996, and International Holocaust Remembrance Day (declared by the United Nations in 2005). |
| 8 May | 1945: the war in Europe ends. |
| 3 October | 1990: German reunification, the national holiday (lesson 2). |
| 9 November | the "day of fate" in German history (see below). |

9 November is called *der Schicksalstag* because four turning points fell on it:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Why 9 November is called the day of fate
  accDescr: Four events on 9 November. 1918: the republic is proclaimed in Berlin and the empire ends. 1923: Hitler's failed putsch in Munich. 1938: the November pogroms, when synagogues, Jewish shops and homes are attacked across Germany. 1989: the Berlin Wall falls.
  T["Der 9. November"] --> A["1918: Ausrufung der Republik in Berlin"]
  T --> B["1923: Hitlers Putschversuch in München"]
  T --> C["1938: Novemberpogrome gegen Jüdinnen und Juden"]
  T --> D["1989: Fall der Berliner Mauer"]
```

In the night of 9 to 10 November 1938, synagogues were set on fire across Germany and Austria, Jewish shops and homes were destroyed, and many people were killed or sent to concentration camps. One reason often given for choosing 3 October rather than 9 November as the national holiday is that a day of celebration couldn't fall on the anniversary of the pogroms.

## Stolpersteine: names in the pavement

Walk through almost any German city and look down. In front of some houses there's a small brass plate set into the pavement, 10 by 10 centimetres, on top of a concrete cube. This is a **[[Stolperstein]]**, a "stumbling stone". Each one carries the name of one person who lived there and was persecuted by the Nazis: most of them murdered, some driven out, a few who survived.

The artist Gunter Demnig laid his first stone in front of Cologne's city hall in 1992; stones with individual names followed from the mid-1990s. In May 2023 the 100,000th Stolperstein was laid in Nuremberg, and there are now stones in many European countries. They're placed in front of the last address the person chose freely, and they're paid for by neighbours, school classes, relatives and local groups, who often research the person's life first. Nobody really stumbles: the idea is that you stop, bend down to read, and so bow to the person.

The stones aren't uncontroversial. Munich, for example, doesn't allow them on public ground: Charlotte Knobloch, president of the Jewish community there, and others objected that people would again tread on the victims' names. Since 2018 Munich has used its own *Erinnerungszeichen*, plaques on walls and small steles at eye level. Both sides want the same thing, to remember each person by name; they disagree about how.

![A street scene: a house front with a door and a window, and in the pavement in front of it a small square brass stone. A magnified circle shows the stone's text: HIER WOHNTE / ROSA ADLER / JG. 1903 / DEPORTIERT 1942 / ERMORDET IN / AUSCHWITZ. A note says the name is invented for this course.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1: Reading a Stolperstein

The stone in the picture is invented for this course, but its text follows the real pattern exactly. Inscriptions use **[[telegraphic style]]**: no articles, no auxiliary verbs, only the words that carry the facts. To understand one, rebuild the full sentences.

1. *HIER WOHNTE / ROSA ADLER* → *Hier wohnte Rosa Adler.* A complete sentence in the simple past; *hier* is in position 1, so the verb comes second and the subject third.
2. *JG. 1903* → *JG.* is short for *Jahrgang*, year of birth: *Sie wurde 1903 geboren.*
3. *DEPORTIERT 1942* → a past participle alone. Rosa Adler didn't deport anyone; she was deported. So the full sentence is a passive: *Sie wurde 1942 deportiert.*
4. *ERMORDET IN AUSCHWITZ* → *Sie wurde in Auschwitz ermordet.*

Full text: *Hier wohnte Rosa Adler. Sie wurde 1903 geboren. 1942 wurde sie deportiert und in Auschwitz ermordet.*

Compare a stone for someone who escaped: *HIER WOHNTE / PAUL ADLER / JG. 1928 / FLUCHT 1939 / ENGLAND / ÜBERLEBT*. Here *Flucht* (escape) is a noun, and *überlebt* is a participle of an active verb: *1939 floh er nach England. Er hat überlebt.* The grammar shows who acted: passive for what was done to people, active for what they did themselves.

## Text: Eine Gedenktafel

Plaques on walls tell a longer story. This one, written for this course, hangs on a fictional house in a fictional town:

> In diesem Haus befand sich von 1919 bis 1938 die Druckerei der Familie Adler.
>
> In der Nacht vom 9. auf den 10. November 1938 wurde die Druckerei von SA-Männern zerstört.
>
> Rosa Adler und ihr Bruder Max wurden 1942 deportiert und ermordet.
>
> Ihr Neffe Paul, der 1939 mit einem Kindertransport nach England gekommen war, überlebte als Einziger der Familie.
>
> Wir gedenken ihrer.
>
> Die Bürgerinnen und Bürger der Stadt Neustadt, 2008

In English:

> From 1919 to 1938 this house was the site of the Adler family's printing works.
>
> In the night of 9 to 10 November 1938 the printing works was destroyed by SA men.
>
> Rosa Adler and her brother Max were deported and murdered in 1942.
>
> Their nephew Paul, who had come to England with a Kindertransport in 1939, was the only one of the family to survive.
>
> We remember them.
>
> The citizens of the town of Neustadt, 2008

Background: the SA (*Sturmabteilung*) was the Nazi party's paramilitary force. The *Kindertransporte* of 1938 and 1939 brought about 10,000 mostly Jewish children from Germany, Austria and Czechoslovakia to Britain; most never saw their parents again.

### Example 2: The grammar of a memorial text

Go through the plaque line by line.

1. *befand sich*: *sich befinden* (to be located) is the formal word for *sein* with places. Simple past, because it's a written history text.
2. *wurde … von SA-Männern zerstört*: passive past with the agent in *von* + dative (lesson 17). The building is the subject; the people who destroyed it are added with *von*.
3. *wurden … deportiert und ermordet*: one *wurden* serves both participles.
4. *der … gekommen war*: a relative clause (lesson 11) in the past perfect (lesson 2), because Paul's arrival in England happened before the rest of the story's point, his survival. *als Einziger* = as the only one (an adjectival noun, lesson 5).
5. *Wir gedenken ihrer.*: *gedenken* takes the genitive, which makes it sound solemn. *ihrer* is the genitive of *sie* (them). In everyday German you'd say *Wir erinnern an sie* (we commemorate them) or *Wir denken an sie* (we think of them).

| solemn, written | everyday |
|---|---|
| *Wir gedenken der Opfer.* | *Wir erinnern an die Opfer.* |
| *zum Gedenken an Rosa Adler* | *zur Erinnerung an Rosa Adler* |
| *in stillem Gedenken* | *wir denken an dich* |

Notice the difference between *sich erinnern an* (to remember, privately: *Ich erinnere mich an meine Kindheit*) and *erinnern an* without *sich* (to remind of, or to commemorate in public: *Die Tafel erinnert an die Familie Adler*).

## Remembering the GDR

Germany also remembers its second dictatorship. At the *Gedenkstätte Berliner Mauer* on Bernauer Straße you can see a piece of the Wall with its "death strip" and read about people who died trying to cross. Since 1992 people can apply to read the files that the GDR's secret police, the Stasi, kept on them; many found out that friends or relatives had reported on them. The words of lesson 2 come back here: *die Grenze, die Flucht, der Zeitzeuge, die Wende*.

Austria's story is different again. For decades after 1945, Austria's official view was that it had been Hitler's "first victim" because of the *Anschluss* of 1938. That view was widely questioned from the 1980s, and in 1991 Chancellor Franz Vranitzky acknowledged in parliament that Austrians shared responsibility for the crimes. (A simplified summary of a long debate.)

## Common mistakes

- *gedenken* with the accusative: ~~Wir gedenken die Opfer~~ → *Wir gedenken der Opfer* (genitive). Or use *erinnern an* + accusative.
- Active instead of passive: ~~Rosa Adler deportierte 1942~~ means she deported someone. → *Rosa Adler wurde 1942 deportiert.*
- *das Denkmal* vs *das Mahnmal*: both are monuments, but a *Mahnmal* (from *mahnen*, to warn) warns: it remembers a crime so that it never happens again. A *Denkmal* can also honour a person or a victory.
- *die Gedenkstätte* is a memorial site, often a former camp or prison: *die KZ-Gedenkstätte Dachau*. It isn't a cemetery (*der Friedhof*).
- *jüdisch* (Jewish) is an adjective: *eine jüdische Familie*. For people, *die Juden / die Jüdinnen und Juden* is the normal, respectful word.

## Key points

- *Erinnerungskultur*: how a society remembers in public. In Germany above all the Nazi era and the Holocaust, and also the GDR.
- Memorial days: 27 January, 8 May, 9 November (1918, 1923, 1938, 1989); the national holiday is 3 October.
- *Stolpersteine* carry one name each, in front of the person's last freely chosen home. Their telegraphic style hides passives: *deportiert 1942* = *wurde 1942 deportiert*.
- Memorial texts use the passive past, the past perfect, relative clauses and the genitive: *Wir gedenken der Opfer.*
- *sich erinnern an* = to remember; *erinnern an* = to remind of, commemorate.

lessons.title: Ein Einwanderungsland: migration history and describing statistics
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 5 you learned the words for people in society: *der Ausländer, die Herkunft, die Bevölkerung, die Mehrheit, die Minderheit*. Lesson 20 added *die Integration* and the nominal style of the news, and lesson 19 the phrases for giving opinions. This last honors lesson uses all of them on one of the big topics of German society: migration. About one person in four in Germany today immigrated or has two parents who did.

You'll learn the main stages of that history, from the "guest workers" of the 1950s to today's citizenship law, and a skill that every B1 and B2 exam and every newspaper reader needs: describing a chart (*eine Grafik beschreiben*) with the right verbs, prepositions and numbers, including the difference between per cent and percentage points.

## From emigration to immigration

For a long time Germans were emigrants (lesson 21's *auswandern*), not immigrants (*einwandern, der Einwanderer, die Einwanderin*); *die Migration* covers both directions. In the 19th century millions left for America. After the Second World War about 12 million refugees and expellees (*Flüchtlinge und Vertriebene*), Germans from the former eastern territories and from Eastern Europe, had to find a new home in the two German states. Then West Germany's economic boom (*das Wirtschaftswunder*) ran short of workers.

### The "guest workers"

In 1955 West Germany signed its first **[[recruitment agreement]]** (*das Anwerbeabkommen*) with Italy. Agreements with Spain and Greece (1960), Turkey (1961), Morocco (1963), Portugal (1964), Tunisia (1965) and Yugoslavia (1968) followed. The workers were called *Gastarbeiter*, **[[guest workers]]**, and the word says what everyone expected: guests go home. Many did. Of roughly 14 million people who came to work in West Germany until 1973, about 11 million returned. In 1964 the Portuguese worker Armando Rodrigues de Sá was welcomed at Cologne-Deutz station as the millionth guest worker and given a moped.

In November 1973, during the oil crisis, the government stopped recruitment (*der Anwerbestopp*). But many workers who had stayed now brought their families, because leaving meant they could never come back. Temporary workers had become immigrants. The Swiss writer Max Frisch summed up the same thing in Switzerland in 1965: *„Man hat Arbeitskräfte gerufen, und es kommen Menschen.“* — "We called for workers, and people are coming."

East Germany had its own *Vertragsarbeiter* (contract workers), mostly from Vietnam, Mozambique and other socialist countries, who often lived apart from Germans in hostels and were expected to leave after a few years.

### After 1990

Since reunification, people have come for very different reasons: ethnic Germans from the former Soviet Union (*Spätaussiedler*), refugees from the wars in Yugoslavia in the 1990s, EU citizens who can live and work anywhere in the EU, refugees from Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq above all in 2015 and 2016, and over a million people from Ukraine after 2022.

The law changed slowly. Only in 2000 did children born in Germany to foreign parents get the right to German citizenship (if one parent had lived there legally for eight years). The first law that openly called itself an immigration law came into force in 2005. The reform of 2024 allowed **[[naturalisation]]** (*die Einbürgerung*) after five years instead of eight and generally allowed dual citizenship; a faster route after three years, added in the same reform, was abolished again in 2025. Laws like these change often, so always check the current rules.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Stages of migration to Germany since 1945
  accDescr: A timeline from top to bottom. 1945 to 1950: about 12 million refugees and expellees. 1955: the first recruitment agreement, with Italy. 1961: agreement with Turkey. 1973: recruitment stop, families follow. 1990s: Spätaussiedler and refugees from Yugoslavia. 2000: children born in Germany can become citizens. 2005: first immigration law. 2015 and 2016: many refugees from Syria and other countries. 2022: refugees from Ukraine. 2024: naturalisation after five years.
  A["1945–1950: Flüchtlinge und Vertriebene"] --> B["1955: Anwerbeabkommen mit Italien"]
  B --> C["1961: Abkommen mit der Türkei"]
  C --> D["1973: Anwerbestopp, Familien kommen nach"]
  D --> E["1990er: Spätaussiedler, Flüchtlinge aus Jugoslawien"]
  E --> F["2000: neues Staatsangehörigkeitsrecht"]
  F --> G["2005: Zuwanderungsgesetz"]
  G --> H["2015/16: viele Geflüchtete aus Syrien und anderen Ländern"]
  H --> I["2022: Geflüchtete aus der Ukraine"]
  I --> J["2024: Einbürgerung nach fünf Jahren"]
```

## Counting: Ausländer or Einwanderungsgeschichte?

Statistics use several groups, and newspapers mix them up:

- *Ausländer* (lesson 5): people without German citizenship. Many were born in Germany; many immigrants aren't in this group, because they have become German.
- *Menschen mit Migrationshintergrund*: the older statistical term: people who weren't born German citizens or have at least one parent who wasn't.
- *Menschen mit Einwanderungsgeschichte*: the measure the Federal Statistical Office now puts first: people who immigrated since 1950 themselves, or whose two parents did. In 2024 that was about 21.2 million people, 25.6 % of the population, according to its first results.

The same country can therefore have "about 15 % foreigners" and "about a quarter with an immigration history" at the same time. Before you compare two numbers, check that they count the same group.

## Describing a chart

At B1 and B2, exams and courses ask you to describe a chart. The structure is always the same: what the chart shows and where it comes from, the main trend, details, and a short conclusion. The chart below was invented for this lesson.

![A bar chart titled Anteil der Einwohner mit Einwanderungsgeschichte in Neustadt, in Prozent. Four bars: 2000: 12 per cent, 2008: 15 per cent, 2016: 20 per cent, 2024: 24 per cent. The vertical axis runs from 0 to 30 per cent. At the bottom: Quelle: Stadt Neustadt (Zahlen erfunden).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Phrases for each part:

| part | phrases |
|---|---|
| introduction | *Die Grafik zeigt …* · *Das Säulendiagramm stellt dar, wie …* · *Die Zahlen stammen von …* · *laut* + dative / genitive: *laut der Stadt Neustadt* |
| going up | *steigen (ist gestiegen)* · *zunehmen* · *der Anstieg* · *sich verdoppeln* |
| going down | *sinken (ist gesunken)* · *zurückgehen* · *abnehmen* · *der Rückgang* |
| no change | *gleich bleiben* · *stabil bleiben* |
| how much | *von 12 auf 24 Prozent* (from … to …) · *um 12 Prozentpunkte* (by …) |
| size | *knapp* (just under) · *rund, etwa* (about) · *über, mehr als* · *fast* · *jeder Vierte* (one in four) · *ein Drittel, die Hälfte* |
| conclusion | *Insgesamt kann man sagen, dass …* · *Zusammenfassend …* |

The two prepositions matter: *auf* gives the new value, *um* gives the difference. *Der Anteil stieg von 20 auf 24 Prozent* = it ended at 24. *Der Anteil stieg um 4 Prozentpunkte* = it grew by 4.

### Example 1: Describing the Neustadt chart

1. Introduction: *Das Säulendiagramm zeigt, wie sich der Anteil der Einwohner mit Einwanderungsgeschichte in Neustadt zwischen 2000 und 2024 entwickelt hat. Die Zahlen stammen von der Stadt Neustadt.*
2. Main trend: *Der Anteil ist in diesem Zeitraum stark gestiegen: von 12 auf 24 Prozent. Er hat sich also verdoppelt.*
3. Details: *Den stärksten Anstieg gab es zwischen 2008 und 2016, nämlich um 5 Prozentpunkte. Heute hat etwa jeder vierte Einwohner eine Einwanderungsgeschichte.*
4. Conclusion: *Insgesamt zeigt die Grafik, dass Neustadt immer vielfältiger wird.* (*vielfältig* = diverse; *die Vielfalt* = diversity; a set of numbers like this is *eine Statistik*.)

Check the numbers before you write: 12 → 15 is +3 points, 15 → 20 is +5, 20 → 24 is +4. So the biggest jump really is 2008–2016. 24 % is just under 25 %, so "about one in four" (*etwa jeder Vierte*) is right, and *knapp ein Viertel* (just under a quarter) would be even more exact.

## Per cent and percentage points

When a share changes, there are two ways to measure the change, and German, like English, has two words.

- A **[[percentage point]]** (*der Prozentpunkt*) is the plain difference between two percentages: from 20 % to 24 % is 4 percentage points.
- A change in *per cent* (*Prozent*) compares the difference with the old value: 4 is one fifth of 20, so the share grew by 20 per cent.

### Example 2: Points or per cent?

A newspaper writes: *Die Partei steigt in der Umfrage von 10 auf 12 Prozent.*

1. Difference: 12 − 10 = 2. The party gained *2 Prozentpunkte*.
2. Compared with the old value: 2 ÷ 10 = 0.2, so its support grew *um 20 Prozent*.
3. Both sentences are true. *Die Partei legt um 2 Prozent zu* would be wrong: it confuses the two.

Now the chart: from 2000 to 2024 the share rose by 12 percentage points (24 − 12). Compared with 12 %, that's an increase of 100 per cent (12 ÷ 12 = 1), which is just another way of saying it doubled. Between 2016 and 2024 it rose by 4 points, that is by 20 per cent (4 ÷ 20). Headlines that want a big number choose per cent; careful writers say which one they mean.

## Common mistakes

- *Prozent* has no plural after a number: ~~25 Prozente~~ → *25 Prozent*. With a plural noun after it, the verb is usually plural: *25 Prozent der Einwohner haben …*
- *auf* and *um* mixed up: ~~Der Anteil stieg um 24 Prozent~~ when you mean it ended at 24 → *stieg auf 24 Prozent*.
- *steigen* and *sinken* take *sein* in the perfect: *Der Anteil ist gestiegen*, not ~~hat gestiegen~~.
- *Die Grafik sagt …* sounds odd. Charts *zeigen* or *stellen dar*.
- Treating *Ausländer* and *Einwanderer* as the same: many foreigners were born in Germany, and many immigrants are German citizens.
- *Gastarbeiter* is a historical term. Use it for the 1955–1973 period, often in quotation marks; today people say *ausländische Arbeitskräfte* or *Fachkräfte aus dem Ausland*.

## Key points

- Germany became a country of immigration in stages: refugees after 1945, guest workers from 1955, the recruitment stop of 1973 and family reunification, migration after 1990, and new citizenship laws in 2000, 2005 and 2024.
- Check what a statistic counts: *Ausländer*, *Migrationshintergrund* and *Einwanderungsgeschichte* are different groups.
- To describe a chart: introduction with source, main trend, details, conclusion.
- *von … auf* = from … to; *um* = by. *steigen, sinken* take *sein*.
- Percentage points are the plain difference between two percentages; per cent compares the change with the old value.
