questions.stem: Finish the sentence "Im Brief steht, …" to say "that the application must be submitted". Put the words in order.
questions.explanation: In a subordinate clause the conjugated modal goes to the very end, so the chain is participle, werden, modal: "eingereicht werden muss". In a main clause the modal is the first verb; in a subordinate clause it is the last.

questions.stem: Match each sign or notice to the sentence with the same meaning.

image.alt: Three signs. A blue sign: Hunde sind an der Leine zu führen. A red sign: Betreten der Baustelle verboten! Eltern haften für ihre Kinder. A green sign: Bitte den Rasen nicht betreten. Die Stadtverwaltung.

left: Hunde sind an der Leine zu führen.
Das Problem ist leicht zu lösen.
choices: Hunde müssen an der Leine geführt werden.
Das Problem kann leicht gelöst werden.
Der Rasen darf nicht betreten werden.
Der Rasen muss nicht betreten werden.
Das Problem muss leicht gelöst werden.
questions.explanation: sein + zu in a rule means "must" (Hunde sind … zu führen, Der Ausweis ist vorzulegen); with leicht it means "can" (ist leicht zu lösen). A ban needs darf nicht; "muss nicht betreten werden" would mean nobody has to walk on the grass.

questions.stem: Which sentences say that something is forbidden? Select all that apply.
choices: Der Rasen darf nicht betreten werden.
Der Antrag muss nicht persönlich abgegeben werden.
Rauchen ist in allen öffentlichen Gebäuden verboten.
Hier dürfen keine Fahrräder abgestellt werden.
Die Gebühr kann bar bezahlt werden.
questions.explanation: darf nicht / dürfen keine and verboten express a ban. "muss nicht" only means it isn't necessary (you don't have to hand it in in person), and "kann bar bezahlt werden" is a possibility.

questions.stem: Complete with a -bar adjective: "Man kann den Pilz essen. Er ist ___." "Man kann die Schrift nicht lesen. Sie ist ___." (der Pilz: mushroom)
questions.explanation: -bar means "can be …-ed": essbar (edible) = kann gegessen werden. un- makes it negative: unlesbar (illegible) = kann nicht gelesen werden.

questions.stem: Complete with a da- or wo-compound: "___ wartest du?" – "Auf den Bus." / "Ich bin ___, dass wir mehr Datenschutz brauchen." (in favour of it)
questions.explanation: warten auf + a thing: the question is "Worauf?", with r because auf starts with a vowel. "in favour of" is für, and before a dass-clause the forward-pointing da-word is "dafür" (no r: für starts with a consonant).

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this social media post.

image.alt: A social media post without labels: a profile picture and the name Tina_Wahrheit, the text of the post, a link box with a source, a row of buttons including Teilen, and a comment by Max B. Five parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 is the profile of the person posting (das Profil), 2 the post itself (der Beitrag), 3 the link with its source (die Quelle), 4 the share button (Teilen) and 5 a comment (der Kommentar). Privacy and data protection are ideas, not parts of the screen.

questions.stem: Match each phrase to what it does in a discussion.
left: Da hast du zwar recht, aber …
questions.explanation: zustimmen = agree; "Das sehe ich anders" and "widersprechen" disagree; "zwar …, aber" grants a point and then objects; "Meiner Ansicht nach" introduces your view; "Was hältst du davon?" asks for the other person's view.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Ich halte das als eine gute Idee.
Es kommt darauf an, ob die Quelle glaubwürdig ist.
questions.explanation: For a person you use preposition + wen (Über wen?), for a thing a wo-word (Worüber?). "Es kommt darauf an, ob …" is the fixed phrase. It is "halten für" (Ich halte das für eine gute Idee), and widersprechen takes the dative: "Ich widerspreche dir".

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "I'm looking forward to seeing you." The capitalised word comes first.
questions.explanation: sich freuen auf + a zu-infinitive: the da-word "darauf" stays in the main clause and points ahead to "dich zu sehen". (In writing, a comma goes after darauf.)

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this diagram of how Germany is governed.

image.alt: A diagram of the German federal system without names. Box 1: Staatsoberhaupt; it appoints box 2: Bundeskanzler(in), Ministerinnen und Minister. Box 3: 630 Abgeordnete; it elects the Chancellor. Box 4: Mitglieder der 16 Landesregierungen, sent by the 16 Bundesländer. Box 5: ab 18 Jahren; these people elect box 3.

questions.explanation: The head of state is the Federal President (1), who appoints the federal government (2: the Chancellor and the ministers). The Bundestag (3) has 630 members and elects the Chancellor; it is elected by the voters (5), from the age of 18. The Bundesrat (4) is made up of members of the 16 state governments.

questions.stem: Match each noun to the verb it comes from.
questions.explanation: Most nouns of nominal style end in -ung (einführen → die Einführung, erhöhen → die Erhöhung, abschaffen → die Abschaffung); some are short forms of the verb (wählen → die Wahl, beschließen → der Beschluss). entscheiden gives die Entscheidung and regieren die Regierung.

questions.stem: Complete with infinitives: in an election you ___ people and parties; in parliament, people ___ über a question.
questions.explanation: wählen is for elections and people (Wen hast du gewählt?); for a yes/no decision on a question German uses abstimmen über: Im Parlament wird über das Gesetz abgestimmt.

questions.stem: Which statements about Germany are true, according to the lesson? Select all that apply.
choices: The Bundestag is elected every four years.
The Chancellor is the head of state.
With the second vote you vote for a party.
The voting age for the Bundestag is 16.
questions.explanation: The Bundestag is elected every four years, the second vote goes to a party and decides the seats, and the Bundestag elects the Chancellor. The head of state is the Federal President, and the voting age for the Bundestag is 18 (16 for European elections and some state and local elections).

questions.stem: Put the three passes for reading a long news sentence in order, from the lesson's method.
choices: Find the main clause and its verb
Spot the passive and the genitive
questions.explanation: First strip the sentence down to its main clause, then see what each relative clause describes, then decode the passive (wird / wurde + participle) and the genitive (des / der), and finally put it all together.

questions.stem: Complete: "Seit 2023 ___ das Rauchen in unserem Stadtpark verboten."
questions.explanation: "Seit 2023" describes a situation that still lasts, so you need the state passive: sein + participle, "ist verboten". "wurde verboten" would be the action at one moment (2023 wurde das Rauchen verboten), "wird verboten" the action happening now, and the passive is never formed with haben.

questions.stem: Which sentence describes the action of passing the law, not the state afterwards?
choices: Das Gesetz wurde am Donnerstag verabschiedet.
Das Gesetz ist seit Mai verabschiedet.
questions.explanation: wurde + participle with a point in time (am Donnerstag) is the event: the vote happened on Thursday. The other three use sein + participle, the state passive: the law is (or was already) passed.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the passive of "Der Bundestag stimmte dem Gesetz zu."?
choices: Das Gesetz wurde vom Bundestag zugestimmt.
Dem Gesetz wurde vom Bundestag zugestimmt.
Dem Gesetz wurden vom Bundestag zugestimmt.
Dem Gesetz ist vom Bundestag zugestimmt.
questions.explanation: zustimmen takes the dative, and only an accusative object can become a passive subject. So "dem Gesetz" stays dative, there is no subject, and the verb is singular: "wurde zugestimmt". "Das Gesetz wurde zugestimmt" turns the dative into a nominative, "wurden" is plural for no reason, and "ist zugestimmt" is neither the Präteritum nor the Perfekt passive (that would be "ist zugestimmt worden").

questions.stem: Complete: "Den Flutopfern ___ schnell geholfen." (die Flutopfer: flood victims)
questions.explanation: helfen takes the dative, so "den Flutopfern" is not the subject. A passive without a subject always has the er/sie/es form: "wird geholfen", even though the dative noun is plural.

questions.stem: Complete with the present passive of "abstimmen": "Im März ___ über das Gesetz ___."
questions.explanation: abstimmen über has no accusative object, so the passive has no subject: "wird … abgestimmt", singular. The prepositional phrase "über das Gesetz" stays as it is. No es, because "Im März" is in position 1.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Es wird im Bundestag über das Gesetz abgestimmt.
Im Bundestag es wird über das Gesetz abgestimmt.
Im Bundestag wird es über das Gesetz abgestimmt.
Im Bundestag werden über das Gesetz abgestimmt.
questions.explanation: In a passive without a subject, es only fills an empty position 1: "Es wird … abgestimmt". When "Im Bundestag" is in position 1, es disappears: "Im Bundestag wird über das Gesetz abgestimmt". The verb is always singular, and it must be in position 2.

questions.stem: Rewrite "Das Problem kann leicht gelöst werden." with sich lassen: "Das Problem ___ ___ leicht lösen."
questions.explanation: sich lassen + infinitive means "can be done". lassen agrees with the subject (das Problem: lässt), sich follows, and the infinitive goes to the end: "Das Problem lässt sich leicht lösen."

questions.stem: Which sentences mean "The windows can't be opened"? Select all that apply.
choices: Die Fenster lassen sich nicht öffnen.
Die Fenster können nicht geöffnet werden.
Die Fenster müssen nicht geöffnet werden.
Man kann die Fenster nicht öffnen.
questions.explanation: sich lassen, the modal passive with können and man + können all mean "can't be opened". "müssen nicht" means it isn't necessary to open them, and "lassen nicht öffnen" is missing sich.

questions.stem: Article 76 of the Basic Law says: "Vorlagen der Bundesregierung sind zunächst dem Bundesrat zuzuleiten." What does it mean?
choices: Government bills can first be sent to the Bundesrat.
Government bills must first be sent to the Bundesrat.
Government bills were first sent to the Bundesrat.
Government bills need not be sent to the Bundesrat.
questions.explanation: "sind … zuzuleiten" is sein + zu. In a rule, without a word like leicht or kaum, it means "must": müssen zugeleitet werden. It is present tense, and it is an obligation, not a possibility.

questions.stem: Put the stages of a government bill in order.
choices: The Bundesrat comments on the bill
Second and third reading, final vote
The Bundesrat deals with the passed law
questions.explanation: A government bill goes to the Bundesrat for comment first, then to the Bundestag: first reading, committee, second and third reading with the final vote. Then the Bundesrat deals with it; after the countersignature the Federal President signs it, and it is published in the Bundesgesetzblatt.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: "to pass a law" is verabschieden, and "coalition" is die Koalition.

questions.stem: A federal law does not name the day it comes into force. When does it come into force?
choices: On the day the Bundestag passes it
On the day the Federal President signs it
14 days after it appears in the Bundesgesetzblatt
On the first day of the following month
questions.explanation: Article 82 of the Basic Law: if a law sets no date, it comes into force on the fourteenth day after the issue of the Bundesgesetzblatt that contains it appeared. Passing and signing are earlier steps.

questions.stem: A politician says: "Es wurden Fehler gemacht." What does this passive leave out?
questions.explanation: The passive without von hides the doer. "Es wurden Fehler gemacht" admits mistakes but names nobody; a careful listener asks "Von wem?"

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Es wurde beschlossen, dass die Bibliothek länger geöffnet bleibt.
Den Experten ist für ihre Hilfe gedankt worden.
questions.explanation: widersprechen and danken take the dative, which stays in the passive: "Der Ministerin wurde widersprochen", "Den Experten ist … gedankt worden". "Es wurde beschlossen, dass …" is correct with es in position 1. "Die Ministerin" wrongly makes the dative a subject, and a subjectless passive is singular: "Den Bürgern wird geholfen".

questions.stem: Complete: "___ Studie zufolge schlafen Jugendliche zu wenig."
questions.explanation: zufolge comes after its noun, which is in the dative: "einer Studie zufolge" (die Studie, dative einer). "Eine" is nominative or accusative, "Einen" masculine accusative, "Eines" genitive.

questions.stem: What does "Der Täter soll etwa 30 Jahre alt sein." mean?
choices: The offender is said to be about 30.
The offender claims to be about 30.
The offender wants to be about 30.
questions.explanation: In news reports, sollen often passes on what others say without confirming it: "is said to be". "claims to be" would be wollen, about the offender's own claim.

questions.stem: What does "Der Fahrer will das Rotlicht nicht gesehen haben." mean?
choices: The driver didn't want to see the red light.
The driver is said not to have seen the red light.
The driver will not have seen the red light.
The driver claims not to have seen the red light.
questions.explanation: wollen + perfect infinitive (gesehen haben) is a claim the subject makes about himself, and the speaker has doubts. "is said to" would be sollen, and "will" in German is not the English future.

questions.stem: Complete with the perfect infinitive of "fahren": "Sie soll nach Spanien ___ ___." (She is said to have gone to Spain.)
questions.explanation: The perfect infinitive is participle + haben or sein, exactly as in the Perfekt. fahren (to a place) takes sein: "sie ist gefahren", so "gefahren sein".

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "He is said to have driven too fast." The capitalised word comes first.
questions.explanation: sollen is in position 2, and the perfect infinitive "gefahren sein" goes to the end, participle first.

questions.stem: Match each adverb to its meaning.
questions.explanation: From most to least certain: tatsächlich, offenbar, anscheinend, vermutlich, angeblich. scheinbar says something only looks true. "hopefully" is hoffentlich.

questions.stem: In careful German, what does "Der Bus ist scheinbar pünktlich." say?
choices: The bus looks punctual, but it isn't.
The bus is probably on time.
The bus is definitely on time.
The bus is said to be on time.
questions.explanation: scheinbar means "only seemingly". "Probably on time" would be anscheinend (many people use scheinbar this way in speech, but careful writing keeps them apart). "Definitely" would be tatsächlich, and "is said to be" would be soll … sein.

questions.stem: A report says: "Ein Sprecher sagte, die Lage sei ruhig." Why does it use "sei"?
choices: It is the past tense of sein.
It shows that the newspaper agrees.
It shows that someone's words are being reported.
questions.explanation: sei is the Konjunktiv I of sein, the verb form of reported speech in written German. It passes on what the spokesman said without the paper confirming it. The past tense of sein is war.

questions.stem: Which of these name a source of information? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: laut, nach Angaben, zufolge and a wie-clause with a verb like mitteilen all say where information comes from. "trotz des Regens" means "despite the rain".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Wie die Polizei mitteilte, niemand wurde verletzt.
Wie mitteilte die Polizei, wurde niemand verletzt.
Wie die Polizei mitteilte, wurde niemand verletzt.
Wie die Polizei mitteilte, verletzt wurde niemand.
questions.explanation: In the wie-clause the verb goes to the end (mitteilte). The whole clause is position 1 of the sentence, so the conjugated verb of the main clause comes right after the comma: "wurde niemand verletzt".

questions.stem: Put the steps of the lesson's method for checking a claim in order.
choices: Ask who says it and look for an Impressum
Check the date and the photo
questions.explanation: First the source, then other sources, then the details (date, photo); only when everything checks out do you share it. If you're not sure, don't.

questions.stem: Read: "Nach Angaben der Stadt wurde der Beitrag über 1.200-mal geteilt. Er soll zuerst auf einer Webseite ohne Impressum erschienen sein." Which statement is right?
choices: The town confirms that the post first appeared on a site without an Impressum.
The newspaper itself counted how often the post was shared.
It is reported, but not confirmed, that the post first appeared on a site without an Impressum.
The town shared the post more than 1,200 times.
questions.explanation: "soll … erschienen sein" is hearsay: the newspaper passes it on without confirming it. The figure of 1,200 shares comes from the town (nach Angaben der Stadt), not from the newspaper, and the town didn't share the post; it was shared that often.

questions.stem: Where does the sentence "Eine Zensur findet nicht statt." come from?
choices: the press code of the German Press Council
a ruling of a German court
the rules of procedure of the Bundestag
questions.explanation: It is part of Article 5 of the Basic Law, which protects freedom of expression and of the press. The Press Council's code contains rules for journalists, such as checking facts and correcting mistakes.

questions.stem: "seriös" means reputable, trustworthy. Which German adjective means "serious" in the sense of "not joking"? ___
questions.explanation: seriös is a false friend: eine seriöse Zeitung is a reputable newspaper. "Are you serious?" is "Meinst du das ernst?"

questions.stem: Complete with the Konjunktiv II: "Wenn ich mehr Geld ___ (haben), ___ (sein) ich glücklicher."
questions.explanation: Wenn ich mehr Geld hätte, wäre ich glücklicher. haben and sein have their own one-word forms, hätte and wäre, which are used instead of würde haben and würde sein. After the wenn clause the main clause starts with its verb: wäre ich.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its one-word Konjunktiv II form (er/sie/es).
questions.explanation: The recipe is simple past stem + umlaut + -e: kam → käme, gab → gäbe, fand → fände. wissen (wusste) and the modal können (konnte) also take the umlaut: wüsste, könnte. kamte and wisste are not German forms.

questions.stem: Which sentences are unreal conditions (the speaker is only imagining)? Select all that apply.
choices: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich kommen.
Wenn ich Zeit habe, komme ich.
Hätte ich ein Auto, würde ich dich abholen.
Wäre das Wetter besser, könnten wir draußen essen.
Wenn es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.
questions.explanation: Unreal conditions use the Konjunktiv II in both clauses: hätte … würde, Hätte … würde (without wenn, verb first), Wäre … könnten. "Wenn ich Zeit habe, komme ich" and "Wenn es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause" are in the indicative: real conditions that may well come true.

questions.stem: What is the job of each numbered word in this unreal condition?

image.alt: The sentence Wenn ich mehr Zeit hätte, würde ich öfter kochen in boxes, with a bracket over the wenn clause marked position 1. Five words are numbered: Wenn, hätte, würde, the second ich and kochen.

questions.explanation: 1 Wenn is the conjunction that sends its verb to the end. 2 hätte is the Konjunktiv II verb at the end of the wenn clause. The whole wenn clause is position 1, so 3 würde, the conjugated verb, comes next, then 4 the subject ich. 5 kochen is the infinitive at the end, completing würde. There is no past participle or separable prefix in this sentence.

questions.stem: Put the parts in order to say "If I had more time, I would travel more often." Start with the wenn clause.
questions.explanation: Wenn ich mehr Zeit hätte, würde ich öfter reisen. The wenn clause fills position 1, so würde comes straight after the comma, then the subject ich, and the infinitive reisen goes to the end.

questions.stem: Complete with hätte or wäre in the right form: "Wenn wir früher losgefahren ___, ___ wir den Zug nicht verpasst."
questions.explanation: Wenn wir früher losgefahren wären, hätten wir den Zug nicht verpasst. losfahren forms its perfect with sein (wir sind losgefahren), so wären; verpassen takes haben (wir haben verpasst), so hätten. The subject is wir, so both need the -en ending.

questions.stem: Markus's story from the lesson: put each sentence on the right path. The left path is what really happened; the right path is what would have happened if he had been on time.

image.alt: Two paths starting from the box Montag, 7.58 Uhr: Der Zug fährt ab. The left path is headed Was wirklich passiert ist (Indikativ) and ends with Heute sind sie verheiratet. The dashed right path is headed Was passiert wäre (Konjunktiv II) and ends with Er wäre in Hamburg geblieben. The first two boxes of each path are empty and numbered 1 to 4.

questions.explanation: The real path uses the perfect: first he missed the train (1), then he met Lena (2), and today they are married. The imagined path uses hätte + participle: he would have taken the train (3), would never have met Lena (4) and would have stayed in Hamburg. "Er würde den Zug verpasst" is not German (würde needs an infinitive), and "Er hat Lena nie kennengelernt" is false: he did meet her.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Wenn ich das gewusst habe, wäre ich gekommen.
questions.explanation: "Ich wäre fast gefallen" (fallen takes sein), "Du hättest mich anrufen können" and "Ich hätte früher losfahren sollen" (double infinitive, always hätte) are correct. gehen takes sein, so it must be "Ich wäre nach Hause gegangen". An unreal wenn clause needs the Konjunktiv too: "Wenn ich das gewusst hätte, …".

questions.stem: Match each sentence to what it expresses.
left: Wenn ich das gewusst hätte, wäre ich gekommen.
choices: a regret about my own mistake
an unreal condition in the past
a real plan for the future
questions.explanation: hätte … sollen about yourself is a regret; hätte … können said to someone else is a reproach; wäre beinahe / fast + participle describes a near miss; wenn … hätte, wäre … is an unreal past condition. None of them is a real plan: they are all about an imagined past.

questions.stem: Put the parts in order to say "If I hadn't partied so long yesterday, I wouldn't be so tired now."
questions.explanation: Wenn ich gestern nicht so lange gefeiert hätte, wäre ich jetzt nicht so müde. The condition is about the past (hätte + participle, hätte last in the wenn clause); the result is about now (present Konjunktiv wäre). After the wenn clause the verb wäre comes first, then ich.

questions.stem: Write the wish with the verb first: "___ ich doch mutiger!" (If only I were braver! — sein)
questions.explanation: Wäre ich doch mutiger! An unreal wish can drop wenn and put the Konjunktiv II verb first. The particle doch (or nur, bloß) makes it a wish. The indicative bin would be wrong here: the speaker isn't brave.

questions.stem: Put the requests in order from the most direct to the most polite.
choices: Können Sie bitte das Fenster schließen?
Könnten Sie bitte das Fenster schließen?
Wären Sie so nett, das Fenster zu schließen?
questions.explanation: The imperative is the most direct. A question with können is polite; the Konjunktiv II könnten is more polite; Wären Sie so nett, … zu …? is very polite.

questions.stem: Which sentences give advice for now, not a reproach about the past? Select all that apply.
choices: An deiner Stelle würde ich kündigen.
Du hättest mit ihr reden sollen.
Wie wäre es mit einem Spaziergang?
questions.explanation: solltest, An deiner Stelle würde ich … and Wie wäre es mit …? are advice the listener can still follow. "Du hättest mit ihr reden sollen" and "Du hättest mich fragen können" use the past subjunctive: it's too late, so they are reproaches.

questions.stem: Match each beginning to the ending that completes it correctly.
left: Er tut so, als ob er krank
questions.explanation: An unreal wish needs the Konjunktiv II: hätte, not habe. An deiner Stelle fills position 1, so the verb comes next: würde ich warten (not ich würde). Würde es Ihnen etwas ausmachen takes a zu infinitive. After als ob, the Konjunktiv II verb goes to the end: als ob er krank wäre.

questions.stem: Complete with the right form of "wünschen": "Ich ___, du wärst hier." (I wish you were here.)
questions.explanation: Ich wünschte, du wärst hier. For an unreal wish, wünschen itself is in the Konjunktiv II: wünschte. "Ich wünsche dir …" is for good wishes (Ich wünsche dir viel Glück), not for wishing that something were different.

questions.stem: Match each word to its fixed preposition.
questions.explanation: stolz auf + A, zufrieden mit + D, abhängen von + D, sich sorgen um + A, das Interesse an + D. aus belongs to bestehen aus and nach to sich sehnen nach.

questions.stem: Complete both sentences with the same preposition: "Ich habe mich schnell ___ das Klima gewöhnt." "Sie ist sehr ___ Politik interessiert."
questions.explanation: sich gewöhnen an + accusative (an das Klima) and interessiert an + dative (an Politik). Both use an, but with different cases: getting used to takes the accusative, interest takes the dative.

questions.stem: Which of these take the dative? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: mit is always dative; vor in fixed phrases is dative (Angst vor dem Hund); zweifeln an takes the dative (an seiner Ehrlichkeit). stolz auf takes the accusative, and sich gewöhnen an the accusative (an das Klima).

questions.stem: Ask about the thing with a wo-word: "___ hängt das ab?" — "Vom Wetter."
questions.explanation: abhängen von + dative, and for a thing you ask with wo + preposition: Wovon hängt das ab? (No r is needed, because von starts with a consonant.) For a person you'd say Von wem …?

questions.stem: Put the parts in order to say "I'm proud that I passed the exam."
questions.explanation: Ich bin stolz darauf, dass ich die Prüfung bestanden habe. darauf points forward to the dass clause; in the dass clause the subject comes right after dass and the verb group goes to the end, with habe last.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this formal e-mail.

image.alt: A short formal e-mail: a bold subject line, Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, a first line starting with a small letter, a paragraph with two questions, a closing sentence, Mit freundlichen Grüßen and the name Daniel Okafor. Six lines on the right are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 the Betreff, a noun phrase without a verb; 2 the Anrede, followed by a comma; 3 the first line, which continues with a small letter after that comma; 4 the main part with the questions; 5 the polite closing sentence; 6 the Grußformel, with no comma after it. The e-mail has no date line, and the name at the end isn't numbered.

questions.stem: Complete with scheinen: "Der neue Kollege ___ sehr nett ___ sein." (The new colleague seems to be very nice.)
questions.explanation: Der neue Kollege scheint sehr nett zu sein. scheinen works like a modal verb, but the infinitive at the end needs zu.

questions.stem: Match each noun to its article. Use the ending to decide.
questions.explanation: -ung and -schaft are always feminine: die Beförderung, die Gewerkschaft. -er for a person who does something is masculine (der Arbeitgeber), and so is -ismus (der Tourismus). -um is mostly neuter: das Zentrum.

questions.stem: Which sentences mean "You don't have to come."? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: brauchen nicht zu and müssen nicht both mean it isn't necessary. dürfen nicht means it's forbidden, müssen means it's necessary, and brauchen nur zu means "you only need to come".

questions.stem: Put the parts of the formal e-mail in order.
choices: mit großem Interesse habe ich Ihre Anzeige gelesen.
Ich wäre Ihnen dankbar, wenn Sie mir kurz antworten könnten.
questions.explanation: Subject line, greeting, a first line that starts with a small letter, the polite closing sentence, and the sign-off without a comma. The small letter in "mit großem Interesse" shows that it follows the greeting directly.

questions.stem: You want to tell a colleague that there is a mistake in her table. Which version is the most diplomatic?
choices: Könnte es sein, dass hier ein kleiner Fehler ist?
Hier ist ein Fehler, das ist falsch.
questions.explanation: "Könnte es sein, dass …?" turns the accusation into a question and leaves room for doubt, and "klein" makes the problem smaller. The other three state the mistake as a fact; "Sie müssen sich verrechnet haben" even says the speaker is sure (must have).

questions.stem: What does "Das dürfte etwa 200 Euro kosten." mean?
choices: That is allowed to cost about 200 euros.
That is probably going to cost about 200 euros.
questions.explanation: In a statement, dürfte is a careful estimate: "probably". It has nothing to do with permission here. "Must" would be muss, and "should have cost" would be hätte … kosten sollen.

questions.stem: Put the statements in order from the surest to the least sure.
questions.explanation: muss = sure (a logical conclusion), dürfte = probable, könnte = possible, kann nicht = impossible, ruled out.

questions.stem: Complete: "Gut, dass du mich erinnert hast, sonst ___ ich den Termin vergessen."
questions.explanation: sonst hätte ich den Termin vergessen. The forgetting didn't happen, so it's imagined: past subjunctive. vergessen takes haben in the perfect, so hätte, and it comes straight after sonst, which fills position 1.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a real warning: something that can still happen?
choices: Zum Glück war ich pünktlich, sonst hätte ich den Zug verpasst.
Ich habe keine Zeit, sonst würde ich mitkommen.
Gut, dass es nicht geregnet hat, sonst wären wir nass geworden.
Beeil dich, sonst verpassen wir den Zug!
questions.explanation: "Beeil dich, sonst verpassen wir den Zug!" uses the indicative after sonst: missing the train is a real danger. The other three use the Konjunktiv II after sonst because the alternative did not or does not happen.

questions.stem: Which sentences soften a statement with the Konjunktiv II? Select all that apply.
choices: Ich würde sagen, wir brauchen noch eine Woche.
Da wäre ich mir nicht so sicher.
questions.explanation: würde sagen, hätte and wäre are Konjunktiv II forms that present the statement as a personal view or an offer. "Ich habe eine Frage" and "Das ist falsch" are direct indicative statements.

questions.stem: What is the difference between "Er hätte es wissen müssen." and "Er müsste es gewusst haben."?
choices: The first is a guess; the second is a reproach.
The first is a reproach (he should have known); the second is a guess (he presumably knew).
Both mean "He should have known it."
questions.explanation: hätte + infinitive + modal infinitive (wissen müssen) is the reproach from lesson 22: he ought to have known. Modal in position 2 + participle + haben (müsste … gewusst haben) is a guess about the past: he presumably knew.

questions.stem: Match each sentence to how sure the speaker is.
left: Das Licht ist an. Sie muss zu Hause sein.
Das Haus dürfte etwa hundert Jahre alt sein.
questions.explanation: muss draws a conclusion from evidence (the light is on), dürfte gives a careful estimate, könnte names one possibility, and kann nicht rules something out.

questions.stem: Turn the order into a polite request with the Konjunktiv II of können: "___ Sie mir die Tabelle noch einmal schicken?"
questions.explanation: Könnten Sie mir die Tabelle noch einmal schicken? Sie takes the -en form: könnten. The plain present können is polite too, but less so.

questions.stem: In the meeting, Herr Brandt says: "Ich hätte gedacht, dass da viele Kunden schon im Urlaub sind." What is he doing?
choices: Saying that he forgot about the holidays
Asking how many guests will come
questions.explanation: "Ich hätte gedacht, …" (I'd have thought …) is a soft way to disagree. He goes on to suggest May instead: "Wäre es nicht sinnvoller, im Mai zu feiern?"

questions.stem: In which sentence does "dürfte" ask permission instead of making a guess?
choices: Dürfte ich kurz Ihr Telefon benutzen?
Es dürften etwa fünfzig Gäste kommen.
Er dürfte den Zug verpasst haben.
questions.explanation: In a question with ich, Dürfte ich …? is a very polite request for permission. In the statements, dürfte means "probably": it'll probably be difficult, about fifty guests will probably come, he has probably missed the train.

questions.stem: Which endings have correct word order after "sonst"? Select all that apply.
choices: …, sonst wären wir zu spät gekommen.
questions.explanation: sonst fills position 1, so the conjugated verb follows immediately: sonst hätte ich, sonst wären wir, sonst verpassen wir. "sonst ich hätte" puts the subject before the verb, which is wrong.

questions.stem: The tracking page says your parcel will arrive tomorrow. Which sentence fits best?
choices: Das Paket kann nicht morgen ankommen.
Das Paket hätte morgen ankommen müssen.
Das Paket muss gestern angekommen sein.
questions.explanation: müsste says it should happen if everything goes as expected, which is exactly what tracking information gives you. "hätte … ankommen müssen" is about something that should have happened but didn't, and the other two contradict the information.

questions.stem: Soften the opinion with the one-word Konjunktiv II of finden: "Ich ___ den Plan etwas zu teuer."
questions.explanation: Ich fände den Plan etwas zu teuer. fand + umlaut + -e = fände, one of the strong forms that is common in speech. With "etwas" and the Konjunktiv, the criticism sounds like a personal view rather than a verdict.

questions.stem: Match each written Konjunktiv II form to its infinitive.
questions.explanation: Simple past stem + umlaut + -e: lag → läge, nahm → nähme, fuhr → führe, brachte → brächte. stehen is one of the few irregular ones: stünde (the regular stände also exists). (führe can also be the ich form of führen in the present, but as a Konjunktiv II it comes from fahren.)

questions.stem: In "Wenn sie nicht so weit weg wohnte, führen wir jedes Wochenende zu ihr.", what is "führen"?
questions.explanation: "to lead" makes no sense with "wir … zu ihr". fuhren (we drove) + umlaut = führen, the Konjunktiv II of fahren: "we would drive to her every weekend". The simple past would be fuhren, without the umlaut.

questions.stem: Why does everyday German use würde + infinitive for weak verbs such as machen or wohnen?
choices: Their Konjunktiv II looks exactly like the simple past.
They have no Konjunktiv II at all.
Their Konjunktiv II needs an extra umlaut.
Their one-word forms are only used in Austria.
questions.explanation: The Konjunktiv II of a weak verb is identical to its simple past (machte, wohnte), so a sentence can sound like a past statement. würde + infinitive makes the imagined meaning clear.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the picture, using words from Kafka's text.

image.alt: A rider on a galloping horse over flat heathland. Six parts are numbered: the rider, the reins, the spur on the rider's heel, the horse's neck, the horse's head and the flat ground.

questions.explanation: 1 der Reiter (the rider), 2 die Zügel (the reins, from his hands to the horse's head), 3 die Sporen (the spurs on his heel), 4 der Pferdehals (the horse's neck), 5 der Pferdekopf (the horse's head) and 6 die Heide (the heath). No saddle (der Sattel) or horseshoe (das Hufeisen) is numbered.

questions.stem: What kind of sentence is Kafka's "Wenn man doch ein Indianer wäre, …"?
choices: A real condition with a main clause at the end
An unreal comparison with als ob
An unreal wish with no main clause
questions.explanation: Wenn … doch … wäre is the pattern of an unreal wish (lesson 23): the Konjunktiv II plus the particle doch, and no main clause follows. The rest of the sentence adds more and more details to the wish.

questions.stem: Which verbs in Kafka's sentence are plain simple past (indicative) forms, not Konjunktiv II forms? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: ließ, wegwarf, sah and gab are simple past forms; their Konjunktiv II would be ließe, wegwürfe, sähe and gäbe. Only wäre is clearly Konjunktiv II. (erzitterte is a weak verb, so its form could be either.)

questions.stem: Write the Konjunktiv II forms Kafka could have used instead: ließ → ___, sah → ___
questions.explanation: Simple past stem + umlaut (where possible) + -e: ließ has no vowel to umlaut, so ließe; sah → sähe.

questions.stem: Which sentence from the essay states a fact, not speculation?
choices: Vielleicht wäre die Reformation ganz anders verlaufen.
Um 1450 entwickelte Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz ein neues Verfahren.
Auch die deutsche Sprache sähe heute vielleicht anders aus.
questions.explanation: entwickelte is an indicative simple past: the essay presents it as history. wären geblieben, wäre verlaufen and sähe are Konjunktiv II forms, which mark the imagined alternative.

questions.stem: Put the parts in order: "If there had been no telephone, people would have sent letters for a long time."
choices: Wenn es kein Telefon gegeben hätte,
questions.explanation: Wenn es kein Telefon gegeben hätte, hätten die Menschen noch lange Briefe geschickt. After the wenn clause, hätten comes first, then the subject, and the participle geschickt goes to the end.

questions.stem: Which is the past subjunctive of the passive, as used in the essay?
choices: wenn der Buchdruck nicht erfunden wäre
wenn der Buchdruck nicht erfunden würde
wenn der Buchdruck nicht erfunden hätte
wenn der Buchdruck nicht erfunden worden wäre
questions.explanation: The passive perfect is ist erfunden worden; in the past subjunctive ist becomes wäre: erfunden worden wäre. Without worden it describes a state ("if printing weren't invented"), würde makes it present, and hätte is the wrong auxiliary.

questions.stem: Match each word from the lesson to its meaning.
questions.explanation: der Buchdruck is the printing process, die Druckerei a print shop, der Mönch a monk, abschreiben to copy (by hand), die Übersetzung a translation. A letter you post is der Brief; the letters of the alphabet are Buchstaben or, in print, Lettern.

questions.stem: Why does the essay say "Bewegliche Lettern gab es in China und Korea schon früher"?
choices: Because Gutenberg learned printing in China
Because movable type existed in East Asia before Gutenberg's invention in Europe
Because the first printed Bible came from Korea
Because Gutenberg's letters were made of wood
questions.explanation: Movable type was used in China and Korea centuries before Gutenberg; the essay mentions it so as not to claim that he invented the idea itself. His invention changed printing in Europe. His letters were made of metal, as the essay says.

questions.stem: Complete with the past subjunctive: "Ohne den Buchdruck ___ sich Luthers Ideen langsamer verbreitet."
questions.explanation: Ohne den Buchdruck hätten sich Luthers Ideen langsamer verbreitet. sich verbreiten takes haben in the perfect, and the subject Luthers Ideen is plural: hätten. The phrase "Ohne den Buchdruck" replaces a whole wenn clause.

questions.stem: Which sentence presents a counterfactual claim responsibly, as speculation?
choices: Ohne Gutenberg gab es keine Reformation.
Ohne Gutenberg gibt es keine Reformation.
Ohne Gutenberg hat es keine Reformation gegeben.
Ohne Gutenberg hätte es die Reformation vielleicht nicht gegeben.
questions.explanation: The Konjunktiv II (hätte … gegeben) marks the claim as imagined, and vielleicht shows it is uncertain. The other three use the indicative and present a guess as a fact.

questions.stem: The five branches of the Sozialversicherung. Name each numbered pillar.

image.alt: A roof labelled die Sozialversicherung resting on five numbered pillars. Under the pillars, from left to right: health, long-term care, pension, unemployment, accidents at work.

questions.explanation: Each name is "what it covers" + Versicherung: Kranken- (the sick: health), Pflege- (care), Renten- (pensions), Arbeitslosen- (the unemployed) and Unfall- (accidents at work). A Haftpflichtversicherung (liability insurance) is a private insurance, not part of the Sozialversicherung, and a Krankmeldung is telling your employer you're ill.

questions.stem: A news report. Type the Konjunktiv I form of "sein": "Ein Sprecher der Klinik sagte, die Lage ___ ruhig."
questions.explanation: The Konjunktiv I of sein is irregular: er/sie/es sei. It marks the sentence as the spokesman's words: "the situation was calm, he said". The indicative would be ist; the Konjunktiv II wäre is also heard in reported speech, but it isn't the Konjunktiv I.

questions.stem: The receptionist asked: "Haben Sie eine Überweisung?" Complete the report: "Sie hat gefragt, …"
questions.explanation: Sie hat gefragt, ob ich eine Überweisung habe. A yes/no question is reported with ob, and ob sends the verb to the end. Sie (you, formal) becomes ich, because you are now reporting about yourself.

questions.stem: Which of these reports are correct German? Select all that apply.
choices: Sie sagt, dass sie kommt morgen.
Er fragt, ob ich Zeit habe.
Er fragt, wenn ich Zeit habe.
Der Arzt hat gesagt, ich soll mehr trinken.
questions.explanation: Without dass, a reported statement can keep main-clause order (sie kommt morgen); with dass, the verb must go to the end (dass sie morgen kommt). A yes/no question is reported with ob, not wenn. An instruction ("Trinken Sie mehr!") is reported with sollen.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning in the health system.
choices: a referral from your family doctor to a specialist
telling your employer that you are ill
the emergency department of a hospital
the hours when a doctor sees patients
questions.explanation: die Überweisung is a referral here (at the bank, the same word means a transfer). die Krankmeldung is the notification of sickness to your employer, die Notaufnahme is A&E, and die Sprechstunde is a practice's consulting hours. A prescription is das Rezept.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the building.

image.alt: A block of flats with six numbered parts: 1 the stairwell in the middle of the building, 2 a small panel with three buttons beside the front door, 3 a box with three slots on the other side of the door, 4 a balcony on the first floor, 5 two bins beside a tree, and 6 the green area next to the building.

questions.explanation: The stairs run up the Treppenhaus (1). Beside the front door are the doorbells, die Klingel (2), and the letterboxes, der Briefkasten (3). der Balkon (4) sticks out from a flat on the first floor, and the bins, die Mülltonnen (5), stand in the courtyard, der Hof (6). The cellar (der Keller) isn't shown, and a tap (der Wasserhahn) is inside a flat.

questions.stem: Complete with the right form of lassen: "Wann ___ du dir die Haare schneiden?"
questions.explanation: lassen changes its vowel in the du and er forms: du lässt, er lässt. The stem already ends in s, so du adds only -t. (lasst is the ihr form.)

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "When did you have the car repaired?"
questions.explanation: Wann hast du das Auto reparieren lassen? The question word comes first and hast second. With another infinitive, the perfect of lassen uses the infinitive lassen, not gelassen, so two infinitives stand at the end: reparieren lassen.

questions.stem: In which sentences does lassen mean "to have something done (by someone else)"? Select all that apply.
choices: Ich lasse mir die Haare schneiden.
Meine Eltern lassen mich allein fahren.
Das Fenster lässt sich nicht öffnen.
questions.explanation: A hairdresser cuts your hair and a tradesperson checks the heating: that's the causative "have something done". Lass mich in Ruhe means "leave me alone", lassen + a person + infinitive (mich allein fahren) means "let", and sich lassen means "can be done": the window won't open.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
choices: paying less rent because of a defect
the company that manages the building
the person who cleans the stairwell
questions.explanation: der Schimmel is mould, undicht means leaking, a Mietminderung is a rent reduction for a serious defect, the Mieterverein is the tenants' association, and the Hausverwaltung looks after the building for the owner.

questions.stem: The speaker is upstairs. Which word describes each numbered movement from her point of view?

image.alt: A two-storey house. The speaker, marked ICH, is in a room upstairs. 1: a person climbs the stairs up to her floor. 2: a key falls from her window down to a friend in the garden. 3: a cat walks into her room. 4: a dog runs out of the front door downstairs.

questions.explanation: her- means towards the speaker, hin- away from her. The person on the stairs comes up to her (herauf), the key goes down away from her (hinunter), the cat comes into her room (herein), and the dog goes out, away from the house she's in (hinaus). hinauf would be up and away (said by someone downstairs), heraus out towards the speaker (said by someone outside).

questions.stem: You are in the cellar. Your friend is upstairs. Call to him, using the full standard form: "Komm bitte ___!" (come down here)
questions.explanation: He should come down towards you, so the word is her- + unter: herunter. hinunter would mean down and away from you. In speech many people simply say runter.

questions.stem: Put the five parts of a short presentation in order.
questions.explanation: Introduce the topic and your plan, tell your own experience, describe the situation in your home country, weigh pros and cons and give your opinion, and finish with a conclusion. This is the structure of part 2 of the Goethe B1 speaking test.

questions.stem: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Austria is divided into nine Bundesländer.
Germany's highest mountain is over 3,000 metres high.
The Alps reach into the far south of Germany.
questions.explanation: Austria has nine Bundesländer and Switzerland 26 Kantone. Germany has 16 Bundesländer, not Kantone. The Zugspitze, Germany's highest mountain, is just under 3,000 metres. The Alps cover much of Austria and Switzerland and reach into the far south of Germany.

questions.stem: Match each phrase to the part of a presentation where it belongs.
left: In meiner Präsentation geht es um …
Bei uns in Brasilien ist es üblich, dass …
questions.explanation: Each part has typical phrases: "es geht um" introduces the topic, "selbst erlebt" signals personal experience, "bei uns in …" the home country, "einerseits … andererseits" weighs two sides, and "abschließend" starts the conclusion.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this formal letter.

image.alt: A formal letter. 1 is next to the sender's name and address at the top left, 2 next to the address of a company below it, 3 before the place and date on the right, 4 after the bold subject line, 5 after Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, and 6 after Mit freundlichen Grüßen.

questions.explanation: The sender (Absender) is at the top, the recipient (Empfänger) below, then place and date on the right and the subject line (Betreff, no full stop). The opening (Anrede) ends with a comma; the closing (Grußformel) has no punctuation. A Fazit is the conclusion of a forum post, and an Anhang is an attachment.

questions.stem: Type the standard closing of a formal letter, without punctuation.
questions.explanation: Mit freundlichen Grüßen is the formal closing (in Switzerland: Grüssen). No comma or full stop follows it in German.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: "Ich schreibe Ihnen, …" (to ask about the course)
questions.explanation: Ich schreibe Ihnen, um mich nach dem Kurs zu erkundigen. um starts the group, the reflexive mich comes early, and zu + infinitive closes it. sich erkundigen nach = to ask about. A comma separates the um … zu group from the main clause.

questions.stem: Which lines are correct in a formal letter to a company? Select all that apply.
choices: Ich schreibe Ihnen wegen meiner Bestellung.
Könnten Sie mir bitte mitteilen, ob der Kurs stattfindet?
questions.explanation: The polite Sie is always capitalized, so "Könnten sie" is wrong. The closing Mit freundlichen Grüßen has no comma. The opening with a comma, "Ich schreibe Ihnen wegen …" and the polite question with Könnten Sie are all correct.

questions.stem: Match each opening or closing to its register.
questions.explanation: Friends get Liebe Mia and Liebe Grüße. People you know but call Sie get Liebe Frau Kraus (closing: Viele Grüße). Companies and offices get Sehr geehrte … and Mit freundlichen Grüßen.

questions.stem: Match each module of the adult Goethe-Zertifikat B1 to its length.
choices: about 15 minutes plus 15 minutes of preparation
questions.explanation: Reading takes 65 minutes, listening about 40, writing 60, and speaking about 15 minutes in pairs after 15 minutes of preparation. No module takes 90 minutes.

questions.stem: Put the stages of the B1 speaking module in order for one candidate.
choices: Planning something together with your partner
questions.explanation: After 15 minutes of preparation, part 1 is planning something together. In part 2 you present your topic, and in part 3 your partner reacts and you answer questions about your presentation. Then the roles change.

questions.stem: You passed. Complete: "Ich habe die Prüfung ___!"
questions.explanation: die Prüfung bestehen = to pass the exam; the participle is bestanden. "Ich habe die Prüfung gemacht" only says that you took it.

questions.stem: Which statements about the adult Goethe-Zertifikat B1 are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Each module is scored out of 100 points.
You must take all four modules on the same day.
A module is passed with 60 points.
The speaking test is done alone, without a partner.
You can repeat only the module you failed.
questions.explanation: The exam is modular: each module has 100 points and is passed with 60, and you can take modules separately and repeat only the one you failed. You can take all four on one day, but you don't have to. Speaking is done in pairs.

questions.stem: Match each word from exam instructions to its meaning.
choices: to match one thing to another
to apply or be true for something
questions.explanation: "Ordnen Sie zu" asks you to match, "Trifft das zu?" asks whether something applies, an Aussage is a statement (for example in a true/false task), and a Gliederung is the outline you plan before writing. A grade is die Note.

questions.stem: Why do news reports often write "Der Bürgermeister sagte, die Brücke sei sicher" instead of "… die Brücke ist sicher"?
choices: sei is more polite towards the mayor
sei is the past tense of ist
sei shows that this is the mayor's statement, not the newspaper's
sei is required after every verb of saying
questions.explanation: The Konjunktiv I marks the statement as reported: the paper passes it on without vouching for it. It isn't a past tense or a politeness form, and it isn't required: the indicative is also correct after a verb of saying, just less distanced.

questions.stem: Type the Konjunktiv I form of "haben": "Die Ministerin erklärte, sie ___ das Problem erst gestern erkannt."
questions.explanation: The original was "Ich habe das Problem erst gestern erkannt." Every past becomes habe/sei + participle, and the third person singular of haben in the Konjunktiv I is habe (indicative: hat).

questions.stem: The tenants said: "Wir haben kein warmes Wasser." Which report follows the replacement rule?
choices: Die Mieter sagten, sie hätten kein warmes Wasser.
Die Mieter sagten, sie haben kein warmes Wasser.
Die Mieter sagten, sie habe kein warmes Wasser.
Die Mieter sagten, sie hatten kein warmes Wasser.
questions.explanation: The Konjunktiv I sie haben looks exactly like the indicative, so it is replaced by the Konjunktiv II: sie hätten. sie habe is singular, and sie hatten is the Präteritum ("they had", in the past).

questions.stem: The workers said: "Wir arbeiten zu viel." Why does the newspaper write "sie würden zu viel arbeiten"?
choices: because the workers were only imagining it
because both sie arbeiten and sie arbeiteten look like indicative forms
because arbeiten has no Konjunktiv I at all
because würde is always used for the plural
questions.explanation: The Konjunktiv I sie arbeiten looks like the present indicative, and the Konjunktiv II sie arbeiteten looks like the Präteritum. So the last step of the replacement rule applies: würde + infinitive. Here würde doesn't mean "would"; it just marks reported speech.

questions.stem: Match each direct statement by Herr Ott to its report in news style.
choices: er sei leider zu spät gekommen
questions.explanation: The present stays present (er komme), the future uses werde (er werde kommen), and every past tense, Perfekt or Präteritum, becomes sei/habe + participle (er sei gekommen). er käme is a Konjunktiv II, only needed when the Konjunktiv I looks like the indicative, which er komme doesn't.

questions.stem: A reporter asked: "Wird die Brücke gesperrt?" Complete the report: "Die Reporterin fragte, …"
questions.explanation: Die Reporterin fragte, ob die Brücke gesperrt werde. A yes/no question is reported with ob; the verb goes to the end, and werde is the Konjunktiv I of werden (indicative: wird).

questions.stem: Which of these verbs suggest that the reporter has doubts about the statement or that it was unpleasant for the speaker? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: behaupten (to claim) keeps a distance: maybe it isn't true. einräumen (to admit) tells you the speaker had to concede something unpleasant. sagen, mitteilen and erklären are neutral.

questions.stem: In a news article: "Viele Ärzte hätten zu wenig Zeit für ihre Patienten, sagte die Sprecherin." What does "hätten" mean here?
choices: would have, if things were different
questions.explanation: In reported speech, hätten often just replaces haben, whose Konjunktiv I would look like the indicative. The spokeswoman said "Viele Ärzte haben zu wenig Zeit". It isn't unreal and it isn't past.

questions.stem: Read: "Der Verband kritisierte die Regeln. Sie seien zu kompliziert. Die Regeln treten am 1. Juli in Kraft." Which information comes from the newspaper itself, not from the association?
choices: that the rules are too complicated
that the rules come into force on 1 July
questions.explanation: "Sie seien zu kompliziert" is in the Konjunktiv I, so it's still the association's view, even without a new "sagte". "Die Regeln treten … in Kraft" is indicative: the newspaper's own information.

questions.stem: You read: "Der Minister erklärte, die Renten seien sicher." How do you pass this on naturally to a friend?
choices: Der Minister hat gesagt, dass die Renten sicher sind.
Der Minister hat gesagt, dass die Renten sicher seien sind.
Der Minister hat gesagt, die Renten sicher sind.
Der Minister sagt, dass sind die Renten sicher.
questions.explanation: In conversation, use the perfect for the speech verb and dass + indicative with the verb at the end. Without dass you'd need main-clause order (die Renten sind sicher), and after dass the verb can't come second.

questions.stem: Find the reporting signals in this article. Name each numbered part.

image.alt: A short news article headed Brücke bleibt gesperrt, with five parts in dashed boxes, each followed by a number. 1 follows the words „Wir arbeiten so, the start of a quotation. 2 follows the word sei. 3 follows the word erklärte. 4 follows Einem Gutachten zufolge. 5 follows the word angeblich.

questions.explanation: The words in German quotation marks („ … “) are direct speech (1). sei is the Konjunktiv I of sein (2), introduced by the reporting verb erklärte (3). "Einem Gutachten zufolge" names the source, with zufolge after a dative noun (4), and angeblich (supposedly) keeps a distance (5). There's no Konjunktiv II and no werden-passive in the article.

questions.stem: Read: "Baubürgermeister Wendt räumte Fehler ein. Die Stadt hätte die Bürger früher informieren müssen." What does Wendt say?
choices: The citizens should have informed the city earlier.
The city informed the citizens early enough.
The city should have informed the citizens earlier.
The city will inform the citizens next week.
questions.explanation: hätte … informieren müssen is the past Konjunktiv II of a modal: "should have informed", a regret. die Stadt is the subject, die Bürger the object. einräumen (admit) fits: he concedes a mistake.

questions.stem: Which verb form is a Konjunktiv I?
questions.explanation: The Konjunktiv I uses the infinitive stem (geb-) + -e: er gebe. Stem-changing verbs keep the infinitive vowel, which helps you spot it. er gibt is the present indicative, er gab the Präteritum, er gäbe the Konjunktiv II.

questions.stem: The police told a resident: "Bleiben Sie im Haus!" Type the Konjunktiv I of sollen: "Die Polizei sagte der Anwohnerin, sie ___ im Haus bleiben."
questions.explanation: Instructions are reported with sollen. The Konjunktiv I of sollen in the third person singular is solle (indicative: soll). For a plural subject you'd read sollten, because sie sollen looks like the indicative.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this official decision.

image.alt: An official letter from the road traffic office of Musterstadt to Elif Kaya, with the section headings removed. 1 is next to the code BP-2027-0418 at the top right. 2 is next to the bold line Ihr Antrag auf einen Bewohnerparkausweis. 3 is next to Ihr Antrag wird abgelehnt. 4 is next to a paragraph explaining that the car is not registered to her and a confirmation was missing. 5 is next to a paragraph saying that a Widerspruch can be lodged within one month.

questions.explanation: The file number (Aktenzeichen, 1) is the code to quote in every reply. The bold line is the subject (Betreff, 2), "Ihr Antrag wird abgelehnt" is the decision (3), the paragraph about the missing confirmation gives the reasons (Begründung, 4), and the paragraph about Widerspruch within a month is the Rechtsbehelfsbelehrung (5). The Grußformel, Mit freundlichen Grüßen, is further down and isn't numbered.

questions.stem: Match each light verb construction to the simple verb with the same meaning.
questions.explanation: In a light verb construction the noun carries the meaning: Antrag → beantragen, Widerspruch → widersprechen, Entscheidung → entscheiden. in Kraft treten means to become valid, and in Anspruch nehmen to make use of something. unterschreiben (to sign) matches none of them.

questions.stem: Match each abbreviation to its full form.
questions.explanation: z. Hd. means "for the attention of", i. V. "standing in for" the person in charge, o. g. "above-mentioned", gem. "in accordance with" and Abs. a paragraph or subsection of a law (§ 556 Abs. 3). beziehungsweise is abbreviated bzw.

questions.stem: You paid a Vorauszahlung of 150 Euro a month for 12 months. Your share of the real costs is 1,920 Euro. How much is the Nachzahlung? Give only the number of euros.
questions.explanation: Advance payments: 12 × 150 = 1,800 Euro. The real costs are higher: 1,920 − 1,800 = 120 Euro, which you have to pay (Nachzahlung).

questions.stem: Your advance payments were higher than the real costs, so you get money back. What is this credit called? Type the noun without the article.
questions.explanation: das Guthaben is the credit you get back (or that is set against the next rent). If the costs were higher than your payments, you'd owe a Nachzahlung.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the service-charge system in order.
choices: You pay a Vorauszahlung every month
You pay the Nachzahlung or receive the Guthaben
questions.explanation: You pay advance payments through the year. When the billing period ends, the landlord adds up the real costs and sends the bill (within twelve months). Only then is the difference settled: a Nachzahlung or a Guthaben.

questions.stem: Which of these are light verb constructions (Funktionsverbgefüge)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: In einen Antrag stellen, zur Kenntnis nehmen and zur Verfügung stellen, the verbs stellen and nehmen have lost their own meaning: the nouns carry it (beantragen, bemerken, bereitstellen). In den Antrag ausfüllen and in die Stadt fahren, the verbs keep their full meaning: you really fill in and really travel.

questions.stem: What does "Im Falle einer Ablehnung erhalten Sie die Unterlagen zurück." mean?
choices: You must send the documents back if you refuse.
If your application is rejected, you get your documents back.
The documents are rejected if they arrive late.
You will receive the documents after the decision in any case.
questions.explanation: im Falle + genitive = in the case of; die Ablehnung comes from ablehnen (to reject). In plain German: Wenn wir Ihren Antrag ablehnen, schicken wir Ihnen die Unterlagen zurück. The office does the rejecting, and you are the one who gets the documents.

questions.stem: A letter says: "Der Betrag ist bis zum 15.07. zu überweisen." What does it mean?
choices: You can transfer the amount if you want to.
The amount has already been transferred.
You must transfer the amount by 15 July.
The amount will be transferred to you by 15 July.
questions.explanation: sein + zu + infinitive in an instruction means "must be done": Sie müssen den Betrag bis zum 15. Juli überweisen. It's an order, not a possibility, and you are the one who pays.

questions.stem: The Rechtsbehelfsbelehrung says: "Gegen diesen Bescheid kann innerhalb eines Monats nach Bekanntgabe Widerspruch erhoben werden." What does it tell you?
choices: You can object to the decision within a month of being notified.
The decision will be announced publicly in a month.
You must pay within a month, or the office will object.
You can apply again after a month.
questions.explanation: Widerspruch erheben (or einlegen) = to lodge an objection; innerhalb eines Monats nach Bekanntgabe = within one month of notification. Bekanntgabe is when the letter counts as delivered, a few days after posting, so act well within a month of the date on the letter.

questions.stem: Why did the office reject Elif Kaya's application for a residents' parking permit?
choices: She doesn't live in the parking zone.
The car isn't registered to her, and the keeper's confirmation was missing.
questions.explanation: The Begründung says: "Das Fahrzeug ist nicht auf Sie zugelassen. Eine Bestätigung der Halterin, dass Sie das Fahrzeug dauerhaft nutzen, lag Ihrem Antrag nicht bei." The car belongs to her sister, and the confirmation was not enclosed.

questions.stem: Which is the best first line for Elif's objection?
choices: Hiermit lege ich Widerspruch gegen Ihren Bescheid vom 03.05.2027 ein.
Hiermit widerspreche ich Sie wegen dem Parkausweis.
Ich finde Ihre Entscheidung nicht so gut, liebe Grüße.
Hiermit lege ich gegen Ihren Bescheid Widerspruch.
questions.explanation: Widerspruch einlegen is separable: lege … ein. The line names the decision by its date, as offices expect. widersprechen takes the dative (Ihnen), not Sie; the third choice is far too informal; and the last one is missing the prefix ein.

questions.stem: Read: "Ihre Vorauszahlungen betrugen 12 × 210,00 € = 2.520,00 €. Ihr Anteil an den Kosten beträgt 2.687,40 €." What is the result?
questions.explanation: The real costs (2.687,40 €) are higher than the advance payments (2.520,00 €), so the tenant owes the difference: 2.687,40 € − 2.520,00 € = 167,40 €, a Nachzahlung.

questions.stem: In Germany, the service-charge bill for the year 2026 arrives in February 2028. What is usually true?
choices: The tenant must pay any Nachzahlung within 30 days.
The tenant gets back all the advance payments.
The landlord can usually no longer demand a Nachzahlung.
The tenant has to ask the Mieterverein before paying.
questions.explanation: The landlord has twelve months after the end of the billing period (here, until 31 December 2027) to send the bill. If it comes later, a Nachzahlung usually can't be demanded. The advance payments themselves aren't refunded, and asking the Mieterverein is a good idea but not a duty.

cards.back: Sudden start, open ending, a turning point, a short time, few characters, everyday language, gaps (Leerstellen). A checklist, not a law.
Rubble literature: German writing soon after 1945 about war, hunger and ruins. Wolfgang Borchert (Das Brot, 1946), Heinrich Böll (Nobel Prize 1972).
Sudden start: no introduction; the reader is dropped into the action.
Open ending: the story stops without telling how things turn out.
Turning point: the moment that changes the situation or what a character understands.
A gap: something important the text leaves unsaid, for the reader to fill in.
The narrator is the voice in the text; the author is the real person who wrote it.
First-person narrator (ich, a character) vs third-person narrator (talks about er and sie).
Present tense; earlier events in the perfect. Never the simple past of the story.
No direct speech, no opinion, own words, main events in order.
In der Kurzgeschichte „…“ von … geht es um … (title, author, text type, theme).
„Hast du gegessen?“, fragte sie. → Sie fragt ihn, ob er schon gegessen hat.

cards.front: die Strophe / die Zeile, der Vers
cards.back: Stanza / line. German Vers is one line, not a stanza.
Couplet rhyme: aabb.
Alternate rhyme: abab.
Enclosed rhyme: abba.

cards.front: How to find a rhyme scheme
cards.back: Give each new end sound a new letter; rhyming lines share a letter. Listen to the sound, not the spelling.
Impure rhyme: close but not identical, e.g. Himmel / Schimmer.
The sentence runs on into the next line: Und meine Seele spannte / Weit ihre Flügel aus. Don't stop when reading aloud.
A dropped sound, often final -e: hätt' = hätte, leis = leise, nach Haus = nach Hause.
Kreuzreim abab cdcd efef. Als hätt' der Himmel … / Als flöge sie nach Haus: comparisons in Konjunktiv II.
Ich weiß nicht, was soll es bedeuten … The "old" legend was invented by Clemens Brentano in 1801.
Find the verb and the subject, then use normal order: was soll es bedeuten → was es bedeuten soll.
Old forms: die Länder; würde fliegen; dass (spelling since 1996). Understand them, don't write them.
Culture of remembrance: how a society remembers its past in public (memorials, memorial days, museums, school).
Coming to terms with the past / working through the past.
1918 republic proclaimed; 1923 Hitler's failed putsch; 1938 November pogroms; 1989 the Wall falls.
1945: Auschwitz liberated. German day of remembrance for the victims of National Socialism since 1996.
A 10 × 10 cm brass stone in the pavement in front of a victim's last freely chosen home; Gunter Demnig, since 1992.
Jahrgang 1903: born in 1903.
Telegraphic style for a passive: Sie wurde 1942 deportiert.
Wir gedenken der Opfer (solemn). Everyday: Wir erinnern an die Opfer.

cards.front: sich erinnern an vs erinnern an
cards.back: sich erinnern an = to remember; erinnern an = to remind of, commemorate: Die Tafel erinnert an die Familie.
Denkmal: any monument, also honouring. Mahnmal (mahnen, to warn): remembers a crime so that it never happens again.
Recruitment agreements: Italy 1955, Spain and Greece 1960, Turkey 1961, Morocco 1963, Portugal 1964, Tunisia 1965, Yugoslavia 1968.
November 1973: recruitment stopped; many workers stayed and their families followed.

cards.front: Man hat Arbeitskräfte gerufen, und es kommen Menschen.
cards.back: Max Frisch, 1965 (about Switzerland): workers are people with lives, not just labour.
No German citizenship / you or a parent not born German / you or both parents immigrated since 1950.
Naturalisation usually after five years; dual citizenship generally allowed. Check the current rules.
von 20 auf 24 Prozent = from 20 to 24; um 4 Prozentpunkte = by 4 points.
20 % → 24 %: +4 percentage points, but +20 per cent (4 ÷ 20).
Der Anteil ist gestiegen / gesunken (sein).
Introduction and source (Die Grafik zeigt … Die Zahlen stammen von …), main trend, details, conclusion (Insgesamt …).
No plural ending after a number; with a plural noun the verb is usually plural: 25 Prozent der Einwohner haben …

cards.front: Futur II: how is it built?
cards.back: werden (position 2) + participle + haben/sein at the end: Sie wird es geschafft haben. Er wird gegangen sein.
The same helper as in the perfect: hat gelesen → wird gelesen haben; ist angekommen → wird angekommen sein.

cards.front: Futur II in a subordinate clause
cards.back: werden goes to the very end: …, dass er den Zug verpasst haben wird.
Finished by a point in the future: Bis Freitag werde ich den Bericht geschrieben haben. (By Friday I will have written the report.)
A guess about the past: Er wird den Zug verpasst haben. = He has probably missed the train.

cards.front: Er wird wohl krank sein. vs Er wird wohl krank gewesen sein.
cards.back: Futur I + wohl: he is probably ill (now). Futur II + wohl: he was probably ill (in the past).

cards.front: Everyday alternative to Bis Freitag werde ich es geschrieben haben
cards.back: The perfect + time word: Bis Freitag habe ich es geschrieben.

cards.front: Everyday alternative to Er wird den Zug verpasst haben
cards.back: Perfect + an adverb: Er hat den Zug wahrscheinlich (wohl, vermutlich) verpasst.
He must have seen it: a modal with the perfect infinitive, a strong conclusion about the past (B2, recognise it).

cards.front: Futur II: the most common mistake
cards.back: Using the bare infinitive: not "wird … schreiben haben" but "wird … geschrieben haben".

cards.front: der Täter, der Verdacht, das Alibi, der Tatort
cards.back: the culprit, suspicion, the alibi, the crime scene.
to investigate (police), to arrest (nahm fest, hat festgenommen), to break in (brach ein, ist eingebrochen).
bei + dative: Als wir ankamen → bei unserer Ankunft.
nach + dative: Nachdem sie zurückgekehrt war → nach ihrer Rückkehr.
vor + dative: Bevor der Bus abfuhr → vor der Abfahrt.
während + genitive: Während er studierte → während seines Studiums.
seit + dative: Seit sie geheiratet haben → seit ihrer Heirat.

cards.front: bis + clause → phrase; sobald + clause → phrase
cards.back: bis zu + dative (bis zu seinem Ruhestand); gleich nach / sofort nach + dative (gleich nach ihrer Ankunft).

cards.front: Three ways to make the noun
cards.back: -ung noun (die Gründung), short noun (die Ankunft, der Beginn; sometimes a different word: sterben → der Tod), or the infinitive as a noun (das Lesen, beim Lesen).
while doing: beim Autofahren, beim Lesen. Capital letter, neuter.

cards.front: What happens to the subject in a time phrase?
cards.back: It becomes a possessive (seit ihrer Heirat) or a genitive (die Heirat meiner Großeltern); von + dative in speech.

cards.front: Turning a phrase back into a clause: the tense
cards.back: Phrases have no tense. Choose it: nach dem Essen → nachdem wir gegessen hatten (one step back).
before (formal), whenever, hardly … when. All send the verb to the end.
wurde geboren for people who have died (Clara Brenner wurde 1891 geboren); for living people ist geboren is the everyday form (Ich bin 1990 geboren), wurde geboren also possible.
Contrast: two different facts side by side (während, hingegen); you can swap the halves. Concession: a fact fails to stop something (obwohl, trotzdem).
while (same time): Während ich koche, deckt sie den Tisch. whereas (contrast): Während ich gern koche, isst sie lieber auswärts. Verb at the end in both.
whereas (formal, only contrast, never time). Verb at the end: Er zahlt bar, wohingegen ich mit Karte zahle.
Linking adverbs. Position 1, verb next: Dagegen ist es in Wien ruhiger. Or after the first element: In Wien hingegen ist es ruhiger.
on the other hand (in a comparison): In Wien dagegen … / against it (da-word of gegen): Ich bin dagegen.
in contrast to, unlike; zu + dative: Im Gegensatz zu meinem Bruder spreche ich kein Französisch. im Gegensatz dazu = in contrast.
however, though: limits what you just said. Die Wohnung ist schön. Allerdings ist sie klein. As an answer, Allerdings! = It certainly is!
unless. Comma + normal main clause (verb second): Wir gehen wandern, es sei denn, es regnet. Or: es sei denn, dass es regnet.
except when, unless. Verb at the end: Ich fahre Rad, außer wenn es schneit.
es sei denn and außer wenn already contain the "not" = wenn … nicht. "es sei denn, es regnet nicht" would mean "unless it doesn't rain".
otherwise, or else. Linking adverbs, verb next: Wir müssen los, sonst verpassen wir den Zug. andernfalls is the formal version.

Sundays and public holidays are protected days of rest; most shops are closed. Opening hours (Ladenschluss) are set by each Bundesland; stations, airports, petrol stations and often bakeries are exceptions.

cards.front: obwohl vs auch wenn vs selbst wenn
cards.back: obwohl: a real fact. auch wenn: fact or possibility (even if). selbst wenn: the extreme or imagined case. All three: verb at the end.
A clause with auch wenn or selbst wenn: the main event happens whatever the condition. Auch wenn es regnet, gehen wir raus.

cards.front: Word order after a fronted auch wenn clause
cards.back: Verb straight after the comma: Auch wenn es regnet, gehen wir raus. (In speech you may hear subject first; avoid it in writing.)
For imagined cases: Selbst wenn ich im Lotto gewinnen würde, würde ich weiterarbeiten.
obwohl is only for facts. A possible event takes auch wenn: Auch wenn es morgen schneien sollte, fahren wir los.
no matter how / what / whether. The main clause usually keeps subject first: Egal, wie teuer es ist, ich kaufe es.
However you look at it (fixed phrase; also Was du auch sagst, … = whatever you say).
Einleitung → Argumente dafür → Argumente dagegen → abwägen → Fazit with your own opinion.
Zunächst … · Außerdem … · Darüber hinaus … (moreover) · Hinzu kommt, dass … · Ein weiteres Argument ist …
Auf der anderen Seite … · Dagegen spricht, dass … · Es stimmt zwar, dass …, aber …
Letztlich … (in the end) · Insgesamt … (all in all) · Zusammenfassend lässt sich sagen, dass … (to sum up)
A complete main clause; the argument follows in a dass clause with the verb at the end: Hinzu kommt, dass Geschäfte weniger Arbeit haben.
Article … noun frame the phrase; the participle (with an adjective ending) stands right before the noun; its own words come before it: der beim Bau entdeckte Schatz.
der Schatz, der beim Bau entdeckt wurde (the treasure discovered during construction)

cards.front: How to read a participle phrase
cards.back: Find an article with no noun after it, jump to the first noun that fits it, take the word before that noun as the participle, and read the middle as its words.

cards.front: Partizip I before a noun: meaning
cards.back: Active, at the same time: die steigenden Preise = die Preise, die steigen.

cards.front: Partizip II of a verb with an object: meaning
cards.back: Passive: die von Kindern gefundenen Münzen = die Münzen, die von Kindern gefunden wurden.

cards.front: Partizip II of a sein verb: meaning
cards.back: Active and finished: der gerade angekommene Zug = der Zug, der gerade angekommen ist.
Verbs with haben and no object (schlafen, arbeiten, lachen) have no Partizip II before a noun. Use a relative clause: der Mann, der geschlafen hat.
the coins that still have to be examined (zu + Partizip I, the gerundive: must or can be done)
a coin about 2,000 years old (adjectives can be extended too)

cards.front: Participle phrases: when to use them
cards.back: Short ones in writing (die gestern bestellte Ware); in speech, use a relative clause.
excavation, to dig up (grub aus, hat ausgegraben)
to come from, to date from: Die Münze stammt aus dem 2. Jahrhundert.
due to, because of (+ genitive; the formal wegen). Without an article: aufgrund von.
as a result of (+ genitive): Infolge des Unwetters fiel der Strom aus.
in view of, given (+ genitive): Angesichts der hohen Kosten …
thanks to (+ genitive or dative); only for a good result.
for lack of (+ genitive): mangels ausreichender Nachfrage
regarding, with regard to (+ genitive): Bezüglich Ihrer Anfrage …
according to (+ genitive or dative); no ending without an article: laut Polizei, laut Plan.
with the help of, on the basis of / using, on the occasion of (all + genitive)
along: den Fluss entlang (after the noun, accusative) or entlang des Flusses (before, genitive)
Agree with the owner; never change; no article after them; preposition in front (mit deren Hilfe); strong adjective ending (dessen neues Auto).
dem Vater sein Haus: spoken and regional, not standard. Write: das Haus des Vaters.
matter, affair: in dieser Angelegenheit

cards.front: Das Gesetz wird verabschiedet vs Das Gesetz ist verabschiedet
cards.back: werden + participle = the action (it is being passed); sein + participle = the state afterwards (it has been passed, it is done).

cards.front: When is the state passive (sein + participle) possible?
cards.back: Only when the action leaves a lasting result: geöffnet, geschlossen, verboten, geregelt, festgelegt. Not possible: Der Minister ist kritisiert (being criticised leaves no lasting state).

cards.front: Passive of a verb with a dative object (zustimmen, helfen)
cards.back: The dative stays, there is no subject, the verb is singular: Dem Gesetz wurde zugestimmt. Den Bürgern wird geholfen.

cards.front: Passive of a verb with a preposition (abstimmen über)
cards.back: The preposition phrase stays: Über das Gesetz wird abgestimmt. Or with a da-word: Darüber wird abgestimmt.
It was decided that … A passive that reports a decision without naming who made it. Also: Es wird erwartet / geprüft, dass / ob …
That can be changed. sich lassen + infinitive = kann … werden.
Es kann gelöst werden. Es lässt sich lösen. Es ist (leicht) zu lösen. Es ist lösbar.

cards.front: Der Antrag ist online zu stellen.
cards.back: Must, not can: The application must be made online. In a rule, without leicht/schwer/kaum/nur, sein + zu usually means must.

cards.front: How a German federal law is made
cards.back: Bill → (government bills: Bundesrat comments) → 1st reading → committee → 2nd and 3rd reading, vote → Bundesrat → countersignature → Federal President signs → Bundesgesetzblatt → in force.
Some laws need the Bundesrat's consent (Zustimmung). For the others it can only object (Einspruch), and the Bundestag can overrule it.
to come into force: on the day set in the law, or 14 days after it appears in the Bundesgesetzblatt.
Mistakes were made: a passive that names no one. When responsibility matters, ask: Von wem?
laut Polizei / laut einem Bericht; nach Angaben der Stadt (+ genitive); einer Studie zufolge (dative, zufolge after the noun). All: according to.
As the police announced, … The wie-clause is position 1, so the verb comes next: …, wurde niemand verletzt.
He is said to be rich. sollen = others say so (hearsay).
She claims to have seen nothing. wollen = a claim about oneself.
Participle + haben or sein (as in the Perfekt): Er soll das Geld genommen haben. Sie soll nach Spanien gefahren sein.

cards.front: Der Sprecher sagte, die Lage sei ruhig.
cards.back: sei (Konjunktiv I) marks reported speech: the paper passes the words on without confirming them.
From most to least certain: in fact; evidently; apparently; presumably; allegedly.
scheinbar = only seemingly (but not really); anscheinend = apparently (and probably true). Many people mix them up in speech.
Who says it (source, Impressum)? Do other, independent sources report it? Do the date and photo belong to this story?
